## **Executive Summary** 

## **Follicular lymphoma** 

- Follicular lymphoma (FL) arises from mature B-cells, and is the most common subtype of indolent lymphoma, accounting for 70% of low-grade non-Hodgkin lymphomas.[1] 

- • About 2,330 people are diagnosed with FL every year in the UK. FL can develop at any age, but is most common in people over 60 years of age.[1] 

- • There are few effective treatment options for individuals with FL, and relapses are common. Treatment options are usually exhausted within two or three lines of therapy,[2] with just over a third of patients progressing to 4L+ treatment from 3L+.[3] At this stage, current strategies often involve recycling ineffective treatments, leading to poor outcomes.[4] 

- • 4L+ FL is an end-of-life disease. Most patients do not survive longer than a year (median ***********) and generally experience rapid disease progression within several months (median **********).[5] 

- • Despite this, there are currently no NICE-recommended treatments specifically at 3L+ FL or beyond and there have been no NICErecommended treatments in FL since 2020.

## **1.3 Health condition and position of the technology in the treatment pathway** 

## **Relapsed and refractory follicular lymphoma:** 

- Follicular lymphoma (FL) arises from mature B-cells in germinal centres and is the most common subtype of indolent lymphoma, accounting for 35% of nonHodgkin lymphomas (NHLs) and 70% of indolent NHLs (iNHL). Approximately, 2,330 new FL patients are diagnosed each year in the UK.[5] 

- • FL patients are at high risk of relapse (lymphoma returning after successful treatment)[11] or refractory disease (lymphoma that doesn’t respond to treatment), with FL becoming increasingly refractory to treatment and more likely to relapse sooner after each line of therapy.[12] Consequently, overall and progression free survival (OS and PFS) decrease significantly after first relapse and with each subsequent relapse.[3,13] 

- • In a UK real world analysis, patients with R/R FL receiving 4L+ therapy had low response rates to current treatment options, with only ***% of patients achieving a complete response.[5] In this context, median OS was **** months and median PFS was just *** months.[5] 

- • Patients with R/R FL have a poor quality of life, experiencing a range of debilitating symptoms including weight loss, fatigue and difficulties walking or swallowing due to swollen lymph nodes.[14] With FL being considered an incurable, chronic disease, patients experience anxiety and depression associated with the uncertainty about relapse.[15] 

## **Current treatment pathways** 

- Multiple-relapsed FL is a life-limiting disease, with treatment aiming to control symptoms and achieve remission. There are no standardised treatment pathways for patients with follicular lymphoma, with limited treatment options available at 4L+. 

- • In many cases, once a patient reaches 4L+ treatment, the only treatment option available is the recycling of previously unsuccessful therapies. Approximately, two thirds of patients who receive third-line treatment will progress to 4L treatment where there is no alternative than to rechallenge with toxic and poorly efficacious chemotherapy containing regimens.[3] Retreatment with multiple rounds of chemoimmunotherapy has a detrimental impact on patient HRQoL that is not wholly captured in QALY outcomes (both physical and psychological).[16] 

- • The lack of new treatment options that allow for deep responses to be achieved has been raised as a concern by patient advocacy groups in multiple previous NICE appraisals.[16-19] 

- • Current treatment options are predominantly administered via IV infusion, resulting in hospital stays and patient monitoring periods, putting pressure on patients, carers and the healthcare system alike. Patients in 4L+ FL currently

spend an average of ******* each year (on an annualised basis) in inpatient settings with overnight stays.[5] 

## **Epcoritamab** 

• Epcoritamab is a novel, humanised IgG1-bispecific antibody that binds the B- cell antigen CD20 and T-cell antigen CD3. • Although the marketing authorisation for epcoritamab is expected to include *************************************************************************, AbbVie are seeking reimbursement in patients who have received three or more lines of prior therapy as these patients have the highest unmet need, i.e. poorest survival outcomes and most limited access to effective treatments. • If recommended, epcoritamab will be the only subcutaneously administered bispecific monoclonal antibody offering quicker and more convenient administration compared with IV chemotherapy, therefore, alleviating pressure on healthcare systems. • Epcoritamab is a chemotherapy-free regimen that maintains patient QoL without the chemo-specific toxicities such as cardiac risk, severe neutropenia and alopecia.[20] In summary, epcoritamab is a novel and alternative treatment for patients with R/R patients at 4L+, offering a tolerable, conveniently administered, effective treatment and durable disease control.

## **1.3.1 Disease Background** 

B-cell development is a vital part of the immune system and results in the production of highly specific antibodies.[21] The development of B-cells is a complex process, regulated by a series of checkpoints.[22] It begins with immature B-cells in the bone marrow and progresses to mature B-cells at secondary maturation sites (the spleen and germinal centres).[23] The expression of CD20, a cell surface protein, is a key marker of mature B- cells.[24] Aberrant B-cell development can give rise to a range of different cancers.[25] Cancers arising from immature cells in the bone marrow are known as leukaemias, whilst those arising from mature B-cells are known as lymphomas. CD20 is expressed on the surface of FL cancer cells, which can be therapeutically targeted by bispecific antibodies such as epcoritamab.[26] 

## **1.3.2 Follicular Lymphoma** 

Lymphomas are broadly categorised into two subgroups, Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). The NHL category covers a wide range of lymphomas, including but not limited to mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), follicular lymphoma (FL) and DLBCL. FL arises from mature B-cells in germinal centres. FL is the most common form of iNHL and is often considered an indolent (slow growing) cancer, with the exception of grade 3B that follows a more aggressive clinical course. Patients are at a high risk of relapse (cancer returning after treatment) or refractory disease (a lymphoma that stops responding to treatment).[3] By the 4L+ stage, R/R FL is no longer considered an indolent disease and is more akin to an end of life disease, with limited treatment options. 

## **1.3.3 Burden of FL** 

Individuals with FL present with B symptoms (a series of symptoms associated with NHLs), including drenching sweats, often at night, intermittent fevers, and unexplainable weight loss. Other symptoms include swelling of lymph nodes, which may be visible in the neck, armpit or groin and fatigue. Currently, there is no cure for FL and it is considered a chronic, life-limiting disease, with treatments aiming to get patients into remission, where their symptom burden is greatly reduced.[27  ] Most patients presenting with advanced stage disease experience recurrent relapses requiring multiple lines of

<!-- page 26 -->

therapy to achieve remission. By their 4L+ of therapy, patients’ life expectancy is typically less than one year.[5] 

Studies investigating health-related quality of life (HRQoL) show significantly reduced HRQoL among patients with FL compared with the general UK population.[28] Studies have also shown that following a FL diagnosis, many individuals are unable to continue work, with this becoming increasingly true in those receiving systemic therapy.[29] Additionally, patients diagnosed with iNHL have lower emotional well-being than those without.[30,31] 

AbbVie recently carried out a study to understand the patient experience of living with FL, which involved asking 15 clinicians and 13 patients or carers from the UK, Germany and Japan about their experiences during 60 minutes interviews.[32] Patients with later stage FL, who were on their second or later lines of treatment, reported feeling disappointed, exhausted and dismayed that they needed to restart treatment. Further, patients with follicular lymphoma reported experiencing shock at their diagnosis and that they lived with high levels of anxiety over the fear of the disease returning.[32] 

Disease relapse has a further significant impact on a patient’s HRQoL with individuals being more likely to report higher levels of depression or anxiety than those in remission.[28] For those with incurable lymphomas, the fear of progression or relapse is also commonly reported and greatly contributes to the debilitating symptomology of the condition, especially in those who reach later lines of treatment where new therapeutic options are limited.[15] Median progression free survival is only ********** at 4L+ with the currently available treatments.[5] This is compounded by the fact that in FL, survival outcomes decrease with each line of therapy due to increasing chemo-refractoriness, an issue particularly pertinent to those who require 4L+ treatment, the target population of this appraisal.[33,34] 

While there is limited available information pertaining to the impact of a FL diagnosis on caregivers, a report looking at lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) in general found that 75% of caregivers, family or friends reported that treatment wait 

times had a moderate to severe effect on their wellbeing.[15] Almost half of the carers Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments

Most of the currently available treatment options are administered via infusions into a vein, a process that occurs over the course of several hours, requiring frequent patient monitoring visits over many months, generating a substantial temporal burden on both the patient, their carers and the health system at large. There is, therefore, a need for effective drugs that convey deep and meaningful responses that can be administered by a more convenient mode of administration. 

There is limited reporting on the economic burden of FL in the UK. A 2018 report, based on patients with FL diagnosed between 2004 and 2011 and followed until 2015, reported an average lifetime cost to the healthcare system of £6,165 to £63,894 per patient.[35] Prevalence-based analysis estimated the annual treatment cost for FL at £6065 million, approximately 10% of the NHS’s annual budget for haematological cancers.[35] The scale of this economic burden in part will be because patients at later lines have no therapeutic options resulting in poor outcomes and high levels of healthcare resource utilisation. Indeed, of the patients reaching 4L+ treatment in the Haematological Malignancy Research Network (HMRN) data set, ***% of patients required inpatient admission with overnight stays.[5] On average, patients required overnight stays for *** days over each 28-day cycle.[5] 

## **1.3.4 Epidemiology** 

FL accounts for approximately 6.2% of all haematological malignancies and for approximately 35% of all NHL and 70% of indolent lymphomas diagnosed in the United States and Western Europe, making it the second most commonly diagnosed lymphoma.[36,37] Approximately 2,330 people per year in the UK are diagnosed with FL with the average age of diagnosis being 67 years.[36] The HMRN is a collaborative network of NHS clinicians and researchers situated across 14 hospitals across the UK, established to provide UK generalisable data for haematological cancers and their precursor conditions diagnosed using the WHO classification at a single 

hematopathology lab. Between 2010 – 2019, the HMRN reported the annual incidence

## **1.3.5 FL grading and staging** 

## **1.3.5.1 Grading FL** 

In 2022, the World Health Organisation classified FL into four grades depending on the number of centroblasts identified via high power field (hpf) microscopy, with these grades being associated with clinical outcomes. Grade 1 FL has 0 to 5 centroblasts/hpf, Grade 2 FL has 6 to 14, Grade 3 can be further classified into Grade 3a, in which centrocytes are present and Grade 3b in which centroblasts present in sheets.[37] 

## **1.3.5.2 Staging FL** 

The anatomical extent (disease stage) of FL is determined by the Lugano classification system using fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) – positron emission tomography (PET) scans, and an adaptation of the Ann Harbor staging system (Table 4).

## **1.3.5.3 Prognosis** 

The FL international prognostic index (FLIPI) was developed based on the clinical characteristics of 4,167 patients diagnosed with FL and validated on a further 919 patients.[38] The FLIPI classifies patients into one of three categories; low risk, intermediate risk and high risk, based on five adverse prognostic factors; age > 60, Ann Arbor stage lll/lV, haemoglobin (Hb) level <120 g/L, number of nodal sites >4 and elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels. In 2009, the FLIPI-2 score was developed; this retained age and Hb level and added bone marrow involvement, elevated levels of beta-2-microglobulin and nodal masses >6cm for prognostic risk classification.[39,40] FLIPI and FLIPI-2 are frequently used to inform the clinical prognosis of FL, but not to guide therapy. 

FL patients are at high risk of relapse (lymphoma returning after successful treatment)[11] or refractory disease (lymphoma that doesn’t respond to treatment), with FL becoming increasingly refractory to treatment and more likely to relapse sooner after each line of therapy.[12] Consequently, overall and progression free survival (OS and PFS) decrease significantly after first relapse and with each subsequent relapse.[3,13] Recent HMRN data indicates that the prognosis for patients at 4L+ is poor, with OS reported at **** months and PFS at *** months.

## **1.3.6 Treatment Pathways** 

There is no standardised treatment pathway for FL, especially as patients move to later lines of treatment. Instead, treatment is tailored to the patient and depends on their previous treatment and responses. About 20% of patients experience disease progression within 2-years of starting immune-chemotherapy.[12] At 4L+, treatment options are limited, with patients frequently receiving further rituximab-based treatments (Figure 1). 

## **1.3.6.1 Treatment of early-stage FL (Stages I and II)** 

Conventionally, early-stage FL comprising stage I-II disease (where the involved nodes are contiguous and can be easily encompassed within a radiation field) has been treated with local radiotherapy. Observation without involved site radiotherapy (ISRT) can be considered for people with limited stage FL who have undergone localised excision and where there may be concerns about radiotherapy of a particular site. Patients with early-stage disease that is discontinuous or are otherwise unsuitable for radiotherapy should be managed as advanced stage disease.[42] 

## **1.3.6.2 Treatment of advanced-stage FL (Stages III and IV)** 

## **1.3.6.2.1 First-line treatment** 

The British Society of Haematology (BSH) guidelines recommends that patients with symptomatic high tumour burden FL are treated with an anti-CD20 antibody (rituximab or obinutuzumab) in combination with chemotherapy (-cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone [-CHOP], or – cyclophosphamide, vincristine and prednisolone [-CVP], or bendamustine) depending on patient characteristics and the evaluation of the treating clinician. R- and O- CHOP chemotherapies are burdensome for both the patient involved and the healthcare system, requiring canulation and IV administration. Rituximab (or obinutuzumab, whichever had been used for induction) maintenance can also be considered for patients who have responded to induction therapy and can prolong PFS.

## **1.3.6.2.2 2L and 3L line treatment** 

There is no defined treatment pathway for individuals with advanced R/R FL at 2L and beyond, instead treatment strategies are informed by the previous treatments a patient has received, along with age, fitness and available options. In cases where patients have experienced a relatively long remission period, the 2020 BSH guidelines recommend a repeat rituximab therapy with the same chemotherapy as previously administered at earlier lines of treatment.[42] In cases where a shorter remission is experienced, rituximab with an alternative chemotherapy is recommend. In cases where patients are rituximab-refractory, the BSH guidelines state bendamustine in combination with obinutuzumab (OB) can be considered, followed by obinutuzumab (O) maintenance.[42] OB is seldom used in UK clinical practice.[2] 

Some patients may be eligible for a stem cell transplant as part of their 2L and 3L treatment. High dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplant (HDT-ASCT), can be considered for the relatively small proportion of fitter patients, where best outcomes have been observed in 2L.[42] 

The 2021 European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) guidelines also recommend a rituximab-based approach to managing R/R FL, with consideration for rituximab maintenance therapy if it had not been previously used. Lenalidomide and rituximab (R[2] ) combination therapy is also an option for patients, especially if they had a short remission to immune-chemotherapy or a short relapse after chemotherapy and may therefore be regarded as chemo-refractory.[43] The ESMO guidelines recommend OB and HDT-ASCT as options for patients at first relapse after a rituximab-containing immune-chemotherapy.[43] 

## **1.3.6.2.3 4L treatment and beyond** 

At 4L+, there is no standard of care for the treatment of FL, with very limited treatment options available for patients. In routine care, a treatment strategy based upon their prior treatments or best supportive care is usually offered. Patients rechallenged with a prior treatment regimen often experience poor outcomes due to acquired treatment

Given the current lack of treatment options at 4L+, clinical trials are also considered for younger and fitter patients at this stage, in many cases requiring referral to tertiary centres adding inconvenience for patients and carers or resulting in inequality of access for those who are unable to travel. 

Despite the significant unmet need in this heavily pre-treated population, there have been limited innovations in recent years that have met the standard required by NICE for approval, with no positive recommendations made since 2020. ## **1.3.7 Unmet need in R/R FL** 

Patients with FL will often receive several treatment courses over several years, with shortening durations of response being observed after each line of therapy; at 1L, 62% of patients still respond to treatment after 5-years, decreasing to 39% and 24%, respectively, for those on 2L and 3L treatments.[4] 

Patient prognosis is particularly poor once a patient reaches 4L+ treatment, by which time there are very limited treatment options available. FL at this stage is often resistant to conventional treatment and can be considered an end-of-life disease, with an estimated median OS for patients at 4L+ of less than a year (**** months) and median PFS of *** months.[5] Patients are often rechallenged with previously administered treatments. Response to these recycled treatments is often poor, with only approximately ***% of patients achieving a complete response (CR).[5] Among responders, duration of response is typically very short. 

Existing chemotherapy-based treatment options do not fully address the immune dysfunction associated with FL and are associated with well-documented toxicities. For example, repeating R-CHOP treatment is not feasible as it is associated with an increased dose-dependent risk of cardiotoxicity .[20] 

There is also a considerable humanistic burden associated with the current FL treatment pathways. Fear of cancer recurrence or progression is considered the most common unmet need by patients with cancer.[52] Among cancer survivors and patients with active cancer, 59% and 19% report a moderate or severe fear of cancer reoccurrence (FCR), respectively.[53] An estimated 46% of patients with lymphoma or CLL fear disease progression or relapse, with higher rates of anxiety being reported in patients experiencing relapse than those who are in remission or disease free, issues which are particularly pertinent in 4L+ R/R FL where median PFS is reported at only *** months in patients with 4L+ R/R FL.[5,54] 

Current chemotherapy treatments are administered via infusion into a vein, which is given slowly over a few hours for the first treatment to prevent side effects.[55] Patients 

treated with R-CHOP should have a blood test either the day of or the day before Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 37 -->

treatment and so may require two trips to a healthcare setting. Therefore, current treatments are time intensive, preventing both patients and carers from conducting their normal daily activities. A recent report by the Lymphoma Coalition found that 23% of individuals (carers, friends or family members of patients with FL) had to stop work, either permanently or temporarily, with a further 22% reporting that they had to reduce their work.[15] 

There is therefore, a significant unmet need for novel interventions that deliver deep and durable response in this high-risk, heavily pre-treated population who have such poor outcomes.[5] An alternative mechanism of action to conventional chemotherapy-based treatments would offer patients and clinicians choice as well as hope for a new treatment beyond recycling therapies to which a patient has already failed to maintain a durable response. Likewise, patients with FL require a treatment that can be delivered via a more convenient mode of administration and has a tolerable safety profile, which will offer patients with a much needed alternative to current treatments options. 

## **1.3.8 Epcoritamab** 

Epcoritamab is a humanised IgG1-bispecific antibody that binds to the CD20 B-cell antigen and the CD3 T-cell antigen, inducing specific T-cell activation and T-cell mediated killing of CD20 expressing cancer cells (Figure 2). As such epcoritamab requires the binding of both B and T-cells to initiate cell death, circumventing the cytotoxicity that can be associated with conventional CD20-targeting therapies. Of note, epcoritamab binds an alternate CD20 epitope to that targeted by rituximab and obinutuzumab. Epcoritamab has proven benefits in treating other haematological malignancies and was recently recommended for the treatment of DLBCL in adults who have received two or more systemic treatments (and where they have either previously received or are unable to receive polatuzumab vedotin) by NICE (TA954, recommended March 2024).[8]

## **1.3.9 Proposed position for Epcoritamab** 

Epcoritamab is proposed for use as a 4L+ treatment for R/R FL. As described throughout Section 1, this is the patient population with the greatest unmet need; therefore, access to an innovative therapy and less invasive therapeutic options will address a key unmet need in patients facing a short life expectancy. 

Currently, there are no treatments approved specifically for the treatment of 4L+ patients. As outlined in Section 2, epcoritamab has the potential to meet this unmet need, providing deep and clinically meaningful responses, delivering improved OS and PFS. 

Epcoritamab offers an alternative to current CD20-based therapies, conveying its benefits through an alternate mode of action to offer increased therapeutic options. In the EPCORE NHL-1 study, epcoritamab demonstrated a manageable safety profile that clinicians will already be familiar with in their experience of treating DLBCL with epcoritamab under NICE approval. Through its subcutaneous administration, epcoritamab reduces the burden on both the healthcare system and patients. These injections are notably faster, less invasive and require less monitoring than traditional intravenous treatments used for 4L+ FL therapies.

## **1.4 Equality considerations** 

It is not anticipated that the provision (or non-provision) of epcoritamab within its licensed indication would exclude from consideration any people protected by equality legislation, lead to a recommendation that has a different impact on people protected by equality legislation or lead to recommendations that will have adverse impact on people with a particular disability or disabilities. 

However, as discussed previously, patients reaching 4L+ are more likely to receive experimental treatments within clinical trials than patients in earlier lines. As access to clinical trials might be more restricted in rural or deprived areas, patients with 4L+ R/R FL are likely to benefit from access to an efficacious therapy as part of routine commissioning.

## **2.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of treatments for adult patients with 3L+ and 4L+ relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (R/R FL). Appendix B reports the full details of the process and methods used to identify and select the clinical evidence relevant to the technology being evaluated. 

Searches were originally run on 3 April 2023, and updated on 13 March 2024 and 7 November, 2024. Relevant studies were identified by searching the following databases: Medical literature analysis and retrieval system online (MEDLINE), Excerpta Medica database (Embase), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR). Proceedings from the following conferences were also searched from 2020-2024: European Hematology Association (EHA), International Conference of Malignant Lymphoma (ICML) Annual meeting, American Society of Hematology (ASH), American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) and the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) annual meeting. Conferences that are not indexed in Embase were hand searched. On-going trials were searched for entries up to 3 April 2023 in the clinicaltrials.gov, the EU clinical trials register, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), the health Canada clinical trials database and European union electronic register of post authorisation studies. 

After de-duplication, 5,515 publications were included for title and abstract screening, 740 of which were included for full-text screening; 345 met inclusion criteria. Of these, 238 publications did not report 3L+ data, resulting in 107 publications, reporting on 54 studies identified in the SLR. Of these 107 publications, 80 reported on 38 studies presenting 3L+ data only, the remaining 27 publications reported on 17 studies reporting on both 3L+ and 4L+ (Figure 3).

## **2.3 EPCORE NHL-1** 

EPCORE NHL-1 was a phase 1/2 open-label, multi-centre, multi-national trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of epcoritamab in various forms of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (BNHL), including FL and DLBCL. The trial was conducted in three parts: a dose escalation part, an expansion part and an optimisation part. Table 9 above provides an overview for trial orientation. 

The key evidence for this submission comes from the dose expansion phase of the trial, designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of epcoritamab in patients with relapsed, progressive or refractory FL, who have had at least two lines of prior therapy. 

## **2.4 EPCORE NHL-1 Dose Expansion Cohort** 

## **2.4.1 Summary of Methodology** 

A summary of the dose expansion part of EPCORE NHL-1 is presented in Figure 5. 

The expansion part of the trial was initiated with parallel enrolment in three cohorts with distinct B-cell lymphoma subtypes: 

- R/R aNHL cohort (LBCL) 

## • **R/R iNHL cohort (including FL Grade 1-3A)** 

- R/R MCL cohort 

These cohorts were treated with the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of epcoritamab. The iNHL cohort is the focus of this submission as this contains the population consistent with the decision problem and the licensed indication for epcoritamab relevant to this submission 

The iNHL cohort was conducted in two stages, illustrated in Figure 5. Only patients with R/R 3L+ FL Grade 1-3A were enrolled into the iNHL cohort in Stage 1. Following an interim futility analysis, additional patients with iNHL were enrolled in Stage 2, including individuals with other iNHL subtypes (small lymphocytic lymphoma [SLL] and marginal

In total, there were 155 patients in the iNHL cohort, of which 128 patients were 3L+ FL 1-3A patients (detailed in Appendix M) and 81 were 4L+ FL patients (Figure 4 & Figure 5). The 4L+ population was a pre-specified subgroup of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, and the safety and efficacy data for these participants are presented as part of this submission. ## **2.5.1 Patient Characteristics** 

The baseline characteristics for the 4L+ FL cohort are presented in Table 11. In total, 65.4% (n = 53) of patients in the 4L+ FL cohort were male and 63.0% (n = 51) were white. Race was not reported in 33.3% (n = 27) patients. Mild to moderate renal impairment was reported in over half of the patients (66.7%, 54 patients). Normal hepatic function was reported in the majority of patients (80.2%, 65 patients). 

## **2.5.2 Baseline disease characteristics** 

Over half of patients in the 4L+ FL subgroup had Grade 2 FL (45 patients, 55.6%). A further 27 patients (33.3%) had Grade 3A FL and 9 patients (11.1%) had Grade 1 FL (Table 11). The majority of this subgroup had a FLIPI score of ≥3 (57 patients, 70.4%), with 13 patients (16.0%) and 11 patients (13.6%) having FLIPI scores of 2 and 0-1, respectively. Over half of the 4L+ patients were double refractory to anti-CD20 and alkylating agents at any treatment line (60 patients, 74.1%).

## **2.5.2.1 Clinical opinion on patient characteristics** 

During interviews conducted by AbbVie in 2024, UK clinical experts provided feedback on the generalisability of the full FL1-3A 3L+ EPCORE NHL-1 trial population. Generally, UK clinicians stated that the baseline characteristics of patients in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial aligned with those of patients in UK clinical practice. Some noted that the overall fitness (e.g. comorbidity profile) of patients is reduced compared with standard trial populations, presenting with high risk features that are typical in real world populations.[5] As discussed in Section 2.15, it is therefore, anticipated that the results observed will closely parallel the responses expected in clinical practice. 

## **2.5.2.2 Prior medication and procedures** 

The patient population enrolled in the iNHL cohort represents a heavily pre-treated, chemo-refractory and high-risk FL population. All 81 patients in the 4L+ subgroup had received prior chemotherapy with combined anti-CD20 and alkylating agents. ## **2.6.1 Trial populations** 

A total of 155 patients, 128 with FL and 27 with other iNHL subtypes were included in the iNHL cohort and treated with epcoritamab. Of the 128 FL patients with two or more prior lines of therapy (3L+), 81 patients were at 4L+. 

The definitions used for the analysis sets are summarised in Table 13. All efficacy analysis were performed on the full analysis set (FAS) (n = 155), the population of patients who received at least one dose of epcoritamab. The data presented within the main Company Submission are for the 4L+ FL (n = 81) population.

## **Time to response (TTR):** 

TTR defined as time from Day 1 of Cycle 1 to the first documentation of objective tumour response (PR or better). TR assessed by Lugano was summarised by descriptive statistics. 

## **Duration of response (DOR):** 

DOR was defined as the time from the first documentation of response (CR or PR) to the date of first report of PD or death, whichever occurs first. This response was assessed by both Lugano and LYRIC criteria. DOR by IRC per Lugano criteria was summarised with descriptive statistics, as well as median, first and third quantile along with twosided 95% CI. DOR by IRC per Lugano criteria, estimated using the KM product-limit method was displayed graphically in FAs. A primary definition of DOR accounted for subsequent anti-lymphoma therapy and censors DOR at the last adequate tumour assessment on or prior to the date of subsequent lymphoma therapy. The secondary definition of DOR did not account for subsequent anti-lymphoma therapy. 

## **Complete response rate, time to complete response and duration of complete response rate** : 

Complete response rate was defined as the proportion of patients with BOR of CR. Duration of complete response was defined as the time from the first documentation of CR to the data of PD or death whichever comes earlier. DOCR was derived for patients reaching CR. DOR by IRC per Lugano criteria was summarised by the number of events, minimum, maximum, median, first and third quantile, and two-sided 95% CI computed based on log-log transformation. 

## **Time to CR (TTCR)** 

TTCR is defined as the time from Day 1 of Cycle 1 to the first documentation of objective tumour response of CR. TTCR was derived for patients who achieve the best response of CR and summarised with descriptive statistics. 

## **Progression-free survival** 

Progression free survival (PFS) was defined as the time from Day 1 of Cycle 1 to the date of PD or death, due to any cause, whichever occurs earlier. Date of PD was defined as the earliest date of documentation progression after which there was no more PR or CR assessment. PFS was determined as for DOR described above. 

Two definitions of PFS were used in the analysis. The primary definition of PFS accounts for a subsequent antilymphoma therapy and patients who are alive without documented disease progression will be censored at the last adequate tumour assessment date or prior to the date of subsequent anti-lymphoma therapy. The subsequent antilymphoma therapies for PFS censoring in general consists of systemic anti-lymphoma therapy and radiation of any target lesion. 

## **Overall Survival** 

Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from Day 1 of Cycle 1 to death from any cause. If a patient is not known to have died, then OS was censored at the last date the patient was known to be alive. Survival status was assessed at least every 3 months after the last administration of epcoritamab and continued until the patient died or withdrew from the study.

## **2.6.2.1 Impact of Omicron wave of the COVID-19 pandemic on the dose expansion part of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial** 

As the EPCORE NHL-1 trial took place throughout the Omicron wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, patients in the trial were susceptible to infection with the Omicron variant – a highly infectious variant of COVID-19 with immune escape properties allowing it to reinfect previously infected or vaccinated patients.[60] As a result, excess mortality was observed in the trial that can be attributed to COVID-19, an external factor to the monitoring of deaths attributed to FL’s natural history and epcoritamab efficacy. As an international trial, EPCORE NHL-1 was exposed to variation in COVID-19 prevalence and the management strategies adopted by different countries. As a result, a higher number of deaths due to COVID-19 were observed in different countries during EPCORE NHL-1, based on the effectiveness of these local management protocols and prevalence, which were beyond the control of the trial investigators. 

It is important to view the survival data from the pivotal study in the context that the UK is no longer experiencing high numbers of COVID-19 infections, and the composite impact of immunity and vaccination status, particularly for immunocompromised patients, means the risk of death from COVID-19 remains low and, in the future, will continue to decline. Given that excess COVID-19 mortality may have been more pronounced during earlier, higher-risk waves with lower vaccine uptake, it is crucial to adjust for this excess mortality to characterise the true therapeutic benefit of epcoritamab in the current UK setting. This excess mortality predominantly related to the Omicron wave was clinically adjudicated in a thorough review of each mortality event in the trial, to identify cases where COVID-19 was the cause of death with certainty. 

Based on the clinical adjudication and review of the trial data and site investigator reports, a total of ** patient deaths were attributable to COVID-19 within the 4L+ population, of which * occurred during the Omicron wave of the pandemic. Of the ** deaths attributed to COVID-19, * had occurred in patients in a CR at the time of their death. Such patients with a CR would typically have significantly extended OS 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 62 -->

compared with patients who achieve a partial response or no response (Figure 30; Section 3.3.2.5.1.1). 

The inclusion of these deaths within the survival analysis produces inappropriately pessimistic estimates of long-term outcomes for patients treated with epcoritamab, given the deaths would likely not have occurred had the trial not taken place during the Omicron phase of the pandemic. As such, and aligned with the conclusions described in the publication by Linton et al 2024,[61] COVID-19 deaths are censored in the survival outcomes (OS, PFS and TTD) presented in Section 2.8 and the MAIC analysis performed in Section 2.12 to best reflect the current real-world situation.

## **2.10  Subgroup analysis** 

There is no subgroup analysis available for the 4L+ FL cohort. The EPCORE NHL-1 trial was not statistically powered to detect significant differences between sub-groups within the 4L+ FL population. 

## **2.11  Meta-Analysis** 

An indirect treatment comparison (ITC) was conducted to compare epcoritamab with treatments currently available in 4L+ care in England as presented in Section 2.12. 

## **2.12  Indirect and mixed treatment comparisons** 

EPCORE NHL-1 was a single arm trial, and no head-to-head trials comparing epcoritamab to relevant comparators were identified during the clinical SLR (Section 2.1 and Appendix B). Therefore, an ITC, in the form of an unanchored matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC), was conducted to inform the relative efficacy estimates for epcoritamab, utilising the COVID-modified data collected from the Dose Expansion cohort of EPCORE NHL-1, versus current 4L+ care in England for this appraisal. 

## **2.12.1.1 Methodology: Data Source** 

The unanchored MAIC was conducted in line with the approach outlined in Signorovitch et al. (2012),[57] and considering the methods described in NICE DSU TSD 18.[58] A SLR was conducted to identify, extract and analyse the relevant clinical evidence for 4L+ therapies in R/R FL, in line with the target population for epcoritamab, in order to 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 79 -->

characterise the current efficacy and safety profiles of current 4L+ care received by this patient group (Appendix B). The studies identified by the SLR are presented in Table 24, alongside a report from the Haematological Malignancy Research Network (HMRN).[5] 

Of the studies identified during the SLR, none were appropriate to estimate relative effects for patients treated with 4L+ care in England due to the inclusion of therapies that are not used in routine NHS clinical practice; therefore, using such data in comparative effectiveness assessments for alternative 4L+ treatments is likely to yield unrepresentative results. In particular, the patient population studied in the SCHOLAR5[64] trial was considered not generalisable to the UK, with approximately 50% of patients at 4L+ having been administered experimental treatments that are not available on the NHS (such as CAR-Ts and bispecific antibodies). Further, SCHOLAR-5 considered transplant as a line of therapy (LOT), which applied to 20-25% of patients. This is incongruous with how LOT is defined in UK clinical practice and in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, where transplant is not considered as a LOT. When evaluating the LEO cohort[65] , patients were exclusively from the United States and only 6% were at 4L+. PFS was not reported as part of the ReCORD-FL[66] trial, and similarly the majority of patients were at an earlier LOT than the Decision Problem for this appraisal. 

The Company are aware that the SCHOLAR-5 data were presented as a relevant source of data for current 4L+ care within TA894 (axicabtagene ciloleucel for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma); however, the EAG raised issues with its generalisability to UK clinical practice. Additionally, in TA894, Kite-Gilead had access to patient-level data from the SCHOLAR-5 study and were, to some degree, able to mitigate these concerns through removal of the DELTA cohort (trial patients with prior idelalisib [a treatment not reimbursed in England]) of SCHOLAR-5. This option was not available to AbbVie during this submission. 

None of the studies identified during the SLR were appropriate for using in an ITC, either as a result of the inclusion of a non-UK generalisable patient population or the inclusion of treatment options which are not available in the UK (i.e. CAR-T, bispecific

## **2.12.1.3 Methodology: MAIC** 

An unanchored MAIC was conducted following the recommendation of NICE guidance on population-adjusted indirect comparisons based on propensity score reweighting methods using individual patient data from EPCORE NHL-1 and aggregate data from the HMRN. Both MAICs and simulated treatment comparison (STC) aim to adjust for differences in population characteristics between data sources when head-to-head trials do not exist, but they utilise slightly different methodologies. In this case, the MAIC approach was preferred over STC for several key reasons, described below. 

STC based parametric or semiparametric regression analyses rely on the number of events (not the number of patients) to determine the degrees of freedom; the lower the number of events, the lower the number of predictors that can be included in the model. As such, this method would not have been appropriate in this submission due to the small number of events recorded in the EPCORE NHL-1 study, which in turn would reduce the number of predictors that could be included in the model. 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 84 -->

MAICs are the preferred method of analysis when analysing time-to-event data for a single target comparator (or single RWE database) across multiple treatment outcomes, whereas STCs are more appropriate for analyses against multiple comparators. Further, conducting an STC on time-to-event outcomes requires a parametric distribution of the best fit and to assess whether the same distribution is applicable to both arms of the analysis. When considering prior NICE TAs, MAICs have been more frequently utilised and accepted in prior NICE appraisals of FL treatments, further supporting the methodological precedent for this analysis. 

A key step in conducting a MAIC is the careful selection of patient characteristics for matching, ensuring that the analysis appropriately accounts for differences between trials to reduce the risk of bias. To achieve this, it is necessary to both establish which patient characteristics are known effect modifiers or prognostic variables (or can be plausibly considered as potential effect modifiers or prognostic variables) and determine whether these variables are imbalanced between the datasets being considered. The selection of characteristics for matching was made considering the availability of these characteristics in the comparator dataset, their inclusion in similar analyses presented in prior NICE TAs, and clinical opinion and empirical tests of whether these variables are predictive of survival or impact the efficacy in epcoritamab trial data. 

MAICs have routinely been presented to and accepted by NICE as valid methodology across various appraisals of lymphoma therapies. The MAIC in this submission was conducted utilising learnings from previous NICE TAs: TA627, TA892 and TA894 and an overview of the approach taken in these appraisals is provided in Appendix K. In summary, following a review of TA627, TA892 and TA894, the unanchored MAIC presented within this submission considers the need to balance: 

- i) reporting limitations of relevant prognostic variables or treatment effect modifiers in the published literature or data set, 

ii)  the risk of overmatching and the impact on effective sample size, 

iii)  the need to include as many potentially relevant adjustment factors as is feasible.

## **2.12.2 Statistical methods** 

Epcoritamab individual-patient data from the 4L+ cohort (n=81) were used together with summary data from HMRN (n=**). Where only summary statistics are available, the Guyot methodology has been recommended by the NICE DSU (TSD 14)[72] in order to re-create patient level data. Therefore, data from the HMRN 4L+ cohort were synthesised to generate event and censoring times for OS and PFS outcomes. These were extracted from the Kaplan-Meier graphs from the HMRN data via a two-step process: 

1. The numerical value of the survival curves at dozens of time points were obtained through a graphical digitisation software, WebPlotDigitizer. 

2. These values were used to create a “simulated” study population using the algorithm published by Guyot et al.[73] This simulated study population is a collection of event and censored times equal to the number of patients in the study population and creating a KM curve whose values are closest to that of the digitised data. These simulated patient-level data sets were then used in the ITC analyses. 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 86 -->

The EPCORE NHL-1 data were reweighted according to patient characteristics identified as the most relevant treatment effect modifiers and prognostic variables by empirical analyses, clinical experts and consistent with prior NICE recommendations.[58] In unadjusted analyses, where the EPCORE NHL-1 data are compared with other treatments irrespective of their baseline characteristics, each patient is given a weight of 1 and the data are unchanged. In adjusted analyses, the EPCORE NHL-1 trial data were reweighted to match the baseline characteristics of those reported in the HMRN dataset, using the method of moments as described by Signorovitch et al.[57 ] 

Whenever indicated to improve the accuracy and precision of final parameter estimates, adjustment weights were incrementally truncated at the following thresholds of their distribution to reduce the occurrence of extreme weights (i.e., generally higher than 5-6 or lower than 0.1),[74] while still preserving the resulting balance in adjusted baseline characteristics, as previously recommended. 

## **2.12.2.1 Endpoints of Interest** 

Comparative efficacy data for epcoritamab relative to current 4L+ care were derived for: 

- PFS (Progression Free Survival) and OS (Overall Survival) Hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) 

- Kaplan-Meier time-to-event survival curves 

- ORR (Overall Response Rate) and CR (Complete Response) Odds ratios (OR) and 95% CI 

The EPCORE NHL-1 data and the reconstructed patient-level outcomes data for current 4L+ care were analysed using a weighted Cox model with robust standard errors, using the “survival” package in the statistical software R. The outcome of the survival ITCs were the HRs and 95% CIs of epcoritamab relative to current 4L+ care. A HR<1 indicates lower risk of progression or death for epcoritamab than for the comparator treatment. Weighted Cox regression is a parsimonious option to account for timedependent effects applicable for small samples sizes. The contributions of each event time to the partial likelihood are weighted according to the product of the survivor function and the inverse cumulative probability of follow-up at that time. Therefore, at 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 87 -->

each event time, their weighting function is proportional to the expected number of participants at risk if censoring had not occurred. 

## **2.12.2.2 Variables for adjustments** 

Selection of variables for adjustment was taken after careful consideration, balancing the need to align populations between evidence sources, reporting limitations and the desire to preserve effective sample size. In consultation with clinical experts and through preliminary investigation of treatment effect modifiers and prognostic variables measurable in the EPCORE NHL1 clinical trial it was determined that it was important to consider variables within the following categories: 

- Age 

- Sex 

- ECOG performance Status 

- Disease Stage 

- FLIPI score 

- Rapid progression on prior treatments 

- Number of prior treatments 

- Previous treatment with specific therapies 

- Refractory status 

These factors are aligned with the variables considered for adjustment in the MAIC analyses conducted vs HMRN in TA627, noting that ECOG and FLIPI are validated prognostic indices (where FLIPI includes age and disease stage). The link between early relapse and survival in FL is described in Casulo et al.,[75] and previous lines of therapy and time from last treatment are likely to reflect the extent and severity of disease. The factors selected for adjustment were, however, limited by the reporting requirements of the HMRN dataset. In the HMRN dataset, several clinical variables were measured at diagnosis but not measured at the start of 4L+ therapy, meaning it was not possible to appropriately adjust for potential imbalances as the proportions at 4L+ were unavailable. This issue was also discussed as part of TA627 and TA1001, 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 88 -->

where HMRN data had been used and where factors such as FLIPI and ECOG were not available at the time of patients initiating their latest LOT.[17,68] Indeed, ECOG had not been adjusted for in any prior ITCs from relevant appraisals (i.e. in heavily-pre-treated FL or where the HMRN dataset had been used to inform the comparator arm)[17,68,19,16] ). 

While ECOG and FLIPI were not measured at the start of 4L+ therapy in the HMRN dataset and therefore not adjusted for (to avoid biasing in favour of epcoritamab), both are composite measures that may be partially represented by the variables that have been adjusted for. For instance, FLIPI includes components such as age and disease stage, which are both accounted for in the MAIC. Similarly, ECOG is generally reflective of overall fitness and functional status, which may be indirectly captured through some of the included variables, such as age. Therefore, the variables included in the adjustment are expected to account for many of the differences between the patient populations that could affect treatment outcomes, as supported by clinical experts. 

The final analysis was conducted using variables of interest following consultation with experts to determine which variables are considered to be confounders, and for which there was a strong degree of evidence for association with survival outcomes (i.e., p≤0.25).[76,77] The final list of variables used for the base case analyses was: 

- Age ( ≥ 60) 

- Disease stage III - IV (At baseline for EPCORE, at diagnosis for HMRN) 

- Sex 

- Prior ASCT 

- Prior CAR-T 

- Prior lines of therapy >4 

- POD24 after first line CIT 

- Refractory to both anti-CD20 and alkylator therapy 

- Refractory to most recent anti lymphoma therapy 

- Prior treatment with R[2]

## **Strengths and weakness of the analyses** 

Using a relevant dataset, an unanchored MAIC was conducted to estimate the relative efficacy of epcoritamab in 4L+ R/R FL based on the EPCORE NHL-1 trial and an equivalent 4L+ cohort from the HMRN data set. The use of data from HMRN allows us to model a representative sample of UK patients receiving relevant treatments as part of current 4L+ care. 

While results from unanchored analyses are sensitive to assumptions of accurately including all available prognostic characteristics and treatment effect modifiers, and the possibility of unaccounted, unobserved residual bias, attempts were made to adjust for all available and clinically relevant baseline prognostic factors and effect modifiers whilst preserving effective sample size. Decisions around variable selection considered clinical expert feedback, tests for significance following investigation of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, prior NICE appraisals in FL and data reporting limitations in HMRN. Unexplained variation in derived relative treatment effects in the ITC could not be tested for and there may be correlated unobserved disease severity characteristics that remain unadjusted in the comparisons. Nevertheless, extensive effort was made to ensure balance between key characteristics between studies taking into account several relevant sources. 

The follow up of the adjusted EPCORE NHL-1 trial data was ***********. With shorter follow-up time, the number of patients being censored is higher than would be expected in a more mature curve, resulting in a low number of patients at risk towards the end of the current curve. Observed events towards the tail of OS and PFS curves, therefore, have greater influence (i.e., large drops in the curves) than would be expected with more mature data. This effect is further exacerbated when applying patient weights as this more rapidly reduces the effective at-risk denominator used for calculating survival probability. Current results toward the end of the curves may not be fully representative of the effect of treatment on survival. 

Although follow-up of patients in HMRN was much longer than in EPCORE NHL-1, the sample size within the HMRN database at 4L+ was relatively small. For the comparison of epcoritamab vs current 4L+ care, the analysis demonstrated a 

substantial and significant improvement with epcoritamab treatment in OS and PFS Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved

Patients treated with epcoritamab in EPCORE NHL-1 were significantly more likely to achieve CR or OR compared with patients treated with current 4L+ care in HMRN. ## **2.14  Ongoing studies** 

This submission presents results from the EPCORE NHL-1 trial (NCT03625037) for the ************* cutoff. To provide further context for the safety and efficacy of epcoritamab, data from the C1-Opt cohort (8 January 2024 data cutoff, *** months median follow-up), is provided in this section. 

## **2.14.1 EPCORE NHL-1 – C1-Opt 4L+ Cohort** 

Following the dose expansion phase of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, a dose optimisation part was conducted to investigate different step-up doses (SUDs) in order to reduce the risk of ≥ grade 2 CRS observed after the first full dose. The optimisation part was conducted in three cohorts (DLBCL, FL Grades 1-3A and MCL).

For the FL1-3A cohort, the optimisation part was conducted in two arms; Arm A and Arm B, the dosing regimens for which can be found in Table 37. Initially six participants were enrolled in each arm, with preliminary analysis revealing a numerically lower CRS rate in Arm A compared with Arm B. As such, Arm A was expanded to include 86 participants. The dosing strategy for Arm A is included in the anticipated marketing approval.

## **2.14.2 Clinical evidence – C1-Opt 4L+ Cohort** 

An overview of the patient baseline demographics and disease characteristics is presented in Table 39. The gender of participants in the C1-Opt 4L+ cohort was well matched (n = 20, 48.8% and n = 21, 51.2% male and female, respectively). Race was not reported in 22.0% of patients (9 patients) with 75.6% of patients (n = 31) being reported as white. Mild or moderate renal impairment was reported in 61.0% (n = 25) patients, with severe renal impairment not being reported in any patient. The majority of patients (95.1%, 39 patients) had normal hepatic function. 

Approximately half of the cohort (53.7%, 22 patients) had FL at histological Grade 2, with Grade 1 and Grade 3A being represented at 26.8% (11 patients) and 14.6% (6 patients), respectively. A FLIPI score of 3 or greater was reported in 63.4% of the cohort (26 patients). Double refractory disease was reported in 65.9% of patients (27 patients).

## **2.15  Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence** 

## **2.15.1 Principal findings from the clinical evidence base** 

Although often considered indolent at an early stage, late-stage FL is an aggressive disease with patient prognosis being poor. Median survival for patients at 4L+ is **** months, with patients often experiencing disease progression or death within a 

median of *** months.[5] Once a patient reaches 4L+ treatment, they have usually 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 111 -->

exhausted the available treatment options and are often rechallenged with agents from prior treatment lines despite diminishing response rates being observed.[4] Consequently, there is a significant need for new treatments for this patient population, a challenge exacerbated by the absence of recent innovations meeting the standards needed for NICE approval. 

Current treatment options for patients with FL are often delivered via intravenous infusion, which confer a significant burden on patients, carers, and the healthcare system due to their invasive administration. As such there is need for a novel therapy, administered in a convenient fashion that offers clinically and statistically meaningful OS and PFS responses.

The clinical evidence presented as part of this submission has been derived from a recent SLR that was conducted according to the principles of systematic reviewing published in the Cochrane handbook.[82] The clinical SLR identified the pivotal clinical trial EPCORE NHL-1 as the primary evidence source for epcoritamab in patients with R/R FL. The results of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial are relevant to the decision problem outlined in the NICE scope, specifically the population of interest; adult FL patients with R/R 4L+ FL. 

Due to an absence of direct trial evidence comparing epcoritamab with current 4L+ care, an unanchored MAIC was used to generate comparative efficacy evidence. After careful consideration, the HMRN registry (which has previously been used in TA604, TA627 and TA1001) was used as a comparator as it is a UK-specific dataset, which was most comparable to the submission population as determined by UK clinical experts.[9,17,68,83] The evidence used to inform the MAIC considered the best data available on the comparator therapies available in UK clinical practice, accurately reflecting the patient population under consideration according to feedback from UK clinicians.[9] The MAIC was conducted following the robust methodologies outlined in the NICE guidance in TSD18.[58] In particular, the effect modifiers and prognostic variables were carefully considered, and were selected based on feedback from UK clinical experts, published literature and testing of prognostic status. This resulted in a high-quality analysis, providing the best estimates for comparative efficacy that could be conducted using the data available. In the MAIC, epcoritamab demonstrated significant and sustained benefits over the comparator arm with OS and PFS hazard rations of ********************************* and *******************************), respectively. 

The EPCORE NHL-1 trial was powered to demonstrate statistical significance. Comparative evidence was generated using a UK dataset (HMRN), as per previous TAs, and the NICE recommended approach to reduce the risk of confounding. Therefore, analyses using EPCORE NHL-1 and HMRN detected a statistically significant improvement in OS and PFS of a magnitude that is clinically important to patients with 4L+ R/R FL. ## **2.15.3  Conclusions** 

There are limited treatment options for patients starting their fourth LOT. By this stage, their FL is an end-of-life disease characterised by frequent hospitalisations and poor HRQoL.[5] Epcoritamab introduces a novel mechanism of action to the current treatment strategy for patients with relapsed or refractory FL grades 1-3A at 4L+, providing a completely new treatment option instead of reusing ineffective available therapies. The convenient method by which epcoritamab is delivered has the potential to reduce the utilisation of hospital resources, decrease appointment times and reduce the overall burden experienced by the patient, their care givers and healthcare system.

## **3 Cost effectiveness** 

## **A cost-utility analysis was performed using a partitioned survival model** 

## **(PSM) structure in line with previous NICE TAs evaluating the cost-** 

## **effectiveness of interventions for FL** 

- The objective of this analysis was to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of epcoritamab in patients with 4L+ R/R FL. The analysis compares epcoritamab with a basket of current 4L+ treatment options identified by the HMRN dataset, validated by UK clinicians and aligned with the treatments described in the scope of this appraisal. 

- A PSM was developed using three health states: 

   - Progression-free: includes patients who are alive and whose disease has not progressed. 

   - Progressed disease: includes patients who are alive but whose disease has progressed. 

   - Death: includes patients who have died either from disease or other causes. 

## **Survival analyses** 

- The proportional hazards assumption was assessed on OS and PFS outcomes from EPCORE NHL-1 and the HMRN dataset using the guidance described in NICE DSU TSD 14.[72] 

- Results of the log-cumulative hazards plot, Schoenfeld residuals and Grambsch-Thurneau assessments found no evidence that the assumption of proportional hazards between EPCORE NHL-1 and HMRN is violated; therefore, PFS and OS for current 4L+ care is generated within the model using HRs obtained from the MAIC and compared with the EPCORE NHL-1 survival curves, outlined in Section 2.12. 

- Base case parametric distributions were selected using guidance from NICE DSU TSD 14, and were based on visual fit, clinical plausibility and fit statistics.[72] 

- TTD data for HMRN were modelled using extrapolated KM data from HMRN due to the difference in regimen treatment schedules which reduces the ability to assume proportional hazards.

## **Utility analyses** 

   - EPCORE NHL-1 included assessment of health-related quality of life during the study, which was used to derive health state utility values. A standardised measure of health status, the EQ-5D-3L, was used, aligned with NICE methods guidance.[84] 

   - As detailed in Section 2, significantly more patients achieve CR on treatment with epcoritamab compared with treatment with current 4L+ care. In line with comments from healthcare professionals that patients achieving CR are expected to have improved HRQoL compared with patients who do not achieve CR, a weighted utility was applied in the base case to the progression-free health state depending on the proportion of patients achieving CR with epcoritamab and current 4L+ care. 

   - • A utility value of ***** was applied for patients in the PF health state receiving epcoritamab, while a utility value of ***** was applied in the PF health state for patients receiving current 4L+ care, reflecting the substantial differences in CR rates observed. 

- To measure HRQoL in the PD health state, a utility decrement from Wild et al. was applied to the current 4L+ care PF value to generate a treatment independent health state utility for PD (*****), as has been accepted in prior appraisals.[85] 

- **Cost-effectiveness results** 

   - All cost-effectiveness results presented within this submission use the current epcoritamab PAS price. 

   - • The comparator arm, current 4L+ care, is associated with 0.9851 QALYs; therefore, considering a patient population with mean age 64.8 years and 34.6% female, the threshold for applying the ×1.2 severity modifier has been met and is considered in this analysis. 

   - • The total costs associated with epcoritamab and current 4L+ care are £******* and £******, respectively. The total QALYs associated with epcoritamab and current 4L+ care are 5.176 and 1.182, respectively (×1.2 modifier applied).

- Sensitivity and scenario analyses demonstrate that the model results are robust to parameter and input uncertainty and consistently show epcoritamab to be associated with ICERs within the range NICE would usually consider to be cost-effective.

- The results of the economic analyses presented in this submission demonstrate that epcoritamab represents a cost-effective use of NHS resources compared with current 4L+ care in patients with R/R FL. 

## **3.1 Published cost-effectiveness studies** 

In line with the NICE technology evaluations manual, an SLR was conducted to identify all relevant cost-effectiveness studies in FL. The SLR was conducted in alignment with the CRD’s guidance for systematic reviews,[86] the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews,[87] Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines,[88] and requirements set out by NICE.[89] Details of the SLR are provided in Appendix E. 

In brief, electronic databases (Embase, Medline and EconLit) were searched from inception to 03 April 2023, and subsequently updated on 07 November 2024. Conference proceedings between 2020 and 2024 were indexed in Embase and were therefore captured in the electronic database search. Additional searches were performed on the websites of HTA authorities to retrieve critical appraisals and key learnings from previous assessments. To identify relevant articles, search terms for FL were used in the website’s search engines. HTA authorities considered for inclusion in the SLR were NICE, Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH), Scottish Medicines Consortium (SMC), Gemeinsamer

## **3.2 Economic analysis** 

The economic case presented in this submission is based on a conventional costutility analysis, assessing the use of epcoritamab for the treatment of adults with 4L+ R/R FL. The analysis considers the simple discount patient access scheme (PAS) available for epcoritamab.

The model considered the R/R FL patient population that has received three or more prior lines of systemic therapy.

## **3.2.2 Model structure** 

In line with previous R/R FL appraisals, a partitioned survival model (PSM) structure was adopted to estimate the cost-effectiveness of epcoritamab versus current 4L+ 

care.[91-94] The cost-effectiveness model was developed in line with NICE guidelines 

related to the methods of technology appraisals.[84] 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 121 -->

The model adopts three health states; 

- Progression-free (PF): includes patients who are alive and whose disease has not progressed. 

- Progressed disease (PD): includes patients who are alive but whose disease has progressed. 

- Death: includes patients who have died either from disease or other causes 

This three-state PSM structure was selected because it offers a data-driven, flexible approach that is well-established in economic modelling of oncological diseases, particularly in R/R FL (Table 44). PSMs have the advantage of directly incorporating observed survival data (such as PFS and OS), which reduces the uncertainty that can arise when estimating separate transition probabilities required in a statetransition (Markov) model. This approach minimises reliance on additional assumptions about intermediate health state transitions—a significant benefit when intermediate endpoint data are limited or potentially biased. Given the single arm nature of the ECPORE NHL-1 trial, patient-level data was not available for current standard of care 4L+ outcomes; the PSM allows for survival-based comparisons using aggregate-level data from HMRN. Additionally, the use of a PSM is consistent with the approach taken in TA604, TA627 and TA1001, where modelling comparative efficacy utilised data from HMRN.[17,68,83] 

The proportion of patients within each health state was determined by OS and PFS curves via an area-under-the-curve approach using data from the EPCORE NHL-1 trial and the comparator data source, HMRN, with outcomes being individually modelled following adjustments performed via a MAIC (Figure 21). The methods and outcomes of the MAIC are described in Section 2.12 

All patients enter the model in the PFS health state and remain in this state until disease progression or death. If a patient’s disease progresses, they move into the progressed disease health state where they remain until their death. Death is an absorbing health state. 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 122 -->

The PFS curve determines the proportion of patients remaining alive and progression-free, and the OS curve determines the proportion of patients that are alive (regardless of their progression status). The difference between the PFS and OS curves informs the proportion of patients that are alive post-progression. 

Background mortality is incorporated in survival extrapolations (described in Section 3.3.2.3) to ensure that the OS of patients within the model does not exceed the survival of an age- and sex-matched population within the UK. 

**Figure 21. Survival curves informing the proportion of patients per health state** 

**==> picture [452 x 151] intentionally omitted <==**

OS, overall survival; PFS, progression-free survival 

Patients accrue costs and utilities for each cycle they spend in each state (excluding death) and the model is run over a defined number of cycles, allowing an estimate of total costs and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) for the cohort over the specified time horizon. The direct healthcare costs include treatment acquisition costs, administration costs, healthcare resource costs per health state, costs of subsequent treatment following treatment discontinuation, AE management costs, costs of disease progression, and costs of terminal care. 

## **3.2.2.1 Time horizon** 

The model considers a lifetime time horizon in the base case analysis. The NICE guidelines recommend that the time horizon is sufficiently long to reflect any differences in costs or outcomes between the technologies that are being compared.[95] With a mean age at the start of the model of 64.80 as informed by the cohort receiving 4L+ treatment in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial at enrolment, this leads to 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 123 -->

a lifetime horizon spanning 35.2 years. The impact of a shorter time horizon is explored in scenario analyses (Section 3.11.3). 

## **3.2.2.2 Cycle length** 

The model adopts a cycle length of one week. This is considered sufficiently short to accurately capture model outcomes, hence no half-cycle correction is applied. 

## **3.2.2.3 Perspective and discounting** 

The model considers a NHS and PSS perspective, and costs and health-related utilities are discounted at 3.5% per annum in accordance with the NICE reference case.[84]

## **3.2.3 Intervention technology and comparators** 

## **3.2.3.1 Intervention** 

As described in Section 1.1, the intervention of interest in this analysis is epcoritamab. Epcoritamab is administered through subcutaneous injection according to the dosing regimen for the optimisation part of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial. This regimen consists of a priming dose of 0.16 mg, intermediate doses of 0.80 and 3.00 mg, and a full dose of 48.0 mg until unacceptable toxicity, disease progression, or withdrawal of consent. The epcoritamab dosing regimen applied within the model is presented in Table 45. 

**Table 45. Epcoritamab dosing regimen applied in the model** 

|**Dose**|**Administration Frequency**|
|---|---|
|0.16 mg|One administration on day 1 of cycle 1 (28-day cycle)|
|0.80 mg|One administration on day 8 of cycle 1 (28-day cycle)|
|3.00 mg|One administration on day 15 of cycle 1 (28-day cycle)|
|48.0 mg|Once weekly from day 22 of cycle 1 (28-day cycle) until cycle 3<br>Once every two weeks for cycle 4 to 9<br>Once every four weeks from cycle 10 and beyond|



At a median of 5.7 (0.4 – 11.8) months study follow-up in Arm A of the dose optimisation part of EPCORE NHL-1, the optimisation cohort was considered adequate to assess any impact of the three step-up dose regimen (including 3.00 mg) on response rates, since the duration of follow-up includes the first scheduled imaging assessments. As is detailed in regulatory documentation to the European Medicines Agency, the response rates in the optimisation cohort using the three step-up dose regimen are similar to those in the expansion cohort using the two step-up dose regimen.[96] Further, pharmacokinetic outcomes are similar between patients who received the three step-up dose regimen and patients who received the two step-up dose regimen in EPCORE NHL-1.[7] Therefore, the clinical efficacy outcomes from the expansion cohort presented in Section 2 are considered suitable with sufficiently long follow-up for use within the economic evaluation.

## **3.3 Clinical parameters and variables** 

## **3.3.1 Evidence synthesis** 

Evidence to describe the characteristics of the patient population and the effectiveness of epcoritamab was primarily derived from the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, an open label, multicentre, phase 1/2 trial in participants aged 18 years or older with 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 128 -->

relapsed, progressive and/or refractory disease. The trial contains an escalation part, an expansion part and an optimisation part, with the expansion part of the study being used to model the clinical efficacy of epcoritamab within this economic evaluation. As EPCORE NHL-1 was a single-arm trial, an SLR was performed to source efficacy data for current 4L+ options in clinical practice. The SLR did not identify any data sources that reported outcomes in UK patients with 4L+ R/R FL who received treatments that resemble UK clinical practice. Therefore, an ITC using data obtained from HMRN was conducted to derive comparator survival and response data as described in Section 2.12. 

## **3.3.2 Survival analysis** 

As described in Section 3.2.2, the proportion of patients in the PFS, PD, and Death health states at each cycle in the model is determined by PFS and OS curves using data from the dose expansion part of EPCORE NHL-1. As this evaluation compares the outcomes for epcoritamab with current 4L+ care over a lifetime horizon, longer than the follow-up duration available from EPCORE NHL-1 and HMRN, the observed PFS and OS curves required extrapolation. In line with the data presented in Section 2.8, these analyses consider COVID-modified outcomes from EPCORE NHL-1. 

## **3.3.2.1 Assessing the proportional hazards assumption** 

The proportional hazards assumption (PHA) was assessed using the epcoritamab survival curves presented in Section 2 to determine whether a constant hazard ratio (HR) could be applied to the epcoritamab curve to extrapolate long-term outcomes for HMRN, or whether alternative methods should be considered. Three assessments were conducted: 

- Visual inspection of log-cumulative hazards against log-time. Approximately, parallel lines indicate the PHA holds, while non-parallel or crossing lines suggest it does not. 

- Visual inspection of Schoenfeld residuals. These residuals reflect the difference between observed covariates and expected value over time, with a plot centred around zero and showing no trend supporting the PHA. 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 129 -->

- The Grambsch and Therneau test. This evaluates the relationship between Schoenfeld residuals and survival time, with a significant p-value (p<0.05) indicating a violation of the PHA. 

The results of all tests described in Table 46 indicate that the PHA is likely to hold for both OS and PFS; therefore, in line with the guidance within TSD14, applying constant HRs is suitable in all cases for long-term extrapolations.[72] This approach also reduces the number of estimated degrees of freedom compared with using independent models, thereby enhancing the precision of the long-term survival estimates. Further details around the assessment of proportional hazards are presented in Appendix J.
