## **3.3.2.2 Extrapolation of survival outcomes** 

To extrapolate survival outcomes over the lifetime horizon, standard parametric curves (exponential, gamma, generalised gamma, Gompertz, log-normal, loglogistic, and Weibull) were fitted to the PFS OS, and TTD curves as per NICE TSD14.[72] 

Curve selection was performed according to the following criteria presented in TSD14, namely: 

- Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) were used to test the relative fit of each parametric model, while also penalising overfitting. Models with an AIC or BIC difference of ≤2 were considered statistically comparable.[97] 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 130 -->

- Each curve was visually compared against the KM data to evaluate the fit. Parametric distributions that deviated substantially or produced implausible projections were discounted. 

- The chosen distributions were compared with landmark survival estimates obtained during individual consultations with UK clinical experts from centres around the country and experienced in using bispecific antibodies for treating FL. Six engagements had taken place. In five of these engagements, the clinicians were able to provide landmark survival estimates at specified timepoints in order to guide the most appropriate model selection. Some clinical experts were not able to provide landmark estimates for all outcomes due to time constraints for the engagements. 

In the base-case analysis, PFS and OS outcomes for current 4L+ care are derived by applying the MAIC-adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) to the unadjusted epcoritamab data, ensuring comparability between treatment arms in an EPCORE NHL-1 trial population.

## **3.3.2.5 Time to treatment discontinuation** 

## **3.3.2.5.1 Epcoritamab** 

As for OS and PFS, parametric distributions were applied to the observed TTD data from EPCORE NHL-1 using the methodology described in Section 3.3.2.2. As observed in Figure 27, all fitted distributions follow the data well and fell within the 95% confidence interval estimates of survival. 

It is noteworthy that the PFS and TTD curves from EPCORE NHL-1 meet within the first 6 months, with the TTD curve briefly being slightly above the PFS curve. This may be caused by different factors, such as the PFS curve being heavily censored during the initial months of the trial and, with PFS being censored at the last PFS measurement, the date of last PFS measurement may be earlier than the date of discontinuation. Additionally, clinicians may not halt treatment for patients immediately after progression or there may be a difference between investigator and IRC-assessed progression, resulting in the patients receiving treatment longer than the IRC-assessed progression date. However, after ~6 months TTD falls below PFS as expected.

These findings are reflected by the landmark estimates in Table 54.

## _**3.3.2.5.1.1 Maximal treatment duration for complete responders**_ 

During engagements on TTD for epcoritamab, clinical experts noted that patients with a CR would be unlikely to continue receiving treatment beyond two years. This can be seen in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, whereby ** patients (****%) with a CR remain on treatment at a median follow-up of **** months. By three years, very few patients with a CR would continue to receive epcoritamab in practice. Clinical experts noted that patient preference, management of adverse events, and experience with bispecific antibodies in other B-cell lymphoma subtypes would influence their decision-making at these time points. 

Data from the EPCORE NHL-1 trial showed that all patients with 4L+ FL remaining on treatment after 15 months are complete responders (Figure 29). Indeed, survival for patients with a CR is durable and OS at three years was shown to be close to **% (Figure 30). Further analysis has demonstrated that patients who achieve a CR, but stop treatment due to reasons other than progression or death (n = *), are likely to maintain their CR, as evidenced by the flat PFS curve within a year of subsequent follow-up (***% PFS at 6 months and 12 months respectively) (Figure 31). This set of results aligns with clinical expectations and experiences with bispecific antibodies in other B-cell lymphoma subtypes. As such, the base case analysis for this appraisal assumes that epcoritamab treatment costs are no longer accrued for complete responders after three years. The impact of this is assessed within the sensitivity analyses (Section 3.11.3.2).

## **3.3.2.5.2 Current 4L+ care** 

Unlike for PFS and OS, it is not appropriate to use a MAIC-derived HR to derive TTD for current 4L+ care because the HMRN treatment basket consists of multiple therapies with different fixed treatment durations, making direct comparisons with the trial treatment less meaningful. Instead, raw HMRN TTD data was used to model patient discontinuation from current 4L+ care. This directly reflects observed treatment discontinuation patterns in UK clinical practice, without relying on the use of hazard ratios. Given that the HMRN treatment basket includes therapies with fixed treatment durations, using raw HMRN TTD allows assessment of how these variations impact cost-effectiveness outcomes. ## **3.3.3 Adverse events** 

The adverse events observed in patients treated with epcoritamab are outlined in Section 2.13. To reflect the impact of AEs, the costs and HCRU associated with AE management are included within the economic evaluation. ## **3.3.4 Background mortality** 

Estimates of the general population mortality (i.e., mortality not related to the disease) are taken from the most recent life tables reported by the Office of National Statistics (ONS) for the year 2020-2022 for England and Wales.[98] The general population mortality was adjusted by the baseline mean age and sex ratio of the 

EPCORE NHL-1 population. 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 147 -->

Background mortality is incorporated in survival extrapolations in the CEM using the internal additive hazards adopted for the epcoritamab survival extrapolations. In this approach, parametric survival fits are used to generate OS data and to calculate a cyclic hazard. Patient background mortality was determined using age- and sexmatched calculations, as previously described. The OS from the preceding cycle was then multiplied by the exponent of background mortality and the hazard of OS for the new cycle. 

EPCORE NHL-1 data were fitted using the internal additive hazards approach, i.e. distinguishing between disease related hazards and background mortality using the most recent national life tables for England and Wales (2020-2022) published by the ONS.[98-100] 

To incorporate the background mortality related hazards for the target population into the CEM, the internal additive hazard approach was adopted using the function presented below.[99] 

ℎ(𝑡) = ℎ𝐺𝑃𝑀(𝑡) + ℎ𝐷𝑆𝑀(𝑡) 

The hazards ( ℎ(𝑡) ) are the sum of the general population mortality (GPM) hazards ( ℎ𝐺𝑃𝑀(𝑡) ) and disease-specific mortality (DSM) hazards estimated by a parametric distribution ( ℎ𝐷𝑆𝑀(𝑡) ).

## **3.4.1 Health-related quality of life data from clinical trials** 

The EPCORE NHL-1 trial included assessment of HRQoL during the study, which can be used to derive utility values for modelling analysis. A standardised measure of health status, the EQ-5D-3L, was used to provide a generic measure of HRQoL.[101]

## **3.4.4.4 Age-adjusted utilities** 

The increasing prevalence of comorbidities in older aged cohorts and the adverse effect on HRQoL directly associated with age must be reflected in economic models with lifetime horizons. It can be assumed that the health state utility values for individuals without a particular health condition will change over the time horizon. 

Hence, the economic model includes the use of age-adjusted utility values over the time horizon of the model to account for this. This has been included in the economic model using age- and sex- adjusted utilities from the UK index of health state utility decline in Ara and Brazier.[118-120]

## **3.5 Cost and healthcare resource use identification, measurement and valuation** 

## **3.5.1 Resource identification, measurement and valuation studies** 

Section 3.1 and Appendix G describe how relevant cost and healthcare resource data were identified. Briefly, an SLR was conducted to identify studies describing the costs and resource use associated with the management of patients with R/R FL who had received two or more prior lines of therapy. The literature search identified 16 studies describing costs and resource across 18 different publications.[121-138] Of the 16 studies, four studies presented evidence among patients receiving therapies in the 3L+ setting.[123,128,130,131] All the studies that presented evidence among patients receiving 3L+ therapy were retrospective analyses. 

Ten studies had a geographical focus in the US, one in Canada, one in Italy, one across multiple locations, and three did not report the geographic focus. All of the studies, except two,[137,138] reported data on direct healthcare costs and none reported on indirect costs. The most common direct costs reported across the studies included medical costs, inpatient costs, outpatient costs, emergency room (ER) costs, physician office visit costs, pharmacy costs, and FL-specific treatment costs. 

All except two[121,124] studies reported on healthcare resource use. The most common resource use reported across the studies included frequency of inpatient hospitalisations, ER visits, physician office visits, and outpatient visits, length of stay in hospital (inpatient stay, ER visits, ICU admissions), number of days in outpatient services, and number of days with drug administration.

## **3.5.2.2 Drug administration costs** 

Treatments may be administered IV, orally or through subcutaneous injection. Drug administration unit costs were obtained from the National Schedule of Reference Costs by the NHS 2023/2024 and are summarised in Table 72.[149] 

Epcoritamab monotherapy is expected to be prescribed in either secondary or tertiary care, with routine follow-up also being performed in the same settings. This is consistent with other treatment options currently available for R/R FL. 

Clinical experts have noted that current 4L+ care often involves extensive inpatient hospital stays due to the need for regular IV infusions, which can be both timeconsuming and taxing on the NHS, patients and carers. Chemotherapy, a large component of this care, can lead to significant side effects and requires continuous monitoring, thereby increasing the burden on healthcare resources and the patient and carer’s quality of life. In contrast, epcoritamab monotherapy is administered subcutaneously and is expected to incur a smaller healthcare resource burden. 

For drugs administered orally, it was assumed that no hospital resources would be required and thus, costs were assumed to be zero.

## **3.5.2.3 Subsequent treatments** 

Following progression on their 4L treatment (epcoritamab or current 4L+ care) patients could receive subsequent therapy (i.e. ≥5[th] line) in the PD state. Since there is no established standard of care for patients reaching 4L+, the escalation treatment pathway for all primary treatments is expected to be identical for epcoritamab and current 4L+ care because patients are expected to continue recycling old regimens, irrespective of the regimen they received at 4L. Further, it is anticipated that having epcoritamab available as a treatment option in the 4L setting would delay patients’ recycling prior treatment regimens by one line of therapy. Therefore, clinical experts have stated that the basket of subsequent treatment should be identical to the basket of current 4L+ care used within the comparator arm, aligned with the approach taken in TA894.[9,19] 

Subsequent therapy costs were calculated based on the dosing schedules for treatments as defined by their SmPC and weighted according to the proportions in Table 71, before being applied as a single cost per cycle for patients receiving subsequent therapy. The cost per cycle is determined by calculating the total cost of each regimen—for drug acquisition and administration costs, respectively, over its full duration and dividing this by the number of cycles within that period. This provides an estimate of the average cost per cycle for each regimen, which is then weighted according to the distribution of subsequent treatments (as per Table 70). This ensures that the cost per cycle appropriately reflects the mix of therapies used in the PD state. The time on treatment and average cost per cycle for each subsequent treatment is displayed in Table 73.

## **3.6 Severity** 

The NICE committees consider the severity of a condition when assessing health technologies.[154] The severity of the disease is considered by calculating the absolute QALY shortfall and proportional QALY shortfall by comparing with QALYs in current 4L+ care. 

The calculation used to determine absolute QALY shortfall is as follows: 

Absolute QALY shortfall = QALYs in current 4L+ care - 

QALYs in age and sex matched general population 

The calculation used to determine proportional QALY shortfall is as follows: 

Absolute QALY shortfall Proportional QALY shortfall = QALYs in age and sex matched general population 

In the base case analysis, with a mean age at baseline of 64.8 years and a proportion of males of 65.4%, the absolute shortfall estimate is 9.92 QALYs and the proportional shortfall is 90.93%, which results in a severity modifier of ×1.2 (Table 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 166 -->

78). This is calculated using the reference case in the York QALY shortfall calculator (using English life tables, the EQ-5D-3L value set and scoring algorithm, and adjusted limited dependent variable mixture models).[118,155-157] This ×1.2 severity modifier is applied to the incremental QALYs in the model base case. The application of a severity modifier in 4L+ FL aligns with clinician and patient feedback where the life expectancy with current 4L+ care in England is low (median OS reached by **** months) and patients will typically be re-challenged with a variant of CIT or chemotherapy.

## **3.7 Uncertainty** 

Due to the limited literature reporting data on patients with 4L+ R/R FL, this analysis is subject to inescapable uncertainty; therefore, the available data may not fully capture the variability and complexity of patient responses and outcomes in 4L+ FL. Although efforts have been made to engage with clinicians experienced in treating patients with 4L+ R/R FL to validate model inputs and patient outcomes, the absence of robust published estimates for resource use and burden of current therapies on patients and caregivers means that this analysis may underestimate the value of epcoritamab compared with existing current 4L+ care options. The benefits of epcoritamab which could not be robustly captured within the economic analysis are detailed in Section 3.13, and include a reduced HRQoL burden relative to treatment with chemoimmunotherapy regimens, less frequent HCRU through more patients achieving CR (where resource utilisation is less intense), anticipated reduction in 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 167 -->

cardiac adverse events compared with treatment using CIT regimens, and alleviated caregiver burden/anxiety. 

Further, although unavoidable due to ethical considerations around treating patients at 4L+, EPCORE NHL-1 is a single arm clinical trial; therefore, no data directly comparing its efficacy with current 4L+ care options are available. This increases the uncertainty within the presented analyses by limiting the ability to establish a direct relationship between treatment effect and observed outcomes and increases the potential for biases in the interpretation of the results. To increase committee confidence in the outputs of the trial and cost-effectiveness analyses, clinical consultations were held to validate the design and outcomes of EPCORE NHL-1, as outlined in Section 3.14.1. Further, to obtain a robust comparison of epcoritamab efficacy compared with current 4L+ care, a MAIC was performed leveraging precedent and recommendations from previous NICE appraisals for similar patient populations and recommendations from clinicians, as detailed in Section 2.12. 

Moreover, the lack of recent positive recommendations from NICE, and the poor outcomes observed in HMRN for treatments in 4L+ FL further highlights the significant unmet need in this patient population. The absence of established guidelines and positive recommendations underscores the urgency for innovative and effective treatments, providing a compelling rationale for the continued exploration and development of new therapeutic options. 

The company has made conscientious efforts to limit the uncertainties within this appraisal. Since epcoritamab represents a promising advancement in the treatment of patients with 4L+ R/R FL, remaining uncertainties should not act as a barrier to ensuring an efficacious treatment is made available to patients, in an area of high unmet need.

## **3.11  Exploring uncertainty** 

## **3.11.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

The probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) assesses model uncertainty by varying model parameters simultaneously over 1,000 iterations to estimate the range of possible outcomes. NICE guidelines state the number of iterations should be chosen such that stochastic results converge towards an equilibrium.[84] 

The distribution chosen for each parameter included in the probabilistic sensitivity analysis PSA (and DSA) is based on the recommendations provided in Briggs et al. (2006).[158] Correlated parameters (such as shares) are modelled through a Dirichlet distribution where applicable. 

Where available, the parameters for the distributions in the PSA were derived from the deterministic value and the SE from these deterministic input estimates. In absence of estimates of variance, an SE level of 10% was assumed in line with prior NICE submissions.[159] 

The findings are presented by means of the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC), cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier (CEAF), and a scatter plot of the incremental cost versus the incremental QALYs. Mean total costs, mean total QALYs, and the mean probabilistic ICER are presented for/versus each comparator. 

## **3.11.1.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis results** 

In the PSA, the model samples values from distributions around the means of input parameters using both the mean and SE of parameters to derive an estimated value using an appropriate distribution.

## **3.11.2  Deterministic sensitivity analysis** 

The deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) is a form of one-way sensitivity analysis that adjusts each parameter one at a time to assess the impact of uncertainty around individual input parameters on the incremental costs, incremental QALYs and ICER. Where available, lower and upper bounds for the DSA were determined by the SE from input estimates. In absence of estimates of variance, an SE level of 10% was assumed. An overview of the parameters varied within the DSA is presented in Appendix L. 

## **3.11.2.1 Deterministic sensitivity analysis results** 

Results of the DSA are presented in Figure 39 and demonstrate the impact of specific parameters on ICER estimates. 

The DSA samples each parameter individually according to their assigned upper and lower bounds; therefore, similar to the PSA, this sensitivity analysis cannot incorporate the severity modifier applied in the base case analysis as variations in individual parameters may impact absolute and proportional QALY shortfall, thereby impacting whether the threshold for implementing a severity modifier is reached. ## **3.11.3.4 Composition of current 4L+ care treatment basket** 

As outlined in Section 1.3.6.2.3 and Section 3.2.3.2, there is no standard of care for patients with R/R FL, particularly at later lines of therapy where patients mostly recycle through prior treatment regimens to which they may be refractory. In the base case analysis, the composition of the current 4L+ care treatment basket is based on data obtained from HMRN to best reflect UK clinical practice. To recognise the variation in treatment regimens available for patients with 4L+ R/R FL, a scenario has been performed to explore possible variations in prescribing patterns in clinical practice (Table 88). The proportion of treatment received in current 4L+ care is also applied to subsequent rounds of treatment to reflect clinical experts’ feedback that the basket of subsequent treatment should be identical to the basket of current 4L+ care used within the comparator arm, aligned with the approach taken in TA894.[9,19]

## **3.11.3.5 Survival extrapolations** 

Survival modelling using long-term extrapolation of parametric functions is subject to considerable uncertainty despite efforts to robustly and transparently provide survival curves that best represent patients in clinical practice. In order to assess the impact of alternative parametric extrapolations on the cost-effectiveness of epcoritamab, scenario analyses were performed by applying distributions generating clinically plausible outcomes. 

This analysis should be viewed within the context of identifying the most appropriate survival extrapolation, as detailed in Section 3.3.2.2. Only extrapolations considered clinically plausible based on engagement with clinicians (Table 49, Table 52 and Table 55) have been included.

## **3.11.3.6 Applying a PFS/TTD HR to derive TTD outcomes for current 4L+ care** 

A scenario analysis was performed to explore the impact of applying a tailored approach that leverages the relationship between PFS and TTD observed within the HMRN dataset for modelling discontinuation of current 4L+ care. First, a HR was calculated between HMRN PFS and TTD (**********). This HR is then applied to the HMRN PFS curve, which itself is generated by applying a MAIC derived HR to the epcoritamab PFS data, to derive the corresponding HMRN TTD curve. This method implicitly captures the impact of matching adjustment because the HR is applied to a PFS curve that reflects the MAIC-adjusted population, and by anchoring TTD to the PFS relationship observed in HMRN, this ensures that TTD is appropriately modelled within the UK clinical practice context while maintaining comparability with PFS and OS estimates.

## **3.13  Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation** 

_New treatment option with a novel mechanism of action_ 

As outlined in Section 1.3.6, there is no standard of care for patients with R/R FL who have received three lines of prior systemic therapy and patients currently recycle through current 4L+ care regimens to which they may already be refractory. Recognising the short life expectancy in patients with R/R FL reaching 4L+, UK clinical experts, patients, and carers, have repeatedly expressed the need for more treatment options, an issue that has been compounded by poor availability of new and innovative medicines due to recent negative recommendations (TA892 and TA894).[9,16,19] Introducing epcoritamab monotherapy as a treatment option in this setting provides a valuable and novel treatment option with a new mechanism of action compared with existing treatment options and may offer increased hope and improved treatment tolerability in patients with relapsed or refractory FL. 

## _Impact of chemoimmunotherapy regimens on HRQoL_ 

The chemoimmunotherapy regimens used within the current 4L+ care basket are associated with severe mental and physical side effects.[70] It is therefore possible that the true impact of these side effects are not fully captured within the QALY calculation when considering the cumulative burden of toxicity (physical and psychological), 

growing treatment resistance and cardiac dysfunction experienced by patients heavily Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 190 -->

exposed to multiple rounds of chemoimmunotherapy, as noted by clinical experts in previous appraisals.[16] In addition, patients re-treated with standard therapy are likely to despair at the lack of available treatment options after three prior lines of therapy. Consequently, this would be expected to negatively impact their emotional and mental well-being, both HRQoL outcomes that could not be fully captured in the costeffectiveness analysis. 

## _Reduced caregiver burden and anxiety_ 

The burden of caring for a family member with R/R FL is also not included within the QALY calculation, but presents a substantial challenge emotionally, practically and financially. Carers often provide transport to-and-from hospital appointments and treatment appointments, which can require time off work, harming personal finances and impacting societal productivity. Current 4L+ treatment regimens are administered by infusion into a vein, over the course of a few hours, presenting a significant time burden on the patient, carers and health care systems. A recent report by the Lymphoma Coalition found that 23% of individuals (carers, friends or family members) had to stop work either permanently, or temporarily, with a further 22% reporting that they had to reduce their work hours.[15] Further, carers also provide emotional support while attempting to navigate an emotionally challenging situation themselves. Most also take on more chores and household tasks. The impact of R/R FL extends beyond temporal and utility burdens, with R/R diagnosis having a significant impact on the mental wellbeing of the patient and carers. Over 3 in 4 caregivers report feeling anxious and physically and emotionally worn out, with some carers and family members requiring counselling and reporting a strain on their relationships.[19] Further, some carers worry that their loved one’s disease has relapsed when they are ill, which can cause daily anxiety.[16] Improved progression-free survival in patients treated with epcoritamab compared with current 4L+ care might introduce benefits for the carer, which are not captured within the QALY calculation. 

## _Reduced HCRU in patients achieving complete response_ 

As detailed in Section 2.8 and Section 2.12, patients treated with epcoritamab achieve deep and durable responses, with significantly more patients achieving CR compared Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 191 -->

with current 4L+ care. During clinical validation exercises, clinical experts experienced in treating patients with 4L+ R/R FL noted that patients who achieve CR would likely incur a lower healthcare resource use compared with patients who fail to achieve CR, in part due to the reduced frequency of CT/PET scans and blood tests. Due to the absence of robust estimates for HCRU in patients achieving a CR, these considerations were not applied within the economic analysis but are expected to provide a meaningful impact on patients, carers and overall healthcare system capacity. 

## _More convenient mode of administration_ 

The availability of epcoritamab as a subcutaneous formulation offers a more convenient mode of administration for patients, carers and healthcare delivery services. Epcoritamab is expected to be prescribed and delivered in secondary and tertiary care settings; therefore, reduced inpatient visits and shorter appointment times will relieve healthcare system capacity and might allow clinicians to increase the number of patients they can treat per day. Whilst the cost-savings associated with subcutaneous administration compared with IV administration are captured in the economic analyses, the benefits of greater flexibility and convenience for patients, as well as the reduced capacity burden for the NHS and opportunity to optimise infrastructure with reduced numbers of IV infusions, is not fully captured. Further, patients regularly receiving IV infusions are expected to experience worsened HRQoL due to the cumulative impact of infusions compared with patients who would receive epcoritamab as a subcutaneous formulation, which is similarly not captured in the base case analysis.[161,162] Patients with 4L+ FL can spend around ******************** in inpatient hospital overnight stays due to treatment administration, monitoring and disease. Over the course of a year, this can add up to more than ************ spent in hospital with overnight stays.[5] Despite this significant burden to patients and carers, it has not been possible to fully capture the HRQoL or resource benefit that epcoritamab, with a subcutaneous mode of administration, can offer.

## **3.14 Validation** 

## **3.14.1 Clinical consultations** 

In order to obtain clinical opinion in advance of this submission, AbbVie organised consultations with six consultant haematologists based around the UK and who are experienced in treating R/R FL with bispecific antibodies. These discussions were held in Q4 2024 and Q1 2025 and included validation of the clinical care pathway at 4L+, assessment of healthcare resource utilisation by health state and response status, selection of effect modifiers for adjustment within the MAIC and landmark survival estimates in patients treated with epcoritamab and current 4L+ care. The outputs of these discussions were implemented within the company’s base case analysis and used to inform selection of survival distributions. 

## **3.14.2 Technical validation** 

In alignment with best practice, validation of the economic model structure was conducted by an independent health economist prior to submission. The validation process also aimed to ensure that a high degree of transparency was maintained throughout the model and so adaptations were carried out where necessary to ensure the validity of assumptions made and methodologies undertaken within the costeffectiveness model. 

## **3.15  Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence** 

## **3.15.1 Summary of evidence** 

In the base case analysis, epcoritamab was associated with 3.994 incremental QALYs and ******* incremental costs compared with current 4L+ care. The corresponding ICER (*******/QALY (when applying the ×1.2 severity weighting) was comfortably within the range NICE usually considers an intervention to be acceptable use of NHS resources. These results are robust to changes in key model parameters, as evidenced in the scenario analyses where ICERs continually ran below £30,000 per QALY gained. Further, the model was robust to parameter uncertainty with the mean PSA results lying close to the deterministic results for the base-case. 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 193 -->

As outlined in Section 3.13, the base case analysis is unable to fully capture many of the benefits of epcoritamab to the healthcare system and patients with R/R FL, namely introducing a new treatment option for patients receiving 4L+ therapy, reduced toxicity burden compared with current therapies, and potential to improve healthcare system capacity through a more convenient mode of administration. Therefore, although epcoritamab provides a cost-effective use of NHS resources, the outcomes of this analysis are likely to significantly underestimate its full potential benefit to patients and payers. 

## **3.15.2 Strengths and limitations of the analysis Model structure** 

The model adopts a PSM structure to capture the clinical benefits of epcoritamab in patients with 4L+ R/R FL. This has the advantage of directly incorporating observed survival data from EPCORE NHL-1, reducing the uncertainty that can arise when estimating separate transition probabilities in a state-transition model and, as detailed in Section 3.2.2, this approach is aligned with previous NICE technology appraisals for R/R FL.[91-94] 

## **EPCORE NHL-1** 

The analyses presented in this submission can be considered generalisable to UK clinical practice and include outcomes data from EPCORE NHL-1 (including sites within the UK) and the HMRN registry, which collects outcomes data for patients across a large geographic region of England. To confirm the generalisability of EPCORE NHL-1 to UK clinical practice, AbbVie engaged with clinicians prior to submission to validate that the patient population enrolled within EPCORE NHL-1 resembles the characteristics of patients treated in UK practice. As part of these discussions, the clinicians noted that the overall fitness of some patients in the trial is poorer compared with standard trial populations and is well aligned with their expectations of a real-world population, albeit with higher risk features. 

Company evidence submission for epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma patients after three or more systemic treatments 

© AbbVie (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 194 -->

While EPCORE NHL-1 provides evidence for the efficacy and safety of epcoritamab as a treatment for patients with 4L+ R/R FL, it is a single-arm trial and so does not provide direct comparative efficacy evidence for epcoritamab versus current treatments in the UK. As a result, ITCs were required to generate comparative efficacy evidence, and the results of these ITCs were used to inform comparative efficacy in the cost-effectiveness model. The ITCs conducted took the form of unanchored MAICs and were conducted in accordance with NICE DSU TSD18.[58] The ITC used robust methodologies previously employed and accepted in other NICE appraisals of R/R FL treatments and adjusted for relevant and observed differences in the patient populations. However, bias due to residual confounding or unobserved differences in populations cannot be excluded. 

As detailed in NICE DSU TSD14,[72] the validity of the PHA was tested to determine whether this approach could be used to model outcomes for current 4L+ care, and concluded that the OS and PFS hazards between EPCORE NHL-1 and HMRN are proportional. Therefore, the base case analysis models the outcomes for current 4L+ care by applying a HR, reducing the number of estimated degrees of freedom compared with using independent models and thereby enhancing the precision of the long-term survival estimates. 

## **3.15.3 Conclusions** 

The life expectancy for patients entering their fourth line of therapy in FL is typically short and most patients do not survive beyond one year after initiating 4L+.[5] Epcoritamab provides hope for patients and carers alike. Analyses presented in this submission show that epcoritamab significantly extends patient life expectancy compared with current care in the UK. Additionally, patients achieve a deep and durable response with epcoritamab, offering certainty and assurance. The results of the costeffectiveness analyses in this submission demonstrate that epcoritamab is a costeffective use of NHS resources and represents a much-needed step change in the care of heavily pre-treated FL.

## **The pharmaceutical company perspective** 

## **What is the SIP?** 

The Summary of Information for Patients (SIP) is written by the company who is seeking approval from NICE for their treatment to be sold to the NHS for use in England.  It is a plain English summary of their submission written for patients participating in the evaluation.  It is not independently checked, although members of the public involvement team at NICE will have read it to doublecheck for marketing and promotional content before it is sent to you.

## **SECTION 1: Submission summary** 

**1a) Name of the medicine** (generic and brand name): 

Epcoritamab (Tepkinly®) 

**1b) Population this treatment will be used by.** Please outline the main patient population that is being appraised by NICE: 

The population that will use this treatment is people with **relapsed** or **refractory** follicular lymphoma who have already received three lines of prior therapy. When a disease is relapsed, it means it that it has become worse again after a period of improvement, and when a disease is refractory it means it is not responding to treatment. 

Follicular lymphoma usually develops fairly slowly. However, after a patient has relapsed or become refractory to treatment and after a patient has received several treatments, the disease becomes more aggressive, with worse symptoms and poorer life expectancy.[1,2]

## **SECTION 2: Current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 

Follicular lymphoma is a slow-growing and generally incurable, chronic type of cancer where **white blood cells** cluster together in the lymph glands. This submission focuses on patients with **relapsed** or **refractory** follicular lymphoma. Approximately 2,330 people a year in the UK are diagnosed with FL with the average age of diagnosis being 67.[3] 

## **Symptoms:** 

The symptoms of follicular lymphoma vary between individual patients, though patients typically experience heavy sweating at night, high temperatures that come and go without cause and rapid, unexplainable weight loss.[4] Other symptoms include swelling of lymph nodes, generally in the neck, armpit or groin and extreme fatigue.[4] Patients with follicular lymphoma also experience high levels of anxiety and depression, especially in patients with disease relapse compared with those in **remission** .[5] 

## **Impact on patients’ and carers’ quality of life:** 

Quality of life describes how healthy, comfortable and able to participate in and enjoy life events a person is. Patients with follicular lymphoma have a reduced quality of life compared with healthy people due to the impact of their symptoms on their daily lives.[5] Following their diagnosis, patients with follicular lymphoma are often unable to continue working.[6] Patients with incurable lymphomas also report anxiety around fear of relapse or progression.[7] 

Current treatment options for patients with follicular lymphoma who have already received 3 or more treatments are invasive and time consuming, which further impacts a patient’s and their carer’s quality of life. The lengthy infusions associated with rituximab-based treatments mean that patients and their carers have to spend several hours receiving treatment at a hospital, over several days during the treatment cycle, which significantly impacts a patient’s ability to participate in their normal daily life. Patients with follicular lymphoma can spend around three days per month in inpatient hospital overnight stays due to treatment administration, monitoring and disease. Over the course of a year, this can add up to more than a full month spent in hospital.[9] Patients and carers also need to travel to and from the hospital, which may result in a financial cost, as well as taking additional time on top of the already lengthy treatment. 

## **Outcomes:** 

Follicular lymphoma can develop fairly slowly, however, after a patient has relapsed or become refractory to several lines of treatment, the disease becomes more aggressive, with worse symptoms. In patients with follicular lymphoma, rates of survival decrease with each line of treatment, and so those who have been treated with several treatments after periods of remission and relapse, have worse predicted survival, than those on their first treatment.[1,2] More than 1 in 5 patients will be treated with 4 or more treatment lines.[8] Patient data from the UK shows that by the time patients need a fourth treatment line, their follicular lymphoma is an endof-life disease and their **overall survival** is less than 1 year. Follicular lymphoma typically progresses in 4 months at this stage.[9] 



<!-- page 211 -->

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

The main test to diagnose lymphoma is a lymph node biopsy, where a doctor removes part or all of the swollen lymph node and sends it to a laboratory where a specialist will look at it under a microscope. The patient may also have some blood tests.[4,10] 

If a patient is diagnosed with follicular lymphoma, they may also need further tests including a PET-CT scan and a bone marrow test.[4,10] These tests help show how much the lymphoma has grown or developed, known as ‘staging’ the lymphoma. Knowing the ‘stage’ of the lymphoma helps the healthcare team know whether a patient should start treatment and decide which treatment is right for the patient. The doctor will also consider other factors, such as a patient’s age, general fitness and the results of their blood tests to determine the best treatment for each patient.[4,10] 

There are no additional tests required for epcoritamab beyond those currently in place to diagnose follicular lymphoma. 

## **2c) Current treatment options:** 

The purpose of this section is to set the scene on how the condition is currently managed: 

- What is the treatment pathway for this condition and where in this pathway the medicine is likely to be used? Please use diagrams to accompany text where possible. Please give emphasis to the specific setting and condition being considered by NICE in this review. For example, by referencing current treatment guidelines.  It may be relevant to show the treatments people may have before and after the treatment under consideration in this SIP. 

- Please also consider: 

   - if there are multiple treatment options, and data suggest that some are more commonly used than others in the setting and condition being considered in this SIP, please report these data. 

   - are there any drug–drug interactions and/or contraindications that commonly cause challenges for patient populations? If so, please explain what these are. 

Patients with follicular lymphoma often go through cycles of treatment, where they stop responding to one treatment and so are given a different treatment. Each one of these treatments is known as a treatment line, with the first treatment being the first **treatment line** , the second treatment being the second treatment line and so on. In follicular lymphoma, there are a limited number of treatments available on the NHS. Therefore, once a patient has stopped responding to their second or third treatment line, they often have to repeat, or “recycle” a treatment they have been treated with before, even though this treatment may be less effective the second time round or they have already failed to respond well to it the first time. 

Some patients with follicular lymphoma will be eligible for a stem cell transplant. This procedure replaces damaged or destroyed stem cells in the bone marrow with healthy ones and may cure a patient’s follicular lymphoma. Patients may receive a transplant as their second or third treatment line. However, this is an intensive treatment with more side effects than other treatment options, and so is only offered to those considered medically fit enough.[11] 

There is no defined treatment pathway for patients with follicular lymphoma, especially as patients need more treatment lines. If a patient fails to respond to their first treatment or stops 



<!-- page 212 -->

responding, there is no defined second, third or fourth treatment. Instead, a clinician will consider what the patient has been treated with before. If a patient still responds to rituximab, then NICE currently recommends rituximab-based treatments, either rituximab with chemotherapy or rituximab with lenalidomide. 

Rituximab is a targeted therapy, which binds to a specific protein on the surface of **white blood cells** called CD20. It is given as an infusion into a vein or an injection into the skin (after at least one infusion). The first infusion is given slowly to reduce any reactions to the drug, with later infusions given over shorter periods of time. Rituximab may be given with chemotherapy, known as **R-CHOP** (rituximab with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone), **R-CVP** (rituximab with cyclophosphamide, vincristine and prednisolone) or **R-Benda** (rituximab with bendamustine), depending on the chemotherapy drugs used. Rituximab may also be given with lenalidomide, another targeted cancer therapy which blocks the development of new blood vessels that cancer cells need to grow. 

If a patient was previously treated with rituximab and no longer responds to this treatment, then NICE recommends treating them with obinutuzumab with bendamustine. Obinutuzumab is another monoclonal **antibody** that targets the CD20 protein on the surface of white blood cells. Obinutuzumab is also given as an infusion into a vein. 

A diagram of the current treatment pathway for patients with follicular lymphoma is provided in Figure 1. 

**==> picture [438 x 286] intentionally omitted <==**

Figure 1: current treatment pathway for relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma 

All of the current treatments offered to patients require frequent hospital visits, with lengthy treatment administration and frequent monitoring.[9] This places a considerable burden on both patients and carers, and can provide challenges due to the time required for each treatment, 



<!-- page 213 -->

which may prevent both the patient and carer from working or pursuing their normal daily activities. 

There are currently no treatments specifically recommended for fourth line treatment of follicular lymphoma and patients often have very limited treatment options at this stage beyond reusing a treatment that they have already been treated with and stopped responding to. All current treatments work in a similar way by binding to the CD20 protein on the cancer cells or as a chemotherapy. As such, by the time patients need a fourth treatment line, their **overall survival** is less than 1 year in the UK.[9] Despite this, there have been limited innovations in recent years that have met the standard to be recommended by NICE in this patient population, with no positive recommendations made since 2020. Epcoritamab would meet a significant unmet need in this patient population, by offering a new treatment for patients that works in a different way to previous treatments. 

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

**Context:** 

- **Patient-based evidence (PBE)** is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. 

In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about **patient needs and disease experiences** . Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

This section summarises some of the key findings from published studies on the impact of follicular lymphoma on patients and their ability to lead their normal lives. A study where patients with follicular lymphoma were asked to complete a survey about their health, work life and normal activities, found that following their diagnosis, patients with follicular lymphoma are often unable to continue working.[6] Patients also reported that they could not do over half of their normal daily activities.[6] The patients reporting a poor overall health status and those receiving systemic therapy had the greatest reduction in ability to work and perform normal daily activities.[6] 

AbbVie recently carried out a study to understand the patient experience of living with follicular lymphoma.[12] This study involved asking 15 clinicians and 13 patients or carers from the UK, Germany and Japan about their experiences during 60 minutes interviews.[12] Patients with later stage follicular lymphoma, who were on their second or later lines of treatment, reported feeling disappointed, exhausted and dismayed that they needed to restart treatment. Patients with follicular lymphoma reported experiencing shock at their diagnosis and that they lived with high levels of anxiety over the fear of the disease returning.[12] 

The Lymphoma Coalition, a non-profit organisation comprised of a worldwide network of patient advocacy groups that supports those affected by lymphoma, conducted a web-based global survey asking patients with lymphomas or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), including those with follicular lymphoma, about their experiences.[13] When asked about their overall well-being, 35% of patients experienced problems with loss of strength, 32% experienced anxiety and/or depression and 22% experienced pain or discomfort over the past months. Patients also reported issues with walking, washing or dressing and fine motor skills, demonstrating the broad impact that lymphomas have on every aspect of a patient’s daily life. Over half of patients (54%) reported that they were unable to do their usual activities without difficulty.[13 ] 



<!-- page 214 -->

During the same survey, 46% of patients reported that they feared relapse or progression during the past 6 months. Similarly, 57% of caregivers, including friends and family members of patients with CLL, reported that they feared disease progression or relapse, with 51% reporting that they felt worried, and 49% reporting anxiety or nervousness. Almost half of caregivers also reported that they had to stop working, either temporarily, permanently or reduce their working hours since the patient was diagnosed.[13] 

The current rituximab-based treatments available to patients require lengthy infusions with regular visits to hospitals for these appointments, which may last for several hours.[11,14] Recent data have showed that patients may spend more than a month each year in inpatient hospital overnight stays by their fourth line of treatment for follicular lymphoma.[9] Administering treatment for follicular lymphoma presents a substantial burden for patients and caregivers and there is demand for new therapies that can be more easily administered. A study asking patients with follicular lymphoma being treated with rituximab whether they preferred to have their treatment via injection or infusion found that patients preferred an injection and that patients had greater satisfaction with the injected version of the treatment.[15] 

Patient-based evidence has shown that there is a high unmet need for a tolerable and effective alternative treatment that can help relieve patients and carers of the burden with current treatments in follicular lymphoma. 

## **SECTION 3: The treatment** 

## **3a) How does the new treatment work?** 

What are the important features of this treatment? 

Please outline as clearly as possible important details that you consider relevant to patients relating to the mechanism of action and how the medicine interacts with the body 

Where possible, please describe how you feel the medicine is innovative or novel, and how this might be important to patients and their communities. 

If there are relevant documents which have been produced to support your regulatory submission such as a summary of product characteristics or patient information leaflet, please provide a link to these. 

Epcoritamab is injected under the skin (subcutaneous) and is a type of protein called a T-cell specific **antibody** which travels in the blood and binds to specific proteins on the surface of other cells in the body. Specifically, epcoritamab is a bispecific antibody and so is specially designed to bind to two target proteins on the surface of other cells: CD20 on the surface of B-cells (the cancer cell), and CD3 on the surface of T-cells (a type of immune cell). 

When epcoritamab is attached to both CD3 and CD20, the immune cell and the cancer cell are brought closely together. Binding of epcoritamab to CD3 also causes the immune cell to make multiple copies of itself which then target and kill the cancer cell.

## **3c) Administration and dosing** 

How and where is the treatment given or taken? Please include the dose, how often the treatment should be given/taken, and how long the treatment should be given/taken for. 

How will this administration method or dosing potentially affect patients and caregivers? How does this differ to existing treatments? 

Epcoritamab is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous), by either a doctor or nurse, preferably in the lower part of the abdomen or thigh.[17] This means that each injection requires the patient to visit a hospital as an **outpatient** . However, the injection itself should be fairly quick, offering more convenience to patients than rituximab-based therapies, which require lengthy infusions. 

Treatment with epcoritamab is given in cycles, where each cycle lasts 28 days. In the first three cycles, epcoritamab is given once a week, which decreases to once every two weeks for cycles 4-9 and then only once every four weeks after that. The dose is increased from 0.16 mg in the first injection, to 0.8 mg in the second injection, 3 mg in the third injection, followed by 48 mg for every injection after that.[17] The dosing schedule is summarised in the table below (Table 1). 

Patients receive epcoritamab until disease progression or until they need to stop treatment due to the severity of any side effects.

In comparison, rituximab-based treatments, are given by an infusion into a vein, which is given slowly over a few hours for the first treatment to prevent side effects.[14] Patients treated with rituximab-containing treatments should have a blood test either the day of, or the day before treatment, and so may require two trips to a healthcare setting.[14] Some patients may receive rituximab as an injection into the skin, if they have already completed one cycle as an infusion.[14 ] 

Patients who are given rituximab with lenalidomide take a lenalidomide tablet every day for the first 21 days of a 28 day cycle, with a seven day rest period.[18] They also receive a rituximab infusion into a vein once per week during their first treatment cycle, and then once every four weeks for the next 2-5 cycles. Each infusion will require a visit to a clinical setting. 

Due to the infusions into veins required for rituximab-based treatments, these treatments require either a temporary tube to be put into a vein in the patients arm or hand (cannula) to be fitted for each treatment or a longer term tube to be inserted,[14] which often requires surgery and can be uncomfortable for patients. This is not needed for epcoritamab.

## **3d) Current clinical trials** 

Please provide a list of completed or ongoing clinical trials for the treatment. Please provide a brief top-level summary for each trial, such as title/name, location, population, patient group size, comparators, key inclusion and exclusion criteria and completion dates etc. Please provide references to further information about the trials or publications from the trials. 

The EPCORE NHL-1 (NCT03625037) Phase 1/2, multi-national trial provides evidence for how effective epcoritamab treatment is in patients with **relapsed** or **refractory** follicular lymphoma after two or more lines of treatment.[19] The trial also provides evidence on the safety profile of the treatment. Most of the patients in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial were from Europe and 9% were from the UK.[19] In this submission, we have focussed on the patients who had previously received 3 or more lines of therapy, as this is where there is the greatest clinical unmet need and where follicular lymphoma is an end-of-life disease. 

EPCORE NHL-1 was an open label trial, meaning that both patients and doctor knew which treatment they were receiving, and all patients were treated with epcoritamab. This study design is common in cancer trials where patients are at a late stage of their disease, as it may not be considered ethical to give patients an alternative treatment in this situation.[20] 

The EPCORE NHL-1 trial enrolled patients with several different types of B-cell lymphoma, including a follicular lymphoma cohort, which was split further into the total cohort and a cohort of patients who had failed 3 or more previous treatments and were on their fourth line treatment. There were 155 patients enrolled in the trial overall, of which, 81 patients were in the follicular lymphoma cohort who had received at least 3 or more lines of treatment previously.[19] 

To be enrolled in the follicular lymphoma cohort with at least 3 or more prior lines of treatment, patients had to be: 

- 18 years or over, 

- diagnosed with follicular lymphoma, 

- had relapsed, progressed or refractory disease after treatment with rituximab, and have been given all other standard treatments.[19] 

The trial started in 2018 and the most recent data are available from April 2024. The trial is still ongoing with the final data expected in 2029. 



<!-- page 218 -->

## **3e) Efficacy** 

Efficacy is the measure of how well a treatment works in treating a specific condition. 

In this section, please summarise all data that demonstrate how effective the treatment is compared with current treatments at treating the condition outlined in section 2a. Are any of the outcomes more important to patients than others and why? Are there any limitations to the data which may affect how to interpret the results? Please do not include academic or commercial in confidence information but where necessary reference the section of the company submission where this can be found. 

## **Clinical Trial Results:** 

The effectiveness of epcoritamab to treat follicular lymphoma in patients who have already received three or more previous lines of treatment was shown in the EPCORE NHL-1 clinical trial. During this trial, all patients were given epcoritamab and so there is no direct comparison of epcoritamab with other treatments. This study design is common in cancer trials due to ethical considerations, given that patients who have received multiple lines of prior therapy  have limited options and poor outcomes with currently available therapies.[20 ] 

During EPCORE NHL-1, most patient’s follicular lymphoma had either gone away or shrunk, known as the overall response rate, after epcoritamab treatment. Over half of patients had no signs of follicular lymphoma after tests and the disease had shrunk by over 30% in a further fifth of patients, meaning over 80% of patients had a clinically meaningful response to epcoritamab treatment.[19] Three years after starting epcoritamab treatment, over half of the patients in the trial were still alive and almost half of patients were still progression free. More details on the results of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial can be found in Section 2.8 of the Company Submission. 

## **Epcoritamab compared with other available therapies:** 

As the EPCORE NHL-1 trial only treated patients with epcoritamab, there is no direct evidence comparing how well epcoritamab works with current care in England. To assess this, a statistical analysis was conducted, where patients’ response and survival after epcoritamab treatment was compared with data from the Haematological Malignancy Research Network (HMRN) where patients were treated with a variety of chemotherapy-based treatments. The analysis was conducted according to NICE guidelines. 

The HMRN is a network established in 2004 by researchers and NHS clinicians working across 14 hospitals in the North of England. The dataset from HMRN provides a UK-specific dataset regarding health outcomes for patients with blood cancers, including follicular lymphoma. 

The results of this analysis demonstrated that patients treated with epcoritamab had significantly better rates for complete response (disappearance of all signs of cancer) and overall response (patients whose cancer has shrunk or disappeared after treatment), than patients who received existing treatments available on the National Health Service (NHS) in the HMRN data set. The analysis also predicted that patients treated with epcoritamab had significantly better **overall survival** and **progression-free survival** (the time between treatment and the cancer starting to grow again), than those treated with current treatments in the HMRN data set. 



<!-- page 219 -->

## **3f) Quality of life impact of the medicine and patient preference information** 

What is the clinical evidence for a potential impact of this medicine on the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers? What quality of life instrument was used? If the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D) was used does it sufficiently capture quality of life for this condition? Are there other disease specific quality of life measures that should also be considered as supplementary information? 

Please outline in plain language any quality of life related data such as **patient reported outcomes (PROs).** Please include any **patient preference information (PPI)** relating to the drug profile, for instance research to understand willingness to accept the risk of side effects given the added benefit of treatment. Please include all references as required. 

The EPCORE NHL-1 clinical trial recorded data on how epcoritamab treatment impacts a patient’s quality of life with follicular lymphoma. It did this by using two questionnaires. 

- The FACT-LymS questionnaire is a tool designed to assess the health-related quality of life in patients with lymphoma, by evaluating physical, emotional, and social aspects affected by the disease and treatment. 

- The EQ-5D-3L is a standardised instrument that is also used to measure health-related quality of life. It features three levels of severity across five areas of health and living: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. 

During the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, quality of life assessed by the FACT-LymS questionnaire was shown to be stable after epcoritamab treatment. Quality of life, assessed by the EQ-5D-3L questionnaire, was slightly improved with epcoritamab treatment. 

## **3g) Safety of the medicine and side effects** 

When NICE appraises a treatment, it will pay close attention to the balance of the benefits of the treatment in relation to its potential risks and any side effects. Therefore, please outline the main side effects (as opposed to a complete list) of this treatment and include details of a benefit/risk assessment where possible. This will support patient reviewers to consider the potential overall benefits and side effects that the medicine can offer. 

Based on available data, please outline the most common side effects, how frequently they happen compared with standard treatment, how they could potentially be managed and how many people had treatment adjustments or stopped treatment. Where it will add value or context for patient readers, please include references to the Summary of Product Characteristics from regulatory agencies etc. 

The EPCORE NHL-1 clinical trial recorded safety events, including any side effects of the treatment or any unrelated patient sickness. 

The most common safety event was cytokine release syndrome,[19] which is when the immune system reacts too aggressively, resulting in patients developing a fever, nausea, fatigue and body aches. It is a common response to many monoclonal **antibody** or immunotherapy treatments. Prompt treatment is required to manage symptoms, however, as this is a common side effect of antibody therapy, clinicians are becoming more familiar with monitoring for and treating this response to treatment. In practice, dosing of epcoritamab has been designed to reduce the risk of cytokine release syndrome (with the introduction of an additional small dose of epcoritamab shortly after initiating treatment). 

After this the most common safety events in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial were COVID-19, injection site reactions, fatigue, diarrhoea, fever, cough and low **white blood cell** count. Of these, only cytokine release syndrome and injection site reactions were deemed to be related directly to epcoritamab treatment.[19]

## **3h) Summary of key benefits of treatment for patients** 

Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key benefits of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. 

- Please include benefits related to the mode of action, effectiveness, safety and mode of administration 

## **There is a lack of effective treatment options in relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma; after three prior lines, patients will typically be offered another intensive chemotherapy-based regimen:** 

Currently there are very limited treatment options in patients with follicular lymphoma who have been treated with 3 or more previous treatments and still have active disease. Available treatment options mostly include cycling through treatments that have already previously been used in earlier lines of therapy and in many cases failed to give a long-term response. Epcoritamab would offer these patients a new treatment option at this late stage of the treatment pathway. As epcoritamab works in a different way to the treatments offered earlier after diagnosis, this provides greater treatment choice and a new way to treat the disease. 

Patients whose disease has stopped responding to treatments report greater levels of anxiety and depression compared with those whose disease is responding to treatment.[5] Therefore, epcoritamab should help relieve some of this anxiety by offering a new treatment option to those whose disease has stopped responding to prior treatments. 

## **Epcoritamab is an effective treatment in follicular lymphoma, extending life expectancy compared with existing UK treatments:** 

During the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, over half of the patients treated with epcoritamab were still alive after almost 3 years. During this time, most of the patients saw a response in their disease, with over half of patients demonstrating no signs of follicular lymphoma after tests and 20% demonstrating that the extent of their disease had decreased by 30%.[19 ] 

A statistical analysis comparing epcoritamab treatment from the EPCORE NHL-1 trial with current NHS treatment options showed that patients treated with epcoritamab had significantly better rates for complete response (disappearance of all signs of cancer) and overall response (patients whose cancer has shrunk or disappeared after treatment), than patients who received current NHS treatment options in the HMRN data set. The analysis also predicted that patients treated with epcoritamab had significantly extended patient life expectancy compared with currently available treatments. The analysis showed that patients treated with epcoritamab were 75% less likely to die than those treated with current options. 

Treatment with epcoritamab during the EPCORE NHL-1 trial was shown to be tolerable with the most common side effects of the treatment being cytokine release syndrome and injection site reactions. Cytokine release syndrome is a common response to this type of cancer treatment that is monitored for and can be treated with established guidelines.[19] 

## **Epcoritamab is a subcutaneous treatment option which can provide a convenient alternative to current intravenous therapies:** 

Epcoritamab is the first and only subcutaneous treatment available for this patient group. This subcutaneous administration enables fast administration across different practice settings when compared with currently available intravenous therapies. Current intravenous therapies are given as an infusion and may require hospital visits on multiple days for additional monitoring. Patients may spend more than a month each year in overnight inpatient hospital stays.[9] Epcoritamab 



<!-- page 221 -->

offers more convenience to both patients and carers as less time is required for each appointment, and therefore, this should reduce any time off from paid work or from societal commitments. These shorter appointment times will also improve the capacity of the healthcare system, allowing clinicians to increase the number of patients they see every day. 

## **3i) Summary of key disadvantages of treatment for patients** 

## Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key disadvantages of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. Which disadvantages are most important to patients and carers? 

- Please include disadvantages related to the mode of action, effectiveness, side effects and mode of administration 

- What is the impact of any disadvantages highlighted compared with current treatments 

Epcoritamab is given as an injection under the skin, which must be given by a healthcare professional in a clinical setting, which requires the patient and their carer to visit this setting once every week for the three cycles, decreasing to once every two weeks and then once every month.[17] However, this is more convenient than the current treatments used to treat late-stage follicular lymphoma, which are given as an infusion which also require a visit to a healthcare setting and take a long time to administer.[14,18] 

The main side effects of epcoritamab treatment are cytokine release syndrome and injection site reactions.[19] More than half of patients reported having cytokine release syndrome after starting epcoritamab treatment, which may have resulted in a fever, nausea, fatigue and body aches. However, all of these cases were low-grade (Grade 2 or below), and so not considered severe, and could be easily managed. These side effects are a common response to this type of cancer treatment that is monitored for and can be treated with established guidelines. 

During the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, a group of patients were treated  with three lower doses of epcoritamab before receiving the full dose, which is the same dosing schdule as patients would receive if epcoritamab were approved. When patients were treated with these earlier doses fewer patients experienced cytokine release syndrome and these were mostly grade 1 and considered mild. The most common safety events were COVID-19, injection site reactions, fatigue, diarrhoea, fever, cough and low **white blood cell** count. Of these, only cytokine release syndrome and the injection site reactions were deemed to be related directly to epcoritamab treatment.[19]
