## **3i) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

## **The economic model and how does it reflect follicular lymphoma?** 

An economic model has been used to assess the value of epcoritamab for patients with follicular lymphoma to the NHS. The economic model estimates long-term clinical and economic cost benefits ( **cost effectiveness** ) of epcoritamab compared with currently available treatments for patients with follicular lymphoma who have received three or more lines of therapy. 

The model considers three patient groups: 

- patients who are progression-free, including patients who are alive and whose disease has not progressed, 

- patients with progressed disease, who are alive and whose disease has progressed 

- patients who have died from either follicular lymphoma or other causes. 

The movement of patients between these groups reflects a patient’s real-world experience as their cancer progresses, or is delayed from progressing as a result of an effective treatment. Movement between the groups is modelled using probabilities calculated using survival and progression data from the EPCORE NHL-1 trial and the HMRN data set, which shows the effect of currently available treatments used in the NHS. 

All patients enter the model in the progression-free group and stay there until they progress or die. While in each group, costs are applied to each patient for the treatment, treatment administration and monitoring of the patient for their follicular lymphoma, as well as costs of any side effects from their treatment or their disease. The model considers patients over their full lifetime. 



<!-- page 223 -->

**==> picture [266 x 150] intentionally omitted <==**

**Figure 1: Overview of model structure used to assess the cost-effectiveness of epcoritamab in patients with follicular lymphoma who have received three or more previous treatments** 

## **How much does epcoritamab extend life?** 

As clinical trials monitor patients over a short period of time, but the effect of cancer and the potential benefits of treatment can affect patients for much longer periods, the economic model requires long-term predictions based on survival outcomes observed in the trial. The need to predict beyond the observation period of a clinical trial is common in appraisals of cancer therapies and allows the long-term effects of treatment with epcoritamab to be estimated over the remainder of a patient’s life. In the economic model for this appraisal, survival outcomes were derived from the EPCORE NHL-1 trial and HMRN data set and showed a significant improvement in life expectancy for epcoritamab compared with current treatments in England. Curves for survival outcomes were extrapolated using guidance from NICE. 

## **How much does epcoritamab improve quality of life?** 

The impact that treatment with epcoritamab has on patients’ quality of life, in combination with how much longer they live after receiving treatment, is captured as part of a metric called **qualityadjusted life years (QALYs)** , where one QALY reflects one year in perfect health. **QALYs** are a health outcome measure that consider both the length and the quality of life provided by a treatment. 

Data related to quality of life was also collected in EPCORE NHL-1 using the EQ-5D-3L questionnaire filled out by patients in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial. Overall, **QALYs** improved in people who received epcoritamab compared with people who received chemoimmunotherapy, reflecting a comparative improvement to patient’s length of life and quality of life after receiving treatment. 

## **How does the model estimate the cost of epcoritamab and its comparators?** 

The economic model estimates the costs associated with medication, including epcoritamab and current care in England and how these treatments are administered. For example, costs are applied for each infusion or injection based on published NHS costs, which account for the nurse’s time. In addition, costs associated with how follicular lymphoma is managed and monitored, which depends on response to treatment and any side effects or other health events, which are dependent of disease progression are included in the model. 



<!-- page 224 -->

## **Is there any uncertainty in the model?** 

During the development of an economic model, companies are required to make assumptions where there is a lack of available evidence. For this model, there was little published literature to inform some of the assumptions, especially data from clinical trials. Instead, some of the assumptions were informed by evidence from real-world clinical practice, which was collected with less well-controlled conditions. Likewise, as patients only received epcoritamab in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial, there was no direct comparison to another comparator, and so the economic model relies on the results of the “unanchored” comparison. These assumptions were tested through sensitivity analyses, where alternate assumptions or values were used in the economic model to determine the impact on the economic results. 

The results of the sensitivity analysis were comparable to the base-case analysis, showing that the economic analysis is robust. 

## **Are there any additional factors to consider?** 

The current treatments that patients receive after their third line of therapy are associated with intense mental and physical side effects. Some of these side effects, such as the increased risk of heart disease after repeated **R-CHOP** treatment,[21] place a considerable physical burden on the patients and are difficult for the NHS to treat. These side effects were not fully considered in the economic modelling during this submission due to a lack of treatment-specific data. The introduction of epcoritamab to this treatment pathway should help reduce the mental and emotional burden to patients compared with re-treatment with a therapy a patient may have already failed to respond to. 

It is also difficult to capture in the model the quality of life impact that a treatment given by an injection has compared with a treatment given by infusion. This is because it is hard to quantify how these treatments impact a patient’s quality of life and so the convenience that epcoritamab offers patients compared with current treatments that are given by an infusion, are not included in the model. Likewise, it is difficult to quantify any benefits to a patient or a carer’s mental health due to the availability of another treatment at a stage when current treatment options are limited to often recycling a treatment the patient has previously failed to maintain a response to. Therefore, the model does not consider the emotional benefit of new treatments becoming available. 

The economic modelling conducted during this submission did not consider the burden of caring for a friend or family member with follicular lymphoma on caregivers, as this is not considered by NICE in their decision making. These caregivers face considerable emotional, practical and financial challenges. Carers often provide transport to-and-from hospital appointments and treatment appointments, which can require time off work and social productivity. Carers also provide emotional support while trying to deal with the emotions surrounding a loved one being seriously ill. Improved response rates and **progression-free survival** in patients treated with epcoritamab could significantly reduce the burden on caregivers, as would the knowledge that alternative treatment options are available to patients who fail to respond to the early treatment lines.

## **3j) Innovation** 

NICE considers how innovative a new treatment is when making its recommendations. If the company considers the new treatment to be innovative please explain how it represents a ‘step change’ in treatment and/ or effectiveness compared with current treatments. Are there any QALY benefits that have not been captured in the economic model that also need to be considered (see section 3f) 

## **Epcoritamab would represent an important advancement in the treatment of follicular lymphoma** 

Currently, there is no standard treatment for patients with follicular lymphoma who have failed to maintain a long-term response after three or more previous treatments. These patients instead cycle through previous treatments, which they may have already stopped responding to, resulting in life expectancy in these patients being less than 1 year.[9] Current treatment options for patients involve lengthy infusions given through invasive ports or cannula, and the time required for each administration places a huge burden on patients and carers. 

Introducing epcoritamab would offer these patients a new treatment option, which works in a different way to the treatments that these patients have previously failed to respond to and so may offer increased hope and be more tolerable, while also providing improved survival rates.

However, patients who have stopped responding to multiple previous therapies are likelier to receive experimental treatments within clinical trials than patients in earlier lines. As access to clinical trials might be more restricted in rural or deprived areas, the patient population in this appraisal would be likely to benefit from access to an efficacious therapy as part of routine commissioning.

## **4b) Glossary of terms** 

**Antibody** : a protein in the blood that helps the body’s defences by identifying and attaching specific foreign substances including germs **Cost-effectiveness:** how effective a drug is in relation to its cost **Follicular lymphoma** : a form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that forms in the lymph nodes, bone marrow and other organs. It is considered an incurable, chronic, life-limiting illness. **Marketing authorisation:** a license that enables a drug to be sold; it is only granted after assessing and reviewing all of the evidence for that drug **Outpatient:** a hospital appointment that does not require an overnight stay **Overall survival** : the length of time from starting treatment that a patient is still alive **Progression-free survival:** the time between treatment and the cancer starting to grow again **Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs):** a unit to measure both the quality of life lived after receiving a treatment and how much additional life that treatment might result in **R-Benda:** a chemotherapy regimen containing both bendamustine and rituximab given by infusions every 28 days **R-CHOP:** a chemotherapy regimen containing rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone **R-CVP:** a chemotherapy regimen containing rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine and prednisolone **Refractory** : when a disease has stopped responding to treatment **Relapsed** : when a disease has become worse again after a period of improvement **Remission** : when the symptoms of a disease have become less severe and are not affecting the patient **White blood cells** : cells in the immune system that protect the body from infectious diseases and foreign invaders.

## **Section A: Clarification on effectiveness data** 

A1. Can the company provide real-world evidence to support the claim that the greatest unmet need lies in 4L+ FL patients? 

In the Company Submission, AbbVie referred to clinical feedback that highlighted the greatest unmet need is among patients with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma (FL) after three or more lines of systemic therapy (4L+). This is due to the poor survival outcomes at this stage of the disease, limited treatment options and reliance on clinical trials, and increased time spent in inpatient hospital settings at 4L+ FL. 

Clinical feedback reflected outcomes seen in available UK real-world evidence (RWE) in 4L+ FL. The Haematological Malignancy Research Network (HMRN) dataset has shown that 4L+ FL is an end-of-life disease; most patients do not survive longer than a year (median ***********).[1] This is aligned with expectations from consultant haematologists in England – i.e. survival in practice is typically less than one year in the 4L+ setting. 

In interviews with clinical experts, it had been noted that there are limited treatment options routinely available for patients with 4L+ FL in the UK. This opinion had also been noted by the professional groups in the appraisal of axicabtagene-ciloleucel (TA894).[2] By the time patients initiate their fourth line of therapy, they have typically exhausted the treatment options available to them. Some younger and fitter patients may be available for enrolment in a clinical trial, though there exists barriers to access for patients who live in rural or deprived areas and who may not be able to access experimental treatments. As such, patients with 4L+ FL are more likely to benefit from access to an efficacious therapy as part of routine commissioning. 

Finally, at this stage of their FL, patients spend a large proportion of their time in the inpatient setting. Data from the HMRN registry showed that patients with 4L+ FL spend around ******************** in inpatient hospital overnight stays due to treatment administration, monitoring and disease. Over the course of a year, this can add up to more than ************ spent in hospital with overnight stays.[1] Indeed, the burden with frequent inpatient visits on caregivers has been noted by Lymphoma Action in a previous appraisal in 4L+ FL:[2] 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 232 -->

“ _Carers often provide transport to-and-from hospital appointments and treatment sessions, requiring time off work... Most also take on more chores and household tasks. Over 3 in 4 caregivers report feeling anxious and physically and emotionally worn out. Some carers and family members report needing counselling_ .” 

Given that the 4L+ FL patient population is also inclusive of patients with four or more lines of prior therapy, it stands to reason that the greatest unmet need lies within this group of patients. 

A2. Why was the 4L+ patient population chosen as the focus when the NICE final scope allows for 3L+? Please provide details of the expertise of the clinicians used to justify the 4L+ unmet need. 

As noted in response to Question A1, the 4L+ patient population was chosen as the focus of the NICE submission as it is the population with the greatest unmet need. The unmet need in 4L+ FL is substantial and has been validated by multiple consultant haematologists who are active in academic research and situated in NHS sites across the UK. Of the consultant haematologists interviewed, all five had previous experience treating 4L+ FL and all had observed the outcomes seen in the HMRN UK real-world evidence reflected in their practice; i.e. that survival is typically less than a year (****  months).[1] 

Specifically, during UK clinical expert interviews conducted by AbbVie, NHS consultant haematologists noted that there is no standard of care in 4L+ FL and there are limited treatment options due to relapse and increasing refractoriness to conventional treatment. Similar observations had also been made by the professional groups in the appraisal of TA894.[2] Patients are often rechallenged with previously administered treatments. Clinical experts noted that patients rechallenged with a prior treatment regimen often experience poor outcomes due to acquired treatment resistance. This is particularly the case if the previous therapy resulted in a non-durable remission. Given the current lack of treatment options at 4L+, clinical trials are also considered for younger and fitter patients at this stage. Accordingly, UK experts stressed the desperate need for new and innovative therapies that are routinely commissioned.

Specifically, the dosing regimen consisted of an initial priming

dose of 0.16 mg (C1D1) followed by a first intermediate dose of 0.8 mg (C1D8) and a second intermediate dose of 3 mg (C1D15), and a full dose of 48 mg on C1D22. The cohort initially consisted of two arms, Arm A and Arm B, *************** whereby 6 patients had been recruited into each arm. On the , preliminary analysis revealed a numerically lower CRS rate in Arm A as compared to Arm B, which was supported by modelling. In addition, the simpler instructions for the 3 mg dose preparation as compared to the 6 mg dose preparation, which requires the use of two 4 mg/0.8 mL vials, was taken into consideration, and further enrolment in Arm A was then prioritised in the FL optimisation cohort.

The EPCORE NHL-1 trial was conducted in three parts: a dose escalation part, an expansion part and an optimisation part. Table 1 below (adapted from Table 9 of the Company Submission) summarises the objectives of the various phases of the study. 

**Table 1: A summary of the objectives for the phases of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial**

|---|---|---|---|

DLBCL, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; FL, follicular lymphoma; MCL, mantle cell lymphoma; MTD, maximum tolerated dose; RP2D, recommended phase 2 dose. 

The purpose of the Phase 1 dose escalation part of EPCORE NHL-1 was to establish the maximum tolerated dose of epcoritamab and the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of epcoritamab, while the purpose of the Phase 2 expansion part was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of epcoritamab at the RP2D. Therefore, in the Phase 2 expansion part of EPCORE NHL-1, patients received the RP2D determined by the dose Phase 1 escalation part, i.e. 48 mg epcoritamab was administered on C1D15/C1D22.

As detailed in the EU assessment report and Section 3.2.3.1 of the Company Submission, pharmacokinetic outcomes are very similar between patients who received the three step-up dose regimen and patients who received the two step-up dose regimen in EPCORE NHL-1.[3] 

As expected, data showed transiently lower trough concentrations after the second intermediate dose in subjects with FL who received the 3-step SUD regimen compared to those after the first full 48 mg dose in subjects with FL who received the 2-step SUD regimen. A15. CS Table 12 reports rates discontinuing treatment for clinical progression, please provide the definition of clinical progression used. 

In FL, clinical progression is conventionally defined using the Lugano and LYRIC response criteria. Table 12 of the Company Submission records * patients (***%) as having ‘Clinical Progression’ as the primary reason for study treatment discontinuation. As per protocol and in the majority of cases, the expected pattern of progression was recorded based on the Lugano and LYRIC response criteria. However, in rare cases, the determination of clinical progression was based on symptomatic deterioration (i.e. without documented progression through the use of objective criteria). It is not expected that patients recorded as having clinical progression by symptomatic deterioration will meaningfully differ from progression recorded by Lugano and LYRIC criteria.

## **A18. Priority Question: Please provide details of how decisions over deaths attributable to Covid-19 were made, and who made the decisions, CS Section 2.6.2.1** 

The significant increase of COVID-19 infections and hospitalisations during late 2021 and 2022 coincided with the active treatment period of the EPCORE-NHL1 trial. As such, the number of COVID-19 related deaths does not accurately represent the current clinical setting in the UK. While the company acknowledges that there is no perfect method for capturing COVID-related deaths, given both the unprecedented nature of the pandemic and limitations resulting from a global lack of standardisation in diagnostic criteria, capacity and the presence of comorbid conditions, a conscientious approach to identifying COVID-19 related deaths was taken in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial. COVID-19 deaths were assigned as per the protocol outlined in the main trial publication[4] , namely, sensitivity analyses were conducted using a stringent criteria with evaluations and adjudications performed by physicians. 

Deaths from clinically compatible illness in a probable or confirmed COVID-19 case were identified using the following criteria: 

- Any death within the standardised MedDRA query of COVID-19 

- Any death related to treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) within system organ classes of respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorders 

- Any death due to ‘other’ with COVID-19 mentioned in free text as a reason for death 

These criteria have been validated by clinical experts in the UK who noted the challenges associated with defining deaths due to COVID-19 more broadly. Cases identified utilising the search strategy outlined above were reviewed for clinical plausibility by the sponsor medical reviewer. Despite the challenges associated with defining COVID-19 related deaths, the approach taken in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial is pragmatic and reflects the interpretation of UK clinical experts. 

Clarification questions

A19. CS Table 18 shows that a proportion of participants were censored for receiving ‘new anti-lymphoma’ therapies. Please explain how these fit in with the data presented in CS Table 22. 

Table 18 in the Company Submission contains an overview of the Duration of Response (DoR) with epcoritamab in 4L+ FL. DoR has previously been defined as the time from onset of response to progression or death due to any reason.[5] Patients initiating a new anti-lymphoma therapy (NALT) after epcoritamab treatment had been censored in assessments of DoR at the last adequate follow-up. Removing this censoring rule would create challenges interpreting whether DoR outcomes after discontinuation can be attributed to epcoritamab or the NALT. Additionally, such an approach risks overestimating outcomes for epcoritamab and creates bias. As such, patients had been censored at the last adequate assessment prior to the start of NALT. 

A20. Please consider the same query above (A19) for those receiving new antilymphoma therapies in CS Tables 19 and 20. 

Tables 19 and 20 in the Company Submission contain overviews of the Duration of Complete Response (DoCR) and PFS, respectively. As per the response to Question A19, outcomes for DoCR and PFS are at risk of bias (favouring epcoritamab) if patients beginning NALT are not censored. As such, a similar censoring rule for DoCR and PFS had been implemented to censor patients at the last adequate assessment prior to the start of NALT.

## _Sensitivity Analysis 1 – ECOG and FLIPI_ 

In the first sensitivity analysis, AbbVie selected variables for matching which aligned with the company base case but also explored the impact of matching for ECOG performance status 0 (i.e. patients with better health status) and FLIPI score 3,4,5 (i.e. patients with worse health status). As described in the Company Submission, both of these factors were noted by clinicians as being important prognostic indicators in FL, but reporting limitations in HMRN meant that these variables were only recorded at diagnosis, rather than at the start of initiating 4L+ treatment. 

After match-adjusting the EPCORE population to HMRN, the effective sample size for epcoritamab patients is 28 (Table 4).

Therefore, AbbVie maintain that the variables selected and adjusted in its base case analysis are conservative and most appropriate.

A26. Could the company clarify whether an STC was attempted and found infeasible, or ruled out a priori? If attempted and found infeasible, was any exploratory STC performed with a reduced set of prognostic variables to assess feasibility? 

As outlined in the Company Submission, simulated treatment comparison (STC)based parametric or semiparametric regression analyses rely on the number of events (not the number of patients) to determine the degrees of freedom; the lower the number of events, the lower the number of predictors that can be included in the 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 258 -->

model. As such, an STC would not have been appropriate in this submission due to the small number of events recorded in the EPCORE NHL-1 study, which in turn would reduce the number of predictors that could be included in the model. In addition, MAICs are the preferred method of analysis when analysing time-to-event data for a single target comparator (or single RWE database) across multiple treatment outcomes, whereas STCs are more appropriate for analyses against multiple comparators.[11] 

Further, conducting an STC on time-to-event outcomes requires a parametric distribution (e.g. exponential, Weibull, etc.) of the best fit to be specified for the outcome, and an assessment performed regarding whether the same distribution is applicable to both arms of the analysis.[12] The choice of the parametric distribution in an STC is a critical assumption, and misspecification of the parametric distribution can lead to biased results. The choice of the parametric curve for the STC would introduce another layer of uncertainty next to the additional aspects of a correct specification of the outcome model and the assumption that the relationship between baseline covariates and the outcome is the same in both studies. 

MAICs have routinely been presented to and accepted by NICE as valid methodology across various appraisals of lymphoma therapies. The MAIC in this submission was conducted utilising learnings from previous NICE TAs: TA627, TA892 and TA894. 

Based on the rationale above, it was determined that a STC would not be an appropriate method for comparing epcoritamab with current 4L+ care and AbbVie did not perform such an analysis. 

## **Survival Analysis** 

A27. Did the company explore flexible models such as piecewise or splines? If so, why were they not presented in the submission? 

AbbVie did not consider flexible approaches to survival analyses to be appropriate for modelling efficacy outcomes in patients with 4L+ R/R FL who received epcoritamab. AbbVie notes that the standard parametric methods applied within the submission produce good visual and statistical fit to the observed data and long-term outcomes that are aligned with survival estimates aligned with clinical expectations, 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 259 -->

as per our consultation with UK clinical experts experienced in treating patients with 4L+ FL; therefore, the use of more complex statistical models such as splines would add little additional value beyond the standard parametric models. 

Implementing semi-parametric approaches (e.g. piecewise or spline-based models) to survival analysis involves subjective choices around the number and placement of cutpoints or knots, as well as the distribution applied to each segment. Further, these approaches to survival modelling risk overfitting to observed data and inherently assume that that the data within each segment are sufficient for robust survival analysis. This assumption is likely to be particularly inappropriate in the tail of the Kaplan-Meier curve where fewer patients are at risk, causing individual events to become disproportionately impactful. As the outputs of flexible survival analyses can be sensitive to these assumptions and arbitrary decisions, implementing flexible survival modelling may lead to additional and unnecessary uncertainty, resulting in outputs that are clinically implausible and lack statistical robustness. 

Overall, while AbbVie acknowledges the value of exploring more flexible approaches to survival analysis in cases where standard models do not fit the observed data well, this is not the case for epcoritamab. As described in Section 3.3.2 of the Company Submission, AbbVie made conscientious efforts to limit the uncertainty associated with the survival analyses by validating long-term estimates with clinicians experienced in treating patients with 4L+ FL; therefore, the company did not feel it was necessary to perform these analyses.

A29. Please fit survival models onto the HMRN curves, and then apply the HRs from the MAIC on those curves to estimate the efficacy of epcoritamab **.** AbbVie have not provided this analysis as it would add additional, unnecessary uncertainty to the modelling. There are three primary reasons for this: 

1. Only summary data is available from HMRN as opposed to individual patient data (IPD) being available from EPCORE NHL-1. As such, fitting survival models to the epcoritamab data where IPD were available and using the HRs from the MAIC to estimate outcomes for HMRN was deemed more appropriate, and allows for more accurate and precise estimation of survival. 

2. The purpose of the MAIC is to align study populations and to estimate relative efficacy in these comparable populations. By then applying the hazard ratio to the epcoritamab survival curves means estimating HMRN efficacy in an EPCORE-NHL 1 population. This allows us to maintain consistency in the reference population for estimation of survival and other model inputs such as utilities, which are taken from EPCORE NHL-1. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 261 -->

3. The sample size in the HMRN dataset (******) is lower than the sample size from EPCORE NHL-1 (N = 81); therefore, it would be inappropriate to use the HMRN curves to fit survival models as this approach would likely lead to imprecise estimates of the efficacy of epcoritamab which would be unsuitable for decision making. 

Producing the analyses in this way is aligned with precedent from previous NICE appraisals and means we can both estimate a relative effect in a comparable population whilst allowing us to retain the benefit of extrapolating from more robust IPD in a reference population that is aligned with other relevant model inputs. Extrapolating from HMRN and applying the inverse HR to generate outcomes from epcoritamab would disregard the availability and use of IPD and introduce unnecessary imprecision and uncertainty into the extrapolations. 

## **A30. Priority Question: Why were the unadjusted epcoritamab curves used for survival models when the HRs applied are from the comparison of the MAICadjusted epcoritamab data versus HMRN?** 

The rationale here is similar to the rationale described in our response to A29 in that analyses have been conducted with the goal of minimising uncertainty and preserving consistency across the reference population used in the submission. 

1. We have applied the HRs to the unadjusted epcoritamab survival data because the adjusted epcoritamab survival data produced as an output of the MAIC is inherently more uncertain given the impact of reduced effective sample size as a consequence of the matching. 

2. To ensure that the estimation of survival considers an EPCORE NHL-1 reference population and to preserve alignment with other important model inputs it was deemed appropriate to apply the hazard ratios to the unadjusted data. 

We acknowledge that a limitation of the MAIC is that it requires adjustment of the EPCORE NHL-1 population to a HMRN population before estimating relative effects. However, there is no reason to believe that this relative effect would not then hold in an EPCORE NHL-1 population and therefore, for the aforementioned reasons it was deemed appropriate to apply the hazard ratios to the unadjusted epcoritamab data. B7 **.** Can the company confirm that the costs of disease progression in the model were applied only to the patients that progressed to the PD state **.** 

AbbVie can confirm that the costs of disease progression were only applied to patients who progressed to the PD state. The calculations for this are in two separate sheets in the model. Firstly, in the Costs & Effects total sheet, cells P7 and P8 calculate the undiscounted costs for both the intervention and the comparator, whilst cells P14 and P15 calculate the discounted costs. The formula in cells P14 and P15 finds the difference between the number of patients with progressed disease in the current cycle and those in the previous cycle. To account for mortality, it then adds the change in deaths between the two cycles. The change in deaths is 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 268 -->

added because any patient who progresses to PD and then dies in the same cycle would never contribute to a net rise in the PD count. By adding deaths back in, it captures those who transition from PD to death and avoids underestimating how many actually entered the PD state. If applicable, these formulas are then multiplied by the discount factor. 

In order to ensure that this calculation is correct. A second calculation is added to the Trace_EPCO sheet, where in column AP this calculation is replicated for every cycle and then summed in cells AP14 and AP15. The totals in these cells are identical to those found in the Costs & Effects total sheet, providing reassurance that the calculations have been completed correctly.

C9. For the SLRs reported in Appendices B, E, F and G, please describe how duplicates were removed from the search results, both across different search updates and between different databases within the same search update or iteration. Searches conducted in ProQuest across the EconLit, Embase and MEDLINE databases were run in parallel. ProQuest automatically removes duplicates between these databases from the exported search results. All exported references from ProQuest were imported into EndNote databases for each SLR. For the clinical SLR, search results from the Cochrane databases were downloaded and combined into the EndNote database. A further deduplication step was then performed within the EndNote database using the find duplicates feature. 

Duplicates across updates were identified by comparing the list of included publications after screening with those from the previous iterations. Any duplicates at this stage were flagged and excluded for the reason of duplicate. 

C10. Please explain how it is possible to have -1 results in Appendix F.1.5, Table 40, line S65, and then 54 results when this is limited by publication date in line S66. This “-1” value is due to an artifact in the ProQuest search platform. It is a known issue that occurs when the results of the individual search line have not had time to load. ProQuest will often display the results of the last search line (in this case line 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 275 -->

S66) before the earlier search lines. When the search strategy is saved as an RTF file directly from ProQuest, any line that has not had time to load displays as “-1”. In this instance, it was an oversight as the RTF file was downloaded too early and hence this “-1” result displayed for line S65. Please note that this has no impact on the results of the final search line S66.

## **Living with the condition** 

||**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition?**<br>**What do carers**<br>**experience when caring**<br>**for someone with the**<br>**condition?**|Living with FL is often described by patients as living with a constant sense of uncertainty and<br>unpredictability. Our patient insights have shown a wide range of experiences, from those on watch and<br>wait with minimal symptoms to others undergoing their sixth line of treatment. The most common fear is<br>that FL will return or transform into a more aggressive form. Fewer patients worry about rapid<br>progression or treatment side effects, but many express concern about running out of treatment options<br>and affording care.<br>Our surveys have revealed that nearly half of patients find coping with uncertainty about the future to<br>be the hardest challenge. Other major difficulties include balancing emotional wellbeing with physical<br>symptoms, and feeling isolated or misunderstood. Constant anxiety, worrying that every new symptom<br>is FL-related, is a common theme.<br>Carers often share these emotional burdens. We hear that carers play a crucial role in daily life and<br>treatment, and they too struggle with anxiety, helplessness, and the need for their own support.|

|**7. What do patients or**<br>**carers think of current**<br>**treatments and care**<br>**available on the NHS?**|The current treatments available for R/R FL patients are very limited, unless they transform to DLBCL,<br>where CAR-T is already approved. |---|---|
|**8. Is there an unmet need**<br>**for patients with this**<br>**condition?**|There is a clear unmet need for patients living with FL, particularly around access to newer, better-<br>tolerated treatments, with the potential for longer remission and ultimately cure.<br>Quality of life is a central priority for FL patients, alongside treatment effectiveness. Our patient insights<br>show that treatment preferences are highly individual; shaped by the time of diagnosis, life stage, and<br>personal experience. Many express a desire to avoid chemotherapy if possible, favouring<br>immunotherapy or targeted treatments. However, a pragmatic approach is also important to them,<br>prioritising efficacy and tolerability over treatment type alone.<br>Information gaps remain a significant unmet need. In our Immunotherapy survey, patients rated their<br>understanding of bispecific antibodies (and CAR-T) at just 2.16 out of 5. This knowledge gap was<br>consistent across the top five countries of residence, including the UK. Patients told us the most<br>valuable information relates to risks, side effects, effectiveness, and the treatment journey.<br>Access is another major concern. In the UK, perceived barriers to bispecifics included limited<br>availability, lack of approval, high costs, and questions around individual suitability. When considering<br>treatment options, patients prioritised effectiveness while closely monitoring side effects, followed by<br>effectiveness irrespective of side effects and their overall well-being—including financial impact and<br>personal comfort.<br>Together, these insights highlight the urgent need for more accessible, well-tolerated treatments, better<br>patient education, and a more individualised, long-term approach to care.|

## **Living with the condition** 

Patient organisation submission Epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after 2 or more systemic treatments [ID6338] 

4 of 17

**6. What is it like to live with the condition? What** Lymphoma is a type of blood cancer where white blood cells known as lymphocytes grow out of **do carers experience** control. It is the 5[th] most common type of cancer in the UK. There are two main types of lymphoma: **when caring for someone with the condition?** non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). NHL is the most prevalent, with around 14,200 people diagnosed each year in the UK. There are many different types of NHL which can be classified in two main ways. Firstly, they can be grouped into low-grade and high-grade based on how fast they grow. Secondly, they can be grouped depending on the type of lymphocyte they developed from: B cells or T cells. Follicular lymphoma (FL) is the most common type of NHL with 2,300 being diagnosed with it every year in the UK. It is a lowgrade lymphoma developing from B cells. The B cells usually develop in clumps called follicles within the lymph nodes. FL can occur at any age but tends to be a lymphoma of older age with most cases occurring in people over the age of 60. These people are often thinking towards retirement and the diagnosis can be devastating as described here, “ _Constant fear basically, it’s not the retirement we had planned and it’s devastating seeing the effect on my wife & family”._ In some people FL has no symptoms and the diagnosis is picked up incidentally when having investigations for something else. However, most people develop lumps, usually in their neck, armpits or groin. These are swollen lymph nodes. People can also experience weight loss, fevers, sweats, frequent infections and fatigue. As FL is a low-grade lymphoma these symptoms tend to develop gradually and it can often take a long time, and many appointments before a patient is diagnosed. Fatigue tends to be a particularly disabling symptom, and one which our patients find has a huge impact on their lives. _“Symptoms of fatigue, weight loss and loss of muscle mass with resulting physical weakness were severe enough to impact daily life…with consequent effects of day-to-day activities, hobbies and concentration, as well as impacting family finances and requiring increased support from family.”_ 

Patient organisation submission 

Epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after 2 or more systemic treatments [ID6338] 5 of 17 



<!-- page 295 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

_“My initial symptoms were severe fatigue, weight loss and night sweats.”_ 

As well as the obvious physical impact, FL can have a profound impact on a patient’s emotional and mental wellbeing. It can be a very anxious time when adjusting to the new diagnosis, as well as waiting for the treatment and hoping that it will work. This psychological impact should not be underestimated. 

_“I ended up having anxiety/panic attacks due to trying to survive alone and with no income.”_ 

_“It’s hard to plan anything or look ahead more than a couple of months and it has a big impact on finances just to add to the pressure… It’s a slow torture really, but you come to terms with it because you don’t have any choice.”_ 

FL can be both staged, which indicates how advanced it is, and graded, which indicates how many large lymphocytes can be seen under a microscope. Grades 1,2 and 3A are all slow growing and are treated in a different way to grade 3B which is fast growing. Our patients reflected that low grade is often viewed as less serious because treatment may not be immediately required, and survival is better. However, by doing this people forget about the emotional burden that having an incurable cancer is. 

_“Because our illness is not curable we are left in active surveillance programmes. We know that the symptoms we deal with are not serious enough to justify toxic chemotherapy regimes and the chance of significant improvement is lower than the risk of side effects. Due to this we learn to minimise what we are dealing with and so it is often overlooked in our medical reviews as evidenced in the latest Lymphoma Coalition Survey.” “It’s hard to plan anything or look ahead more than a couple of months and it has a big impact on finances just to add to the pressure.”_ 

## Patient organisation submission

When a person is diagnosed with FL this diagnosis does not just have an impact on them. They will have friends, spouses, children or grandchildren, and their lives can also be turned upside down. _“It's absolutely awful for my wife. Her life has basically been ruined…she can no longer come with me to clinics or treatments, she did for the first few years but that has taken its toll and she now finds it too traumatic.” “My partner feels the same emotional impact of living with the uncertainty of an incurable cancer as I do. In addition, he has to deal with the financial and emotional impact of having to support me. His lifestyle, hobbies and activities are as altered as mine. I think the situation of a carer for someone with an incurable chronic cancer could be argued to be harder than that of the patient.”_

Patient organisation submission

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

> **7. What do patients or** If a person is diagnosed with early-stage FL, which is about 1 in 5 people, they may not need to be 

> **carers think of current** started on treatment straightaway. People can go years like this in what is known as ‘active 

> **treatments and care** surveillance’, or ‘watch and wait’. Whilst people avoid the symptoms of active treatment it is still a very **available on the NHS?** difficult time and can be referred to by patients as ‘worry and wait’. If treatment is required in earlystage disease this may be radiotherapy or rituximab antibody treatment. Most people at diagnosis have advanced stage disease. Despite this if they do not have troublesome symptoms, they may be treated the same as early-stage disease. If treatment is required, this is usually in the form of chemotherapy combined with antibody therapy. Chemoimmunotherapy, although often successful, can be very intense, requiring multiple visits to the hospital. It can also cause a number of short and long-term side effects such as fatigue, sickness, diarrhoea, hair loss and recurrent infections. _“Chemo caused many issues living alone. Feeling ill whilst alone is hard work (physically, emotionally and mentally). Still unable to work (self-employed) and unable to claim benefits added more stress.” “Chemo…..had the usual side effects of nausea, constipation, headaches, fatigue etc.”_ If a patient responds well to chemoimmunotherapy they will usually be offered maintenance treatment. This involves having an injection of the antibody used in the chemoimmunotherapy every 2-3 months for up to 2 years. The aim of this is to keep the FL under control and make the remission period last as long as possible. This is because FL is unfortunately not curable, and almost everyone will relapse at some stage. Knowing that their disease is likely to come back whilst struggling with the side effects from treatment can be incredibly tough. _“There is an emotional impact both from dealing with these symptoms and their impact but also dealing with the knowledge that my type of lymphoma is currently incurable and carries a risk of transformation to a more aggressive form of lymphoma.”_ 

Patient organisation submission 

Epcoritamab for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after 2 or more systemic treatments [ID6338] 9 of 17 



<!-- page 299 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

The treatment for relapsed disease depends on a number of things such as previous treatment used, the side-effects and impact of this treatment and how quickly the disease relapsed. Options for treatment are the same chemoimmunotherapy regimen, a different chemoimmunotherapy regimen, radiotherapy, obinutuzumab with bendamustine, or rituximab with the targeted treatment lenalidomide. If there is a good response to treatment, a course of higher dose chemotherapy with a stem cell transplant may be offered. One patient pointed out the effect repeated courses of chemotherapy can have, “ _The need for repeated courses of chemotherapy can lead to cumulative toxicity which is particularly important as many patients can live for many years post treatment”._ Unfortunately, none of these treatments, even the most intense, will cure FL and relapse is likely to happen at some point. This knowledge can have a profound impact on the mental wellbeing of the patient and their loved ones. 

_“It’s also really terrifying to think I will probably run out of treatments one day, or a treatment available in the USA or EU might not be available to me, and the consultant will say no more can be done…It’s a slow torture really, but you come to terms with it because you don’t have any choice.”_ 

_“My quality of life has totally changed. I was a very fit self-employed person doing sprint triathlons, running, gym etc.” “I know have to manage energy (as most of us do) I’m very weary of crowds, people with coughs etc Since I’ve relapsed for the 3rd time, I have no way of knowing if the treatments have been of any benefit.”_

_“A perfect treatment would be a curative therapy with no long-term toxicity that would enable me to live a healthy future free of lymphoma and the worry of transformation.”_ Patients also feel that there needs to be more options available to enable them to have choices available to them with as little long term side effects as possible.

## **Other issues** 

> **13. Are there any other** All of our patients wanted the committee to consider the fact that there is an urgent need for further 

> **issues that you would like** treatment options in the management of FL. One patient had this to say: **the committee to consider?** _“I would like to see a more accurate cost analysis of epcoritamab that addresses the long-term costs of effects of other chemotherapy regimens and the psychosocial impact of complex prolonged cycles of treatment.”_ 

It is also important to our patients that the committee understands the importance of having treatment options available which are well tolerated with few side effects. This was backed up by the recent Lymphoma Coalition survey. This survey on lymphomas was completed by 1204 UK respondents in 2024. Follicular lymphoma was the most common subtype reported (25%). 

The survey results reflected how important living as well as possible with lymphoma is to patients. Among the respondents, 93% selected 'improved quality of life' as one of the most important aspects of treatment, second only to ‘improved / longer survival’ and ‘bring about a remission / response’, both 96%. ‘Fewer side effects / more tolerable side effects’ during treatment was also a key consideration, selected by 72% of respondents.

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

1. **Efficacy of Epcoritamab** : Epcoritamab offers clinically meaningful activity in patients with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma, achieving an overall response rate of 82% and a complete response rate of 62.5% in the pivotal cohort. Responses were observed across high-risk subgroups and heavily pretreated patients. 

2. **Safety Profile** : Epcoritamab has a manageable safety profile, with most adverse events being low-grade.  The cycle 1 optimisation cohort further reduces the incidence and severity of cytokine release syndrome, with no grade 3 or worse events reported in the trial, and eliminated mandatory hospitalisation for monitoring. 

3. **MRD Negativity and Long-Term Outcomes** : High rates of measurable residual disease (MRD) negativity were observed in the trial, which were associated with improved progression-free survival, highlighting the potential for durable responses. 

4. **Convenience of Subcutaneous Administration** : Epcoritamab's subcutaneous dosing offers practical advantages over intravenous therapies, improving patient experience and healthcare resource utilisation. 

5. **Potential as a Novel Therapy** : Epcoritamab represents a promising alternative to current treatments for relapsed or 

refractory follicular lymphoma, with indirect treatment comparisons demonstrating clear benefits over standard treatments.

## **20. Do the clinical trials on the technology reflect current UK clinical practice?** 

- If not, how could the results be extrapolated to the UK setting? 

- What, in your view, are the most important outcomes, and were they measured in the trials?

Otherwise, the treatment is extremely well tolerated. late infections due to hypogammaglobulinaemia are established due to other treatment pathways, and its mitigation and management are well established. 

To date, the only published data for Epcoritamab has been its evaluation in single arm studies. The primary endpoint for the pivotal cohort was overall response rate which for third line onwards treatment is acceptable. Progression free survival and adverse events which are the most relevant to the UK setting were key secondary endpoints, and showed excellent outcomes with low toxicity. The results can be extrapolated to the UK setting, especially as they were conducted and influenced b the covid 19 pandemic. No adverse effects that were not apparent in clinical trials have come to light. 

- Are there any adverse effects that were not apparent in clinical trials but have come to light subsequently?

**Follicular lymphoma is a living hell in many ways. Life is nothing like you planned and it’s heartbreaking to see the impact on your wife and family. It’s difficult to look more than three months ahead. Every scan is terrifying with the constant fear is of another relapse and then the sickening blow when it comes back. To add to the stress, it’s very expensive being ill with months of no income. It’s also tough to see others enjoying life, retirement, holidays and not living with endless worry. On the other hand, what’s equally true, ten years on and I’m still here. This is much better than the alternative! You have to be strong for your family which is no bad thing. I refuse to let it spoil my day. I’m probably as optimistic now as I’ve ever been since diagnosis because the new immunotherapy treatments are coming through just in time. I’ve had most of the chemotherapies, now it’s time for new and better drugs to increase the options available. Without new treatments I will run out of options. I’m lucky that I’m genetically optimistic. It would have been a real waste not to have made the best of those ten years, but it’s a huge mental challenge. My wife can no longer come with me to clinics or treatments, she did for the first few years but that has taken its toll and she now finds it too traumatic. Her mental health is as badly affected as mine. I saw someone comment the other day “we watched our savings turn to dust”. We sold our house after my first treatment and traded down so we had no mortgage. Only people who’ve been through all this will really understand how brutal it is.**

## **Executive Summary** 

## **1 Executive summary** 

This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the External Assessment Group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision making. It also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental costeffectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 provides an overview of key model outcomes and the modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER. Sections 1.3 to 1.6 explain the key issues in more detail. Background information on the condition, technology and evidence and information on non-key issues are in the main EAG report. 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of NICE.

The key differences between the company’s preferred assumptions and the EAG’s preferred assumptions are as follows: 

- The EAG prefers to use a naïve comparison to inform relative efficacy of epcoritamab. In this approach, the PFS and OS outcomes for current 4L+ 

9 



<!-- page 352 -->

care are directly extrapolated from HMRN data, without the use of a MAIC. For epcoritamab, data that are not adjusted for Covid deaths are used in the naïve comparison, to maintain consistency with the unadjusted HMRN data. Other differences include: 

- Application of same utility weights for PFS, in both treatment arms, without adjusting for complete response status 

- Incidence of AEs in current 4L+ care estimated based on weighted AE incidence for O-Benda, R-CHOP and R[2] instead of R-CHOP only. 

- Increased haematologist’s consultant visits in first month for Epcoritamab arm. 

- No severity weighting 

## **1.2** _**Overview of key model outcomes**_ 

NICE technology appraisals compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

## Overall, the technology is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Utility values assigned to the different health states 

- Source of data and method of informing relative efficacy 

   - Relative efficacy is informed using a naïve comparison between epcoritamab and the HMRN 4L+ FL data. Epcoritamab outcomes are based on EPCORE NHL-1 study data, unadjusted for COVID-19 deaths, while comparator outcomes are directly extrapolated from observational HRMN data without adjustment or indirect treatment comparison. 

## Overall, the technology is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Source of data and method of informing relative efficacy 

   - Costs are influenced by treatment duration and health state occupancy, which are informed by progression-free survival, overall survival, and time to 

10 



<!-- page 353 -->

treatment discontinuation from the EPCORE NHL-1 study for epcoritamab and the HRMN observational real-world data for the comparator arm. 

- Frequency of adverse events 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- Estimating PFS and OS outcomes for comparator (current 4L+ care) directly from HMRN data and informing relative efficacy via a naïve comparison

**Issue 2: Evidence uncertainty from the included epcoritamab study** 

|**Report section**||**3.2**|

|**Description of issue**<br>**and why the EAG has**<br>**identified it as**<br>**important**||There are limitations with the epcoritamab study. EPCORE<br>NHL-1 is an ongoing, single-arm, open-label trial. The data<br>are from subgroups relating to number of prior lines of<br>treatment and some data from the latest data cuts could<br>not be validated . It has not been possible to fully validate<br>all data in the CS. The company focus on adjusted<br>analyses to account for COVID-19 deaths, but also<br>presented un-adjusted analyses. ## _**issues**_

## **External Assessment Group Report** 

## **2 INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND** 

## **2.1** _**Introduction**_ 

The EAG has reviewed and critiqued the company submission (CS) submitted to NICE by AbbVie Ltd. This report evaluates the clinical and cost-effectiveness evidence for epcoritamab (Tepkinly) in treating adult patients with relapsed or refractory (R/R) follicular lymphoma (FL) grade 1 – 3A, after three or more prior lines (4L+) of systemic treatments. 

## **2.2** _**Background**_ 

## **2.2.1 Background to the condition** 

The company provides a description of epcoritamab and of the relevant health condition (B.1.2 – 1.3), however, some citations were either inaccurately represented or lacked sufficient context as discussed below. This section provides a critique of the company overview of the disease, the technology, and the positioning of epcoritamab within the treatment pathway. 

## **Follicular lymphoma** 

The CS cites relevant references in their description of the health condition (B.1.3.1). FL is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) that is a mature B-cell-derived, indolent disease (with the exception of grade 3B, which is more aggressive) characterised by relapses and remissions. It can be treatment refractory (resistant), with a heterogeneous clinical course.[1-3] When indolent, some patients may not require treatment for prolonged periods, while others may develop more aggressive forms that are refractory to standard treatment options.[3] The EAG notes that the CS includes a population that is relapsed, progressive or refractory. The EAG clinical experts highlight that “progressive” implies disease worsening despite treatment and can also be considered refractory; “refractory” can also include stable disease (not progressing). “Relapse” refers to disease returning after a response. Therefore, relapsed or refractory are used by the EAG in this report, unless otherwise stated. 

22 



<!-- page 365 -->

The CS (section 1.3.2 and 1.3.7) states that “ _by 4L+ stage, R/R FL is no longer considered an indolent disease but more akin to end of life disease with limited treatment options.”_ The EAG notes that this statement lacks citation. The CS notes that by the 4L+ of treatment, patients with R/R FL have a median overall survival of less than 12 months, based on observational data.[2, 4] 

## **FL grading and staging** 

The company states that FL is graded according to the 2022 WHO classification into four distinct grades based on centroblast count per high-power field (CS section 1.3.5). The EAG notes that the updated WHO-HAEM5 classification makes grading of FL optional,[5] due to concerns about poor reproducibility, lack of standardised methodology, and limited clinical significance in distinguishing between grades 1, 2, and 3A. 

CS section 1.3.5.2 states that the Lugano classification system (using fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography scans and an adaptation of the Ann Harbor staging system) is used to determine the staging of FL and provides additional information (CS Table 4). The EAG notes that no citation is provided. 

## **Prognosis** 

Both the Follicular Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (FLIPI) developed in 2004[6] and FLIPI2 (2009)[7] are prognostic tools used in the assessment of FL.[8] While FLIPI is based on five clinical factors: age >60, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, haemoglobin <120 g/L, involvement of >4 nodal sites and elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), FLIPI2 retains age and haemoglobin but replaces LDH with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) - a more specific marker of tumour burden - and adds bone marrow involvement and nodal mass >6 cm. The CS (CS section 1.3.5.3), highlights that both are used to inform clinical prognosis but not guide treatment. The EAG clinical experts agree that some prognostic factors such as bone marrow involvement are not routinely used, therefore FLIPI is the most currently used tool in UK clinical practice. 

Response criteria in FL is commonly assessed using the Lugano classification system, which includes the Lymphoma Response to Immunomodulatory Therapy Criteria (LYRIC) developed specifically to evaluate responses to immune-based 

23 



<!-- page 366 -->

treatments.[9] These criteria define complete response, partial response, and progressive disease based on imaging results such as PET/CT scans and changes in lesion size (CS Table 5). The company’s EPCORE NHL-1 study,[10] applies both the Lugano and LYRIC criteria to evaluate these treatment outcomes, see Table 5 for further details. 

## **Burden of FL** 

CS section B.1.3.3 addresses the HRQoL burden of FL and states that quality of life declines in comparison with the UK general population.[11] However, the cited reference provides population norms only and does not include a direct comparison with FL patients. The EAG notes that the three studies cited by the company in section B.1.3.3[12-14] do not specifically report on the burden on R/R FL patients. For example, the study by Cheung 2009[12] evaluates work productivity among a mixed cohort of indolent NHL patients at different stages, including those with R/R FL, but does not report results for this subgroup. Similarly, Major 2022[13] reports on HRQoL in newly diagnosed patients with indolent NHL, including FL, but excludes patients with R/R disease. The study by Lee 2013[14] provides HRQoL data across all cancer types, with 84% of patients diagnosed with stomach or lung cancer; the remaining cancer types, including FL, are not specified. The company describes a study they conducted into patient experience of living with FL.[15] While this qualitative study addresses the emotional burden experienced by patients at 1L to 3L of treatment, it is based on interviews with a small number of patients / caregivers (n=13), 3 of whom were from the UK and only one patient was at 3L. Furthermore, no standardised instruments were used to assess or report emotional burden. 

## **2.2.2 Position of the technology** 

The company describes treatment pathways for FL in CS section 1.3.6 and presents an overview of current treatment options in CS Figure 1 (not reproduced here). Apart from a few exceptions the EAG clinical experts confirm that the representation is reasonable. Symptomatic high tumour burden stage III and IV (advanced-stage) FL follows British Society of Haematology (BSH) treatment guidelines[8] with an antiCD20 antibody treatment (rituximab or obinutuzumab) in combination with chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone 

24 



<!-- page 367 -->

[CHOP], or cyclophosphamide, vincristine and prednisolone [CVP], or bendamustine). The EAG clinical advisors agree with the company that there is no standardised treatment pathway for relapsed / refractory FL at later lines of treatment. Treatments used will depend on prior treatments used, responses to those prior treatments as well as clinical judgement about fitness.  For some, a repeat rituximab with chemotherapy option is used as per the BSH guidelines,[8] but other treatments include rituximab with an alternative chemotherapy, lenalidomide with rituximab (R2) or other regimens such as bendamustine, gemcitabine, cisplatin with different centres using more or less intensive regimens. Obinutuzumab in combination with other therapies is rarely used at later treatment lines in the UK. 

As there is no standard of care for the treatment of 4L+ FL, currently used treatments are aimed at controlling the disease rather than achieving remission.  Although the EAG experts agree with the CS that there is an unmet need at 4L+, unlike the company experts, the EAG experts consider that there is a greater unmet need at 3L+ and that it is desirable to consider using epcoritamab at 3L+.  They suggest that as most patients will have already received rituximab and chemotherapy and then rituximab with lenalidomide, the choice of the next line of therapy is difficult and that it would not be desirable to give bendamustine later because of how it affects T-cell function; it would therefore be of benefit for patients to have the option of epcoritamab at third line. 

Best supportive care (BSC) was not considered an appropriate comparator by the company because they expect that BSC would be for those not fit enough for an active intervention. The EAG clinical experts confirmed that fitness would be based on performance status. The EAG clinical experts considered that some people at 4L+  who would not be fit enough for chemotherapy would be eligible for epcoritamab treatment instead of receiving BSC and that therefore, the exclusion of BSC as a comparator is not appropriate. 

Current NICE recommendations for FL are presented in CS Table 7. The EAG clinical experts agree that it is unlikely that any of these interventions would be used in 4L+ or 3L+ as they would have already been used as second-line in the majority of cases. 

25 



<!-- page 368 -->

The CS outlines their case for the unmet need at 4L+ in Section 1.3.7. The EAG experts agree that FL at later stages is often resistant to conventional treatment and that the CS estimates of median overall survival (OS) at 4L+ of less than a year (**** months) and median progression free survival (PFS) of *** months is reasonable.[4] 

The CS reports that there are limited treatment options at 4L+. The CS also reports that existing chemotherapy-based treatments do not fully address the immune dysfunction associated with FL and have a number of toxicities which mean they’re not suitable to be repeated. The CS cites a systematic review of cardiovascular events at first line CHOP or R-CHOP chemotherapy in NHL, rather than FL specifically, where the review identified that cardiac dysfunction is reported in more than 10% of individuals post-chemotherapy.  The EAG clinical experts agree with these issues but note that they are not specific to 4L+ FL. 

CS Table 2 reports details of epcoritamab. Epcoritamab is a humanised IgG1bispecific antibody that binds the B-cell antigen CD20 and T-cell antigen CD3, encouraging destruction of abnormal FL cells. The marketing authorisation is for adult patients with R/R FL after two or more lines of systemic therapy. Epcoritamab is administered subcutaneously (sc), whereas other treatments are administered intravenously. The company has submitted a new indication application to the UK Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and a decision is expected in *********. The epcoritamab dose is increased during the first 4-week cycle to 48 mg from 0.16 mg on day 1, 0.8 mg on day 8, 3 mg on day 15 and 48 mg on day 22. 

## **2.3** _**Critique of company’s definition of decision problem**_ 

The decision problem in the company’s submission has some differences to the final NICE scope. The population in the company’s decision problem is narrower than the NICE scope and the UK marketing authorisation and the EAG considers there to be an unmet need in the wider population, in line with the NICE scope, see Table 3 for more discussion.  The comparator in the company’s decision problem is also narrower than the NICE scope, which the EAG considers is appropriate.

## **3 CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS** 

## **3.1** _**Critique of the methods of review(s)**_ 

The company conducted an SLR to evaluate the efficacy and safety of treatments for adult patients with 3L+ and 4L+ relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (R/R FL), reported in CS Appendix B. 

## **3.1.1 Search strategies** 

Searches were originally undertaken in April 2023, with updates in March and November 2024. The EAG ran targeted searches for any studies relevant to the NICE scope that may have been added to databases since November 2024; this identified no additional, relevant studies. An appropriate selection of bibliographic databases, recent conference proceedings and clinical trials registries was searched. Reference lists of previous SLRs, pooled analyses and meta-analyses were also checked (CS Appendix B, Table 13), although reference lists of included studies do not appear to have been checked for additional studies. One further included publication was found via ‘Supplementary evidence publications included for data extraction’; it is not clear what this means and the company’s response to Clarification C12 is also unclear. 

The database search strategies (reported in Appendix B, Tables 1-4 and Clarification C8 Appendix, Tables 8-1 to 8-10) combine terms for relapsed/refractory or 2L+ follicular lymphoma with interventions of interest and study type filters for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomised studies. The EAG considers that since both interventional and observational studies were to be included in the review, the search strategy would have been more comprehensive had it not included study type filters, perhaps only excluding specific unwanted study or publication types such as case reports and letters (Appendix B, Table 13). 

Publication date limits have been used in update search strategies to exclude results published before the date of the previous search. This is not best practice and risks missing relevant results, as publications are not added to Embase/Medline as soon as they are published. More appropriate date fields such as “date created” or “date 

31 



<!-- page 374 -->

delivered” can be used for a comprehensive search. Additional limitations affecting the sensitivity of the search strategies include missing Emtree or MeSH headings for the relapsed/refractory concept ( ‘refractory cancer’, ‘cancer recurrence’, ‘salvage therapy’, ‘recurrence’), not including trade names nor alternative names for drug interventions, not using the drug trade name field in Embase, and not searching the keywords field (using title and abstract fields only for free text searches). 

The company’s searches were for FL, therefore did not identify an epcoritamab study that reported results for of the LBCL group (Thieblemont 2024).[17] The EAG considered this publication useful for reporting of adverse events (see section 3.2.7). 

## **3.1.2 SLR methods** 

The company conducted the SLR from a global perspective and included comparators that are not relevant to the NICE decision problem. The population specified by the eligibility criteria (CS Appendix Table 13) is wider than both the UK marketing authorisation (adult patients with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma (FL) after two or more lines of systemic therapy) and the population defined by the company’s decision problem (after 3 or more systemic treatments). The reporting of the results of the SLR is not clear, with a number of errors acknowledged by the company at clarification (Clarifications C5, C6, C11). In addition, full citations of the 490 excluded reports listed in CS Appendix B.7 and details of 238 additional publications subsequently excluded for not reporting 3L+ data were not provided with the initial submission (Clarifications C4 and C3, respectively). 

Searches of clinical trial registries were undertaken. However, the methods stated that results were not extracted from studies reported only in clinical trial registries, which is a potential source of publication bias. The CS does not report details of relevant studies from clinical trial registries, but the company confirmed in Clarification C13 that there were no additional trials identified. 

The company excluded conference abstracts if data were published in a more recent abstract or in a peer-reviewed publication. This is reasonable, but it is not clear from 

32 



<!-- page 375 -->

the reasons for exclusion what the linked publication was for abstracts excluded for ‘study design’, making checking difficult. 

Although the company included 54 studies reported in 107 publications (Clarification C5), only 38 studies are discussed in Appendix B.2 and no results for these 38 studies are reported. Most of these 38 studies assessed interventions that are not relevant to this appraisal. It is not clear why the CS omits the other 16 studies. 

The EAG has checked all included and excluded publications lists, identified any studies with relevant interventions and checked for 3L+ and 4L+ data. There were a number of studies that were relevant to the decision problem (Table 4), but the EAG agrees with the company that none were appropriate for use in the MAIC for the 4L+ population. No studies with BSC were identified. 

If the 3L+ population were to be considered, the following studies should be reassessed: 

Coiffier 2011[18] Salles 2022[19] Hao 2023[20] Wästerlid 2024[21] Johnson 2024[22] Johnson 2025[23] Vitolo 2025[24]

## **3.2** _**Critique of trials of the technology of interest, the company’s analysis and interpretation (and any standard meta-analyses of these)**_ 

The study providing safety and efficacy information for this indication of epcoritamab is EPCORE NHL-1 (NCT 03625037). 

## **3.2.1 EPCORE NHL-1 study design** 

The EAG summary of the key characteristics of the EPCORE NHL-1 study, based on the company submitted information, is summarised in Table 5. The EAG has summarised the relevant parts, cohorts and subgroups of EPCORE NHL-1 in Table Table 6 and the data-cuts and sources of information in Table 7. 

Table 5 combines data obtained and checked by the EAG from the CS and the available CSRs, NCT record,[27] company protocol version 14, the publication relevant to the EPCORE study[10] and the abbreviated dataset provided at clarifications (A4). 

EPCORE NHL-1, is an ongoing open label single arm phase 2 study, conducted in US, Australia, Asia and Europe to evaluate the safety and efficacy of epcoritamab in relapsed/refractory patients with B-cell lymphomas (diffuse large b-cell lymphoma: DLBCL; high-grade b-cell lymphoma: HGBCL; primary mediastinal b-cell lymphoma: PMBCL: follicular lymphoma, grade 3b: FL grade 3B; marginal zone lymphoma: MZL; small lymphocytic lymphoma: SLL and mantle cell lymphoma: MCL). The subgroup of relevance to the decision problem in this submission is patients with FL grades 1 to 3A. Eligible patients are ≥ 18 years old, who were relapsed, progressive and/or refractory to at least two prior lines of treatment  (including anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody), having exhausted or are ineligible for standard treatment options and have an ECOG PS score 0 – 2. 

The study consisted of 3 parts; an initial dose-escalation part which is not applicable to the decision problem; a dose expansion part and a dose-optimisation part which are the focus of this submission. The optimisation part of EPCORE NHL-1 had two arms, arm A (as shown in CS section 2.2, Table 9) which is relevant to this 

36 



<!-- page 379 -->

submission while arm B (n=6) was irrelevant due to a difference in the step-up dose (6mg at day 15) from that in the anticipated licenced escalation. 

Epcoritamab was administered subcutaneously per cycle (1 cycle was equivalent to 28 days).  Participants received epcoritamab subcutaneously in 4-week cycles (i.e., 28 days) at varying doses as follows: 

- Cycle 1: dose escalation, Day 1: 0.16 mg, Day 8: 0.8 mg, Day 15: 48 mg (Dose Expansion Part) or Cycle 1 Day 1: 0.16 mg, Day 8: 0.8 mg, Day 15: 3 mg, Day 22: 48 mg (Dose Optimisation Part) 

- Cycle 2-3: Days 1, 8, 15, and 22 (once weekly) 48 mg 

- Cycle 4-9: Days 1 and 15 (every 2 weeks) 48mg 

- Cycles 10 to progressive disease (PD), unacceptable toxicity, or end of trial: Day 1 (every 4 weeks) 48 mg 

The EAG notes a difference in the dose escalation between the expansion part (which informs the main evidence of this submission) and the optimisation part (and anticipated licensed escalation), see Table 5. In the latter, an additional dose of 3.0 mg at day 15 is included and the 48 mg dose commenced from day 22. In response to clarification question A10, the company explained the rationale for the difference and agreed that the expansion part did not include the 3 mg step used in the optimisation part and anticipated licenced escalation which is to improve tolerability. The company report that pharmacokinetic outcomes are very similar and that the 3- step regimen does not undermine the efficacy or safety data. The EAG clinical experts did not consider the different dosing escalations to have any bearing on clinical, or safety results seen. 

The CS focuses primarily on the 4L+ subgroup. Data pertaining to the 3L+ subgroup are presented separately in CS Appendix M, Table 83 for completeness. As detailed in Section 1.3, the 3L+ population is consistent with the NICE scope. 

The clinical data in the CS are based on the most recent data cut of *************, (median follow-up **** months) in the expansion part and 8 January 2024 (median follow up 5.7 months) in the optimisation part. The expansion part primary endpoint of relevance to the decision problem was overall response rate (ORR) per Lugano 

37 



<!-- page 380 -->

criteria and assessed by independent review committee (IRC), with secondary endpoints including response rates, PFS, OS, safety and HRQoL, see Table 5 for further details. Primary endpoints in the optimisation part included Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) events and safety, while secondary endpoints were similar to those of the expansion part but excluded HRQoL, Table 5.
