## **3.2.2 Baseline characteristics** 

The EPCORE NHL-1 trial was a single arm study divided into three parts, two of which are relevant to the efficacy of epcoritamab; the CS presented data for two different subgroups from each part as discussed earlier (EAG report section 3.2.1). In this section, the EAG summarises the baseline characteristics of the 4L+ and 3L+ subgroups, from both the expansion and optimisation parts of EPCORE NHL-1. Data for the 4L+ subgroup of the expansion and optimisation parts were obtained from the CS, Section 2.5.1 – 2.5.2.2, Table 11 and Section 2.14.2, Table 39, respectively. Additional data for these subgroups was also available from CS Appendix M. The EAG was unable to validate these data from any publications or the submitted CSR and requested documents for the 4L+ subgroups at clarification (Clarification 

question A4). In their response, the company stated that there were no publications or CSR available for the 4L+ cohorts and instead provided an abbreviated dataset. The EAG was able to validate these data for the 4L+ expansion phase and notes that for the optimisation phase, some of these data were only in a summary document provided by the company.  Data for the 3L+ expansion and optimisation cohorts were obtained from CS Appendix M and validated with CSRs, and the publication.[10] An overview of the patient characteristics is summarised in Table 8 and key points discussed below. 

The EPCORE NHL-1 study subgroups submitted in the CS were the expansion part 4L+ (n = 81) and 3L+ (n = 128), and the optimisation part 4L+ (n = 41) and 3L+ (n = 

41 



<!-- page 384 -->

86). These are not mutually exclusive groups, the 4L+ groups are subsets of the respective 3L+ groups.  The EAG summarises key prognostic characteristics from across these subgroups to consider representativeness of the participant cohorts, rather than for any comparison. The mean age of participants ranged from 62.8 to 65.5 years, indicating a predominantly older population consistent with the typical age profile of FL.[29] The expansion part subgroups showed a higher proportion of male participants, which aligns with the known epidemiological pattern of FL in the UK (i.e., male-to-female ratio ~1.4:1).[29] In contrast, the optimisation cohorts 4L+ group showed more balanced sex distribution.  Most patients included had ECOG PS 0 – 1 across all cohorts, indicating a generally fit population. A small proportion of patients in the expansion subgroups had an ECOG PS of 2 (3.7% and 5.5% for the 4L+ and 3L+ subgroups respectively) and none in the optimisation subgroups had a PS above 1, see Table 8. Minor differences were also observed across cohorts in histological grade, FLIPI score, and refractory status, these are summarised in Table 8. 

The EAG notes that patients were heavily pre-treated, particularly in the 4L+ groups, with 49.4% of patients receiving ≥4 prior lines of therapy (expansion 4L+) and 41.5% in the optimisation phase. Some patients had received later-line treatments such as lenalidomide (up to *****). Approximately *** of patients underwent stem cell transplant and fewer than 10% of patients in each subgroup had received prior CART. As the EPCORE NHL-1 protocol excludes those with prior CAR-T therapy within 30 days of enrolment, the EAG asked the company for more details about the participants who had received prior CAR-T (clarification A14). The company response reports on the participants from the 4L+ expansion subgroup (n=*; ****) and noted that these individuals had relapsed and were considered high-risk. As such, no long-term benefit from prior CAR-T was expected.

## **3.2.3 Risk of bias of EPCORE NHL-1** 

The company SLR reported that the Down and Black risk of bias checklist was applied to EPCORE NHL-1; however, this was not included in the CS.  The company presented a table with risk of bias questions which was not referenced.  Some of the questions are those used in the NICE methods guide[30] but there were also some additional questions. The EAG has undertaken an assessment with these same questions in Table 9 below.  In response to clarification question C1, the company provided the full quality assessment of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial using the Down’s and Black checklist. The EAG in Table 10, compares their responses to the Down’s and Black checklist criteria with that of the company’s assessment. Overall, the EAG has no major concerns on the EPCORE NHL-1 risk of bias. The EAG notes that, due to the study design (single-arm study), several items in the Down and Black checklist were not applicable, including randomisation, comparability between groups, and blinding. 

There are some differences between the EAG and the company’s assessments (Tables below). The EAG disagrees with the company’s assertion that patient characteristics for those lost to follow-up were described. The EAG notes that characteristics of censored patients (e.g., those receiving new anti-lymphoma therapy or affected by COVID-related mortality) were not detailed, thus limiting ability to fully assess the impact of incomplete follow-up. Details of characteristics for COVID-censored patients were presented by the Company at Clarification Questions (Appendix 1) and were described in response to Question A25. The EAG also notes a difference between the dose escalation used in the expansion phase (efficacy data) and the licensed, optimised regimen. The company assessment of representativeness of the study population was ‘unclear’, whereas the EAG considered that the study population may not represent the entire population from which participants were recruited. For example, the company did not state the source population for recruited patients and while the CS stated the eligibility criteria, it did not describe how the patients were selected. 

45 



<!-- page 388 -->

The EAG considered the data presented for the subgroups to be pre-specified and unlikely to be related to data dredging; it is interesting that the company assessment was unclear. 

In addition, the EAG notes that p-values were not reported for patient-reported outcome data, despite before and after comparisons being presented.

## **3.2.5 Results** 

## **Overview of results** 

Key results from the EPCORE NHL-1 study are summarised in Table 12. These are presented for the expansion part and the optimisation part of EPCORE NHL-1. The CS focused on outcomes for the 4L+ subgroup; but as discussed in Section 2.3, the EAG has also considered outcomes for the 3L+ subgroup. 

At clarifications (A4) the company confirmed that no CSR was available for the 4L+ data from the expansion or optimisation part. The company provided an unpublished document containing the formal tables, listings and figures for the key characteristics and outcomes for the 4L+ subpopulation which the EAG has used to validate data where possible. There are no published sources of the 4L+ subgroup analyses.  For the 3L+ expansion part, the data cut presented by the CS is *************.  The data cut in the submitted CSR is 21 April 2023, corresponding to the published data in Linton 2024.[10] The EAG is therefore unable to validate the data for the 3L+ subgroup from the most recent data cut presented in the CS. 

As the data for the main submission are from subgroup analyses which are not mutually exclusive groups, the EAG requested (clarification A5 and A8) summary efficacy data for the subgroup who only received third-line treatment (3L-only) from both parts of EPCORE NHL-1 for completeness. This would permit the EAG to consider any limitations in the data such as inconsistencies in the effects seen. The company declined to present these data only noting that data for the 3L+ population were presented, which includes the 3L-only subgroup. Although the EAG 

52 



<!-- page 395 -->

summarises the 3L+ data, unfortunately this does not permit any consideration from the contrasting data to the 4L+ subgroup. 

Results from the expansion part are from independent review committee (IRC); results from the optimisation part are investigator assessed (INV). The CS does not explain why the outcome assessment was different, however, the EAG note that in the study protocol the mantle cell lymphoma cohort of the optimisation part was assessed through IRC. CS Table 13 summarises the analysis sets used for the outcomes in EPCORE NHL-1, the EAG is not able to confirm which analysis sets are presented but assumes from the descriptions these are from the full analyses sets. 

The length of follow-up was a median of **** months for the expansion part and 5.7 months for the optimisation part. The median follow-up for the earlier 2023 published data cut was 17.4 months and 5.7 months for the expansion part and optimisation part, respectively.[10] 

The CS presents results that were adjusted to censor deaths related to the COVID19 pandemic during the expansion part of the EPCORE NHL-1 study. The CS reports that each mortality event was clinically adjudicated to identify cases where COVID-19 was the cause of death with certainty and censoring for these COVID-19 deaths applied in the survival outcomes (OS, PFS and TTD). The EAG has some reservations about this and asked in clarification A18 for details of how decisions over deaths attributable to Covid-19 were made, and who made the decisions. The company response confirms the decision criteria but does not fully report details of who made the decisions, only that evaluations and adjudications were performed by physicians.  The company also states that there are challenges with defining deaths as COVID-19 but that they took a pragmatic approach which was based on the interpretation of their own clinical experts. The EAG clinical experts considered that while it is useful to have the adjusted analyses, there are likely difficulties with confirming that COVID-19 was the cause of death.  In addition, the EAG experts considered that there is the possibility that epcoritamab itself increased infection risk and while COVID-19 infections are lower now, there are other infections which can impact mortality.  The EAG also notes that in the peer reviewed publication of EPCORE NHL-1 and the CSR from the 2023 data-cut (3L+), the COVID-19 adjusted 

53 



<!-- page 396 -->

analyses were presented as sensitivity analyses, not the main analyses.  The EAG was not able to locate details of these COVID-19 adjusted analyses in the statistical analysis plan (version 3.0 dated 8 June 2023) submitted by the company. The EAG view is that the COVID non-modified data is more appropriate but for completeness the EAG also summarises the COVID-modified data as sensitivity analyses.

The company adjusted the OS results to account for COVID-19 deaths as outcomes in EPCORE NHL-1 were recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic. A total of ** deaths were clinically adjudicated, by the company’s experts, as attributable to COVID-19, of which * occurred during the Omicron wave, and * of these ** patients were in CR at the time of death. The company argued that since patients in CR typically exhibit significantly better long-term survival, the inclusion of these deaths skews the OS curve downward, underestimating treatment benefit. 

Therefore, the company censored these patients at the times of their death, instead of treating them as a death, in this new COVID-modified dataset. A comparison of the KM plots for both datasets, original and COVID-modified, is presented in Figure 3. As with PFS, a visible separation emerges in the KM curves between the unmodified and modified OS estimates between 12 to 15 months, suggesting that COVID-19 had an impact on survival outcomes. The company report that ** deaths were attributable to COVID-19, representing ****% of the starting population. The company states that * of these people were in complete response when they died. This approach was aligned with the method used in Linton et al. 2024, which conducted COVID-19 sensitivity analyses using stringent adjudication criteria for censoring. The Linton appendix outlines how deaths were identified for censoring, including: 

- Deaths in patients with probable or confirmed COVID-19, 

- Deaths linked to relevant medical system organ classes (e.g. respiratory or cardiac) in COVID-positive patients, or 

- Any death with COVID-19 mentioned in free-text cause. 

In those cases, if no alternative non-COVID cause of death was clearly present, the death was censored at the date of death for all time-to-even outcomes. 

The EAG is unsure of the frequency of monitoring, and how recent the CR was confirmed. Without knowing how up to date their response status was, there remains some uncertainty about the accuracy of assuming these patients would have remained long-term responders.

## **3.3** _**Critique of trials identified and included in the indirect comparison and/or multiple treatment comparison**_ 

EPCORE NHL-1 is a single-arm study and the company’s SLR did not identify any studies that were suitable comparators in the 4L+ population (see section 3.1 [Critique of methods of review]). As outlined in the company’s decision problem (section 2.3), the most appropriate comparator was considered to be a basket of care. The company therefore engaged with the Haematological Malignancy Research Network (HMRN) to establish a dataset for use as a comparator in the MAIC. A confidential report was provided by the company.[4] 

## **HMRN** 

The HMRN region covers Yorkshire and the Humber & Yorkshire Coast Cancer Networks in the UK, with a total population of 3.8 million. The HMRN provides information and statistics primarily based on a population-based cohort which comprises all patients diagnosed with a haematological malignancy or related precursor condition; patients enter the cohort on the day they are diagnosed and are regularly followed up. The cohort has a similar age and sex profile to the UK, and a comparable socioeconomic and urban/rural distribution, which the HMRN says means that the findings can be generalised to the whole country.[4] The HMRN receives funding from non-commercial sources. 

The analysis conducted for the company identified people newly diagnosed with FL between 1st September 2004 and 31st December 2021, aged ≥18 years at diagnosis, and who had received ≥3 lines of chemotherapy. 

The EAG has cross-checked data cited in the CS (PFS, OS, baselines in CS Table 28) against the HMRN report.[4] 

Baseline characteristics are discussed further in section 3.4.2. 

The EAG notes that some of the interventions received at 4L+ are not in line with the NICE scope for this appraisal, however this is not unexpected given the inclusion 

69 



<!-- page 412 -->

period (2004 to 2021) and the lack of SOC at this line. These are summarised in section 3.4.2. 

Key results from the HMRN report for 4L+ FL patients are presented in Table 18 and Table 19. Of the ** patients in the 4L+ setting, ****** patients achieved a complete response, ** achieved a partial response, * patient had stable disease, and ** patients progressed disease. *** patient’s response to treatment was not evaluable, though the reason was not given, and ******** patient did not discontinue and was still ongoing treatment. 

The results from the HMRN indicate the ************* did not respond well to treatment, potentially underscoring the unmet need in the 4L+ setting. ************** of the patients experienced progressive disease, suggesting limited effectiveness of the current batch of available treatments in this real-world cohort. Furthermore, 

******************* had discontinued treatment, suggesting that the current available treatments were either not tolerable, not effective, or both.

## **3.4** _**Critique of the indirect comparison and/or multiple treatment comparison**_ 

No meta-analysis was performed by the company due to EPCORE NHL-1 being a single-arm study, and no head-to-head trials were identified by the company’s search strategy. Therefore, the company performed a matching adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) using individualised patient data (IPD) from EPCORE NHL-1 to match the population of the COVID-modified dose-expansion cohort of EPCORE NHL-1 to current 4L+ care in England. 

MAICs involve reweighting IPD from one study to match the baseline characteristics of a comparator study, enabling a fairer comparison between treatments. In this STA, IPD were used from EPCORE NHL-1 to reweight the COVID-modified doseexpansion cohort to match important treatment effect modifiers (TEMs) from the HMRN. The quality of the comparison after adjusting for TEMs depends on the overlap between populations, indicated by the choice of variables used for matching and how the effective sample size (ESS) post-matching changes from the original sample size of the study in question, in this case EPCORE NHL-1. An unanchored MAIC, such as this, also requires all prognostic factors to be included in the analysis. 

The company considered implementing a simulated treatment comparison (STC). STCs, like MAICs, are also used when head-to-head clinical trial data are unavailable. The company’s reasons for not doing a STC include the small number of events in EPCORE NHL-1 which limits the feasibility of an STC, which relies on 

71 



<!-- page 414 -->

the number of events to determine how many predictors can be included; MAICs are thought to be better for assessment of effectiveness against a single comparator or single real world evidence (RWE) result  (as in HMRN) whereas STCs are better suited for multiple comparators; STCs require selecting a parametric distribution adding further complexity; and MAICs have frequently been accepted in prior STAs of FL treatments. 

The EAG presents a summary of the trials included in the MAIC.  The safety and efficacy of epcoritamab was from the COVID-modified dose-expansion cohort of EPCORE NHL-1, and the safety and efficacy of the current 4L+ care in England was from a report by the Haematological Malignancy Research Network (HMRN). 

## **3.4.1 Comparison of included studies** 

There are several important differences between the EPCORE NHL-1 trial and the HMRN dataset that raise concerns regarding the validity of the company’s MAIC, see 

Table 20. EPCORE NHL-1 is a multinational, phase 2, open-label clinical trial where data is collected prospectively, compared to HMRN which is a retrospective, observational dataset limited to two regions in England. The studies differ in sample size and median follow-up, and the difference in study period might generate differences in outcome simply due to changes in clinical practice and standards of care. 

The patient populations may also differ due to the inclusion criteria. EPCORE NHL-1 included a more selectively defined group (4+ prior therapies and relapsing remitting (R/R) disease), whereas the HMRN included patients with 3+ lines of therapy, potentially capturing a broader and more heterogeneous group – though the MAIC included the 4L+ patients in HMRN. Treatments received in the HMRN report were also more varied with no defined standard comparator, compared to EPCORE NHL1 which used epcoritamab as the only treatment option.

## **3.4.3 Variables included in MAIC** 

The company discusses the choice of variables in CS B.2.12.2.2 and originally considered: age, sex, ECOG performance status, disease stage, FLIPI score, rapid progression on prior treatments, number of prior treatments, previous treatment with specific therapies, and refractory status. These factors aligned with the TEMs considered in the MAIC conducted in TA627. 

The reliability of the MAIC was limited by the lack of reporting in the HMRN dataset, where some variables were not reported or others like ECOG status or FLIPI, were measured at baseline but not at the start of 4L+ therapy. The company noted that age and disease stage are components of the FLIPI score and therefore were indirectly adjusted for through inclusion of FLIPI in the analysis. As such, the company did not consider their omission to substantially bias the analyses. The EAG clinical experts stated that the reliability of an indirect comparison would be further negatively impacted by missing these important prognostic factors, in addition to the differences in inclusion/exclusion criteria applied to the two populations. 

The final analysis was conducted using the following TEMs: age (≥60 years), disease stage 3-4, sex, prior  autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), prior chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR-T), prior lines of therapy ≥4, progression of disease within 24 months (POD24) after first line chemotherapy inducted therapy (CIT), refractory to both anti-CD20 and alkylator therapy, refractory to most recent anti lymphoma therapy, and prior treatment with combination of rituximab and lenalidomide (R[2] ). Table 27 of the CS presents the selection of the TEMs with reasons for inclusion or exclusion. 

Prior to matching, there were notable differences between the epcoritamab trial population and the HMRN comparator cohort across several key baseline characteristics. The percentage of patients in HMRN with advanced-stage disease (stage 3-4) was ******************** than in EPCORE NHL-1 (**** vs *****, respectively). Prior CAR-T therapy was reported in **** of EPCORE NHL-1 patients, but was ****** in HMRN, suggesting a ********** in access for advanced treatments. Prior treatment with R2 (lenalidomide and rituximab), was ************* in EPCORE NHL-1 than in HMRN with limited 95% CI overlap, as with patients with 4+ prior lines of therapy. These differences raise concerns about residual imbalances in disease

severity and prior treatment exposure, which may affect the validity of the estimates derived from the MAIC. 

There were no statistically significant differences between the other TEMs, which included the proportions of people aged 60 years and over, males, prior CAR-T, POD24 after 1L chemoimmunotherapy (CIT), and refractory to both anti-CD20 and an alkylator.

## **3.4.5 EAG Critique of MAIC** 

The EAG has a number of concerns about the MAIC which question its suitability for decision-making. Firstly, the small effective sample size for the MAIC weighted population, plus the small sample size of HMRN cohort means the true estimate of relative efficacy is unlikely to be represented and could be influenced by the outcomes of a small number of individuals. Secondly, the methodology of the MAIC is unlikely to account for the differences between a trial and real-world population, particularly the stricter inclusion/exclusion criteria of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial. Known key prognostic factors are unable to be included in the MAIC. While the MAIC may be a theoretically appropriate method in the absence of direct comparative data, its implementation in this submission is fundamentally limited by data constraints and uncertain assumptions. 

Finally, the EAG considers it implausible that the application of weights to a trial dataset, when matching to real-world evidence, would improve the efficacy of epcoritamab. The EAG interprets this as evidence that the MAIC results lack face validity. 

For these reasons, the EAG considers the MAIC to be unhelpful and potentially misleading for decision-making purposes. Whilst a naïve comparison clearly has its limitations, the EAG considers this the strongest evidence to inform relative efficacy. The company could explore applying a simulated treatment comparison[34] however this would be limited to the same covariates as the MAIC, so is not an obvious improvement over a naïve comparison. 

The company’s preference to use of the COVID-modified cohort is also a concern. The EAG understands that the HMRN cohort was also likely impacted by COVID, and so to remove these events in one source may introduce bias to the analysis by increasing the likelihood of more negative outcomes in the HMRN group. Additionally, COVID deaths were adjudicated using prespecified and physician-led criteria; however, censoring all deaths in this category may still risk introducing bias, 

81 



<!-- page 424 -->

particularly as COVID-related deaths were not similarly censored in the HMRN comparator cohort.. The EAG prefers to use the non-COVID adjusted analysis in a naïve comparison. 

## **3.5** _**Additional work on clinical effectiveness undertaken by the EAG**_ 

The EAG updated the company’s MEDLINE and Embase searches, to check for any new publications. Two additional studies were identified as potentially relevant (Day 2025[35] and Gao 2025[36] ), but were excluded after examination of the full paper. Two recent abstracts were also identified (via Google Alerts) that may be useful if the 3L+ population is to be considered.[23, 24] 

The EAG also conducted targeted searches to check for any relevant studies missed due to identified limitations in the company’s search strategies. Only one publication of relevance was identified, a RWE study of quality of life in patients with FL in Europe (including the UK) and USA (Johnson 2024).[22] The EAG considers that this study could be useful should there be a focus on the 3L+ population, although notes that HRQoL was not assessed in response to a treatment and that various treatments had been given at 1L and 2L so may not reflect the current treatment pathway. Search strategies for additional searches run by the EAG can be found in Appendix 8.1.1 

## **3.6** _**Conclusions of the clinical effectiveness section**_ 

The CS presents direct evidence from the EPCORE NHL-1, an ongoing open label multinational single arm phase 2 study evaluating the safety and efficacy of epcoritamab in R/R patients with B-cell lymphomas, including FL grades 1 – 3A among adults having exhausted all previous lines of therapy (subgroup of relevance to the decision problem in this submission). The study was divided into three parts of which the expansion and optimisation parts within the 4L+ and 3L+ subgroups of patients with FL relevant to this submission. While the CS focussed on outcomes for the 4L+ subgroups, the EAG also considered those of the 3L+ subgroup. 

Primary efficacy outcomes across subgroups are reported as follows: In the expansion 4L+ subgroup (latest data cut), an overall response rate (ORR) of ****************************** was observed. ORR for the 3L+ subgroup was not 

82 



<!-- page 425 -->

reported in the latest data cut, but an ORR of 82% was noted in an earlier analysis. No ORR data were reported for the 4L+ optimisation cohorts, while the ORR for the 3L+ optimisation cohort was ***************, at **** compared with the expansion part. A complete response ******* and ***** partial response was also observed in the expansion cohort 4L+ subgroup, while in the 3L+ subgroup: ***** and ***** achieved CR and PR, respectively. Rates for CR and PR in the 3L+ optimisation phase were ***** and *****, respectively.  The EAG consider the non-adjusted COVID-19 data for the survival analysis to be the more appropriate source of evidence, as it better reflects real-world trial conditions and avoids introducing bias by selectively censoring deaths, given the uncertainty around the timing and confirmation of CR in those who have died of COVID-19. 

The most frequent adverse events for each subgroup were CRS (expansion 4L+ *******3L+********optimisation******), fatigue (expansion 4L+********3L+ *******optimisation 3L+ *****), COVID-19 (expansion 4L+********3L+ *******optimisation 3L+ *****), and injection site reactions (expansion 4L+*******************optimisation******). 

Overall, the EAG has no major concerns about the EPCORE NHL-1 risk of bias. However, the EAG notes that patient characteristics of those lost to follow-up were not described, neither were characteristics of censored patients, thus limiting the ability to fully assess the impact of incomplete follow-up. Although there was a difference between the dose escalation used in the expansion phase (efficacy data) and the ********* optimised regimen, the EAG clinical experts did not consider this difference to have any bearing on the clinical, or safety results. 

HRQoL outcomes for the expansion 4L+ subgroup were presented in the CS, while data for the 3L+ subgroup were only available in the CSR. No HRQoL data was presented for the optimisation cohorts. The EAG notes that changes generally did not exceed the MID. 

The EAG considers it difficult to fully ascertain the generalisability of the EPCORE NHL-1 study to UK clinical practice in patients with FL. In part, this is due to the small sample size; however, the EAG notes that there are some differences in the sample from the UK only and the wider sample which may indicate some generalisability issues.  Despite this, however, the EAG clinical experts did not have major concerns

with the representativeness of the EPCORE NHL-1 participants to the populations seen in UK clinical practice.

## **4 COST EFFECTIVENESS** 

## **4.1** _**EAG comment on company’s review of cost-effectiveness**_ 

## _**evidence**_ 

The company undertook SLRs to identify cost-effectiveness studies, health-related quality of life (HRQoL) studies and cost and healthcare resource data in patients with R/R FL in a second-line or later setting. These are reported in Appendices E, F and G respectively of the CS. Searches for the cost-effectiveness and costs/healthcare resource use SLRs were undertaken together. 

## **4.1.1 Search strategies** 

Searches were originally undertaken in April 2023, with updates in February and November 2024. An appropriate selection of sources was searched, including bibliographic databases, HTA agencies’ websites and recent conference proceedings. Given that the CRD databases are no longer updated, the EAG would recommend searching the International HTA Database provided by INAHTA to ensure comprehensiveness and currency.  Reference lists of previous SLRs, pooled analyses and meta-analyses were also checked (Appendices F and G, Tables 43 and 52), though reference lists of included studies do not appear to have been checked for additional studies. 

The EconLit, Embase and MEDLINE search strategies (reported in Appendix E Tables 23-25, Appendix F Tables 39-41 and Clarification C8 Appendix ‘Economic SLR search strategies’) use multiple search terms for relapsed/refractory or 2L+ follicular lymphoma. In Embase and MEDLINE, these were combined with a comprehensive selection of Emtree/MeSH terms and free-text keywords relating to economic evaluations, cost effectiveness, HRQoL, costs and resource use. 

Publication date limits have been used in update search strategies to exclude results published before the date of the previous search. This is not best practice and risks missing relevant results, as publications are not added to bibliographic databases as soon as they are published. More appropriate date fields such as “date created” or “date delivered” can be used for a comprehensive search. Additional limitations affecting the sensitivity of the search strategies include missing Emtree or MeSH headings for the relapsed/refractory concept ( ‘refractory cancer’, ‘cancer 

85 



<!-- page 428 -->

recurrence’, ‘salvage therapy’, ‘recurrence’) and not searching the keywords field (using title and abstract fields only for free text searches). 

The EAG ran targeted searches in MEDLINE and Embase (see Appendix 8.1.1 for search strategies) to check for any studies relevant to the NICE scope that may have been missed by the company’s searches, whether due to limitations in the search strategies or because they were published in recent months. These searches identified no additional, relevant studies 

## **4.2** _**Summary and critique of the company’s submitted economic evaluation by the EAG**_ 

The eligibility criteria were suitable for the SLR performed. The results of the SLR appear comprehensive enough despite the limitations highlighted above. As the EAG’s targeted searches failed to yield additional relevant data, the EAG considers the submitted economic evaluation evidence by the company comprehensive.

## **4.2.2 Model structure** 

The company constructed a de novo cost-utility model with a weekly cycle length and a 35.2-year time horizon, using partitioned survival, to assess the costeffectiveness of epcoritamab versus current 4L+ care. Three health states - 

87 



<!-- page 430 -->

progression free (PF), progressed disease (PD), and death are described by the model (Figure 4). 

All patients started in the PF state and remained there until disease progression or death. Patients whose disease progressed remain in the PD state until death (absorbing health state). 

**==> picture [452 x 151] intentionally omitted <==**

**Figure 4:** Partition survival model (PSM) and survival curves informing the proportion of patients per health state (OS, overall survival; PFS, progression free survival) 

Source: CS Figure 21 

The partitioned survival model (PSM) method uses “area under the curve” approach, where health state occupancy at a given time point is taken directly from survival curves fitted to the clinical data. The PFS curves, indicate, at each timepoint, the proportion of patients alive without disease progression whilst the OS curves represent proportion of patients alive at any given timepoint. The proportion of patients in the PD state was calculated as the difference between the proportion of living patients (OS health state) and the proportion of patients who are both living and pre-progression (PFS health state). The OS and PFS curves were determined by fitting parametric models to the EPCORE NHL-1 study data adjusted to the HMRN dataset through a MAIC analysis. MAIC-adjusted hazard ratios were applied to the unadjusted epcoritamab data to obtain the PFS and OS outcomes for the current 4L+ care (see section 4.2.6 for details). 

Background mortality was used in the survival extrapolations in the model to ensure that the OS of patients does not exceed the survival of an age and sex matched population within the UK. 

88 



<!-- page 431 -->

TTD for epcoritamab was assumed not equal to PFS in the base case analysis. Patients stopped treatment due to progression or other reasons with a stopping rule of 3 years applied to complete responders. Clinical experts to the EAG indicated it’s reasonable to consider stopping point because of AEs that could occur at this time the longer patients are on treatment. The EAG therefore considers it a logical approach as consideration is given to treatment discontinuations prior to disease progression for reasons such as toxicity. For the comparator arm (current 4L + care), TTD was obtained directly from the HMRN raw data reflecting the impact of the varied fixed treatment durations of the therapies within the basket on costeffectiveness outcomes. 

The company did not apply treatment waning in the model. The EAG’s clinical experts indicated that, when considering the population studied as a whole, one would expect that treatment does wane. One of the EAG’s experts stated that “ _the duration of complete responses curves do go down with time with just over 50% of the population who achieve CR remaining alive and in CR 3 years after achieving CR_ .” 

## **EAG Comments** : 

- A PSM is widely used in oncology trials to model clinically important endpoints such as OS and PFS and is suitable for use in this appraisal. Whilst the company’s justifications for using a PSM appear reasonable the EAG believes the company should have considered a state transition model (STM) since they used complete response (CR) to adjust for PFS status (as seen in the estimation of utilities). This modelling approach would enable the transition of patients between sub-states (PFS with CR, PFS without CR, PD, and death), a proper estimation of proportion of patients with and without CR, the duration in CR/no CR in each model cycle and the associated outcomes. 

- The lifetime horizon of 35.2 years, considering the mean age (64.80) of patients in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial at enrolment, is long enough to capture differences in costs and benefits associated with the strategies being compared. 

89 



<!-- page 432 -->

- A weekly cycle length used in the model was short enough to accurately capture the model outcomes. 

- TTD for epcoritamab was capped to PFS and OS to maintain consistency in the model. For the current 4L+, TTD was not capped but the EAG notes that the TTD curve was consistently below the PFS and OS over the modelled time on treatment. 

- Treatment waning was not applied to the company’s base case analysis or explored in scenario analysis. EAG’s clinical experts’ opinion is that treatment waning would occur and applying treatment waning in the economic model is a reasonable assumption.  The EAG was unable to incorporate any treatment waning scenarios at the time of report submission as we awaited further input on clinically plausible treatment waning assumptions to explore. 

## **4.2.3 Population** 

The economic model considered adult patients with R/R FL after three or more lines of systemic therapy, i.e., 4L+ R/R FL 1-3A patient population. As discussed in section 1.3, the population partially aligns with the NICE scope and the UK marketing authorisation (MA) for epcoritamab. The anticipated MA is for adult patients with R/R FL after two or more lines of systemic therapy (i.e. R/R 3L+ FL). 

The base line characteristics of patients were informed by the EPCORE NHL-1 study’s expansion cohort (n=81), a subset with R/R iNHL who have received three or more prior lines of systemic therapy (4L+). The EPCORE NHL-1 was an open label, phase 1/2, multicentre, multi-national single arm study evaluating dosage, efficacy and safety of epcoritamab in various forms of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (FL, DLBCL, and MCL). The trial was performed in three parts: dose escalation, dose expansion and dose optimization (see CS, section 2.3). The dose expansion FL cohort were made up of 3L+ FL population who had received 2 or more lines (n=128) with 81 at 4L+ with the primary outcome being ORR.  As mentioned above, the model considered the R/R FL patient population that had received three or more lines of systemic therapy. 

90 



<!-- page 433 -->

- The EAG considers that the 3L+ FL (n=128) broader population aligns better to the MA and NICE scope. 

The baseline characteristics used in the cost effectiveness model (CEM) are mean age 64.80kg, gender distribution 34.6% female, mean weight 77.40kg and BSA 1.90m[2 ] . Baseline mean age and gender distribution were used to obtain age and sex specific mortality for the general population. All doses in the model that are weight and body surface area (BSA) dependant were adjusted using the mean weight and BSA respectively 

- The EAG’s clinical experts indicated that baseline characteristics used in the economic model are reflective of the patient population seen in NHS clinical practice. 

## **4.2.4 Interventions and comparators** 

## **4.2.4.1 Intervention** 

The intervention in this appraisal is epcoritamab. Epcoritamab is administered as a subcutaneous injection  until disease progression, toxicity or withdrawal of consent. Whilst all efficacy analyses are based on the dose expansion cohort, the dosing data for epcoritamab used in the economic model is consistent with the optimisation part of the EPCORE NHL-1 trial for cycle 1. This was a priming dose of 0.16mg in day 1 cycle 1, two intermediate doses on day 8 (0.8mg) and day15 (3mg) of cycle 1 and full dose (48mg) on day 22 of cycle 1 and then weekly until the end of cycle 3. The full dose (48mg) is administered every two weeks in cycles 4-9 and every four weeks in cycle 10 and beyond (a cycle is 28days). In response to clarification A10, the company noted that the dosing in the optimisation part of the EPCORE NHL-1 reflects the anticipated UK MA and this step-up dosing had been explored in the optimisation part to reduce incidence of CRS. The company noted that 

pharmacokinetic outcomes had remained similar between patients who received the three step-up dose regimen and patients who received the two step-up dose regimens in EPCORE NHL-1.  The EAG’s clinical experts confirmed that the dose differences do not affect interpretation of results as the second intermediate dose (3mg on day 15) was given to mitigate AE of CRS. 

91 



<!-- page 434 -->

- The EAG is satisfied with the dosing schedule used in the model for epcoritamab. 

## **4.2.4.2 Comparators** 

The company modelled the comparator through a basket of care noting that there is no standard of care for patients with R/R FL 4L+ in UK clinical practice and treatments for these patients are individualised. The most prevalent option in each sub-basket as identified from the HMRN data was used to represent each subbasket. For example, in the R-chemotherapy sub-basket,****% of patients received R-bendamustine, followed by R-CHOP (***%) and R-GDP (***%), the company chose R-bendamustine to represent the sub-basket in the current 4L+ care basket (Figure 5).  In other + experimental sub-basket, obinutuzumab + bendamustine was selected to reflect UK clinical practice. A summary of the selected therapies used to represent each sub-basket is presented in Table 25 

Clinical advice to the EAG also indicated no standard care for 4L+ and that treatments are based on whatever worked previously. Also, as new treatments get approved, treatment options start being used at earlier lines. As a result, best supportive care (BSC) would be an appropriate comparator as it is being considered in most 4L+ setting primarily due to lack of effective treatments for 4L+ patients. 

The company has not considered best supportive care as a comparator as included in NICE scope because it is expected that patients who would receive BSC would not be considered fit enough to be eligible for an active intervention such as epcoritamab. Clinical advice to the EAG indicates BSC should be a comparator because some patients at 4L+ who are not fit enough for chemotherapy would be eligible for therapy with epcoritamab instead of BSC. 

92

## **4.2.5 Perspective and discounting** 

NHS and PSS perspective was used for estimating resource use and costs with an annual 3.5% discount rate applied to all costs and utilities in the model base case in line with NICE reference case. 

93 



<!-- page 436 -->

## **4.2.6 Treatment effectiveness and extrapolation** 

To inform the health-state occupancy of the economic model, the company fitted parametric models to data from EPCORE NHL-1 to predict the future efficacy of epcoritamab PFS and OS, and applied hazard ratios from the MAIC analysis to predict the relative efficacy for the comparator group. 

The company submission states that the overall survival modelling is described as incorporating background mortality by not permitting the modelled hazard rate to fall below the age and sex matched population of the UK. The EAG notes that the implementation of background mortality in the model does not exactly match this description and instead represents a relative survival approach where the impact of background mortality is applied in addition to trial mortality via an internal additive approach. 

## **4.2.6.1 Epcoritamab** 

## **4.2.6.1.1 PFS and OS** 

For PFS and OS, the company fitted parametric survival models (exponential, Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic, Gompertz, and generalised gamma) to the COVIDmodified dose-expansion 4L+ cohort PFS, OS, and TTD data from EPCORE NHL-1 (n=81), in line with NICE TSD14. Based on assessment of clinical plausibility and goodness-of-fit statistics, the company selects the log-normal extrapolation for both PFS and OS. 

The EAG is content with the choice of PFS curve, however the OS extrapolation was deemed optimistic by the EAG clinical experts. If maintaining the use of the COVIDmodified data, the EAG prefers to use the exponential extrapolation as it has the lowest goodness-of-fit statistics and produced the most pessimistic extrapolation of the models fitted to this data. The limited amount of information in the data owing to the limited sample size and number of events also aligns with selecting an extrapolation with fewer parameters being less prone to overfitting. 

However, the EAG preference is to use the COVID-unmodified data from EPCORE NHL-1 for PFS and OS. Firstly, the EAG considers the extrapolations coming from the COVID-censored data to be too optimistic based on feedback from the EAG clinical experts. Secondly, the EAG is concerned about the potential for COVID to have affected the HMRN cohort and so should be maintained in the EPCORE NHL-1 

94 



<!-- page 437 -->

data for balance. Thirdly, it is unclear whether COVID is solely attributable for all COVID-related death events. Following the same approach as the company, but using the COVID-unmodified data, the EAG also selects log-normal extrapolations for both outcomes. 

The company consulted four clinical experts who provided predictions of future PFS and OS for epcoritamab. No estimates were shared with the EAG for the comparator population. The EAG is unclear over the context these estimates were generated in (i.e. what data were presented to the experts and whether it was specific to COVIDcensored EPCORE NHL-1 population, or to UK real-world use of epcoritamab). The EAG’s clinical experts commented that these predictions were optimistic for UK realworld population given the comorbidities and older age of this population, and uncertainty around long-term efficacy. The mid-values reported by the company were considered an upper bound by the EAG experts. The EAG notes that for 15 years and beyond, the company’s OS extrapolations exceed the estimates of their experts. 

Hence, the EAG is satisfied that their extrapolations using the COVID-unadjusted data result in less optimistic outcomes for epcoritamab, consistent with the expectations of their clinical experts.

## **4.2.6.2.2 TTD** 

The EAG accepts the approach to extrapolation of HMRN TTD data, which fits an exponential model to the HMRN data, and does not consider any alternatives. Note, that time on treatment for the comparator is not capped.

## **4.2.6.3 Additional EAG comments on time-to-event modelling** 

Whilst the EAG does not object to the selection process of the company’s individual models, the EAG notes that the combination of models prefered by the company has some unexpected results. Firstly the post-progession survival for epcoritamab exceeds the pre-progression survival time for epcoritamab. Secondly, the mean post-progression survival for epcoritamab is far in excess of the equivalent time for current 4L+ care. Under the EAG’s preferred approach to modelling, the epcoritamab post-progression survival time is less than the pre-progression survival time, and more similar to the comparator.

## **4.2.7 Health related quality of life** 

## **4.2.7.1 Health-related quality of life data identified in the review** 

A SLR was conducted to identify HRQoL studies from electronic data bases as discussed in section 3.1. The search identified nine studies from 11 publications that included data for 2L+ R/R FL of which two reported patients receiving 3L+ therapy, three studies with data for R/R NHL: two reporting results of mixed population (> 80% FL) and one for a subset of FL. 

The most used instrument to assess the HRQoL in the included studies is EORTC QLQ-C30 (n=5). Other instruments used are SF-36 (n=3), EQ-5D (n=3), and Functional Assessment of cancer Treatment-Lymphoma (FACT-Lym) (n=3). 

Searches of previous NICE HTAs were also performed to identify and compare utility values used across the different appraisals. Utility values used for PFS were seen to be comparable. 

The company selected the studies by Wild et al[37] and Cognet et al[38] from those identified in the SLR for their analysis. The utility decrement applied to the PFS to obtain the PD utility was based on Wild et al, 2006,[37] following precedents set in other FL NICE appraisals. Although this study is frequently used in NICE TAs of FL, it is still a conference abstract with no full text available. Utilities from Cognet et al[38] and TA892[39] were applied in scenario analysis but no justification provided for their preference. 

EAG additional search did not find any relevant study.

## **EAG comments:** 

The concerns of the EAG are: 

- Linear mixed model analysis: As highlighted in section 4.2.7.2, the company said they performed a LMM twice, the first one accounted for health state PFS/PD which they reported lacks face validity.  The second LMM was conducted on a subset of patients in PFS exploring the covariate “CR status”. The EAG could not validate both analyses because the company failed to provide the requested LMM output (Clarification response B14). 

   - The EAG understands from the result presented (CS, Table 64) that CR status was applied to obtain utilities by using mean estimates of the patients who had CR and no CR from the trial data. The results do not reflect LMM regression results as no intercept or coefficients were presented for any variable. 

- Using CR to adjust for PFS utility for both arms: Whilst the EAG experts agree with the PF utility by CR as disease status is a determinant of HRQoL, they noted that the impact of TEAEs on HRQoL in the PFS should also be considered because patients who achieve CR remain on treatment for a longer period in the epcoritamab arm. The EAG considers this approach might have created a form of bias in favour of epcoritamab. 

   - The EAG prefers to use the same PFS utility for both arms in their base case analysis. A utility of ***** obtained by the company from the trial data without using CR status was applied for the PFS for both arms and a utility decrement used by the company from Wild et al was applied to the PFS utility to obtain PD utility. 

104 



<!-- page 447 -->

- Exclusion of adverse events disutilities: Utility decrements from AEs were not included in the CEM base case analysis, and no justification was provided. It is worth noting that there have been inconsistencies in the application of utility decrements from AEs across NICE STAs of lymphoma. Whilst some appraisals have considered the use of AE disuilities in their economic model like in TA627, others like TA502 have not included it because the utility captured using the EQ-5D instrument within the clinical trials already accounted for decrements due to occurrence of AEs. Across literature different approaches have been applied. Some authors are of the opinion that the utility values of disease states already reflected the impact of AEs.[43] NICE TSD 12[44] states that a clear justification should be provided for either inclusion or exclusion of disutilities for adverse events in decision-analytic models. Consequently, the EAG performed a scenario analysis including AE disutilities to the company’s base case to ascertain the impact of their base case assumption. The result suggests a negligible increase to the ICER. 

## **4.2.7.4 Adverse Events** 

Adverse events (AEs) of grade 3 or 4 that occurred in ≥ 5% of patients were included in the economic model. The source of AEs for epcoritamab is the EPCORE NHL-1 dose expansion 4L+ cohort (n=81) and that of the comparator was sourced from TA894. The company notes lack of safety data for chemotherapy made it difficult to model AE outcomes through the basket of care. AE reported for R-CHOP in a previous NICE TA894 appraisal was used to represent the AE for the current 4L+ care basket because R-chemo was the second largest sub-basket in the current 4L+ care. 

Table 35 presents the TEAEs that were applied in the model. AEs that were recorded in EPCORE NHL-1 and not reported for R-CHOP were set to zero.

## **EAG comment:** 

- The EAG is concerned that the approach used by the company to assign AEs to the current 4L+ basket of care does not accurately capture the probabilities of AEs that represent the therapies in the basket. The EAG believes that using varying proportions across the different therapies in the basket to provide a weighted value for each AE will better represent the AEs for the current 4L + care arm which is consistent with a previous NICE TA1001 appraisal where HMRN therapy basket was also used as comparator. This approach has been applied in the EAG base case. 

- Another area of uncertainty is the exclusion of CRS AE from the epcoritamab arm which would have underestimated the costs of AEs resulting from the use of epcoritamab. Though in the CS, CRS grade 3+ occurred in only one patient (1.2%) in the EPCORE NHL-1 study expansion phase (n=81), grade 2 CRS required treatment with tocilizumab and other care provided for CRS patients. The EAG believes epcoritamab use may lead to some patients, necessitating treatment with tocilizumab in practice and prefers that all grade 2 CRS 

106 



<!-- page 449 -->

requiring treatment with tocilizumab be included in the CEM. This approach is consistent with previous NICE appraisal TA894 of R/R follicular lymphoma and has been included in the EAG base case. 

## **4.2.8 Resources and costs** 

## **4.2.8.1 Resource use identification, measurement and valuation studies** 

The CS stated a SLR was performed to identify costs and resource use data that might be relevant to this appraisal. 16 studies were identified across 18 publications which included four retrospective studies that reported patients on 3L+ therapy. Fourteen studies reported on direct health care costs and resource use and no study reported any indirect costs. 

- Direct costs reported across the studies are medical costs, inpatient costs, outpatient costs, emergency room (ER) costs, physician office visit costs, pharmacy costs and treatment costs specific to FL. 

- Resource use reported are frequency of inpatient hospitalisation, ER visits, physician office visits, length of stay in hospital; inpatient and ICU, outpatient visits including number of days in outpatient services, and drug administration days. 

No study was found that reported data for a UK population. The studies reported were for US (10), Canada (1), Italy (1), multiple location (1) and 3 did not have any geographical focus. 

A detailed critique of the search strategy is provided in section 4.1. In the EAG additional search, no relevant study was identified.

## **4.2.8.3 Costs of subsequent treatment** 

In the CEM, patients in both arms received subsequent treatments (i.e. ≥ 5[th ] line of therapy (LOT)) upon progression to the PD state. The treatments were assumed to be the same for both arms because there is no standard treatment pathway for those reaching 4L +. While the EAG were concerned with this assumption, advice from their clinical experts confirmed its rationality, due to the absence of a standard treatment for patients at 4L+ and typical recycling of prior treatments. 

The costs of subsequent treatments were applied as a single costs per cycle throughout the time patients are in the PD state. These costs were estimated from the drug acquisition and administration costs of treatments within the basket based on their dosing schedules as defined by their SmPC divided by the number of cycles (time on treatment) for each therapy to obtain the average costs per cycle (Table 42). The average costs per cycle were weighted according to share of patients on each therapy to obtain the basket cost per cycle which was then applied throughout the cycle duration that patients remain in the PD state. All patients (100%) that progressed were assumed to receive subsequent treatment in the CEM. The EAG considers the assumptions used in estimating the costs of subsequent treatment to be appropriate. 

The company explored the impact of changing the basket mix of subsequent treatment by using current 4L+ care basket proportions obtained from TA894 as outlined in section 4.2, Table 43.

## **EAG comments** : 

The EAG deems the estimation of resource use and costs reasonable, but concerns included: 

- Clinical benefits of subsequent treatments used in the EPCORE NHL-1 study captured without corresponding presentation of associated costs: The company assumed both arms received the same subsequent treatments for reasons highlighted in section 4.2.8.3. This assumption was validated by the company and the EAG experts as the subsequent treatments reflect UK clinical practice. Considering that in the EPCORE NHL-1 study the FL 4L + (n=81) patients received different subsequent treatments; systemic antilymphoma therapy (****%), allogenic stem cell transplant (***** and CAR-T therapy(****), the EAG is concerned that the effect of epcoritamab might have been overestimated in the clinical efficacy data used in the CEM for patients who were not censored (**** who received CAR-T). Not adjusting for treatment effects of the subsequent treatments received by these patients would have inherently biased the results of the analysis in favour of epcoritamab. 

- Resource use in the epcoritamab arm: Resource use for haematologist consultation was thought to be underestimated for epcoritamab. EAG clinical expert advised that patients on epcoritamab will have weekly visits in the first month and then monthly visits thereafter. Also, the use of PET scan every 12 months. The EAG have considered the increased haematologist consultant visits in its base case and explored inclusion of PET scans in a scenario analysis. 

- Adverse event costs in the epcoritamab arm: Adverse event costs were thought to be underestimated for epcoritamab because of exclusion of CRS which is a major AE associated with the use of epcoritamab. The EAG notes that in the EPCORE NHL-1 study, some patients who had grade 2 CRS were treated with tocilizumab. Therefore, EAG have added costs of all grades 2 

117 



<!-- page 460 -->

CRS that required treatment with tocilizumab in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial expansion part (4L+) in their base case analysis. 

118

## **4.2.9 Severity** 

The company quantified disease severity through two different but related measures of disease severity – the absolute QALY shortfall and proportional QALY shortfall - in line with NICE’s Health Technology Evaluations manual.[60] Absolute shortfall represents the number of future QALYs that are lost by people living with the disease and _on current standard of care_ whilst proportional shortfall represents the proportion of future QALYs that are lost by people living with the disease and _on current standard of care_ . The severity modifier reflects a spectrum of disease severity and allows a QALY weight of (x1, x1.2 and x1.7) to apply depending on the QALY shortfall (AS or PS) (Table 46). The multiplier is applied to the incremental QALYs associated with a technology before the calculation of ICERs implying the £20,000 to £30,000 threshold is retained regardless of QALY weight chosen. 

## **Table 46: QALY weightings for severity** 

|**QALY weight**|**Proportional QALY shortfall**|**Absolute QALY shortfall**|
|---|---|---|
|1|Less than 0.85|Less than 12|
|X1.2|0.85 to 0.95|12 to 18|
|X1.7|At least 0.95|At least 18|



The number of QALYs that the general population living without the condition would be expected to accrue for the rest of their lifetime was estimated to be 10.91 and was based on the characteristics of the EPCORE NHL-1 4L+ study subpopulation i.e., age = 64.80 years and proportion females = 34.60%. The remaining QALYs accrued by people with _relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after three or more systemic treatments_ and on current standard of care were 0.985 and estimated using the company’s base case cost-effectiveness model. The resulting QALY shortfalls (absolute and proportional) are shown in Table 47 below. Since the absolute QALY shortfall is below 12 but the proportional QALY shortfall greater than 85%, the company appropriately concluded that, based on their base case assumptions, a x1.2 multiplier for disease severity was appropriate for this appraisal as per NICE guidance. 

119

**Table 47: Summary of QALY shortfall analysis  (table 59 CS)** 

|**Approach**|**Expected**<br>**total QALYs**<br>**for the**<br>**general**<br>**population**|**Total QALYs that**<br>**people living with a**<br>**condition would be**<br>**expected to have**<br>**with current**<br>**treatment**|**Absolute**<br>**QALY**<br>**shortfall**|**Proportional**<br>**QALY**<br>**shortfall**|**QALY**<br>**weight**|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|Company|10.91|0.985|9.93|91%|x1.2|
|EAG|10.91|1.70|9.21|84.4%|x1|



The EAG replicated the QALY shortfall analysis, but using the EAG’s preferred base case assumptions in the economic model and arrived at a different conclusions. Based on the EAG’s preferred assumptions, the remaining QALYs accrued by people with _relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after three or more systemic treatments_ and on current standard of care are estimated to be 1.70 vs. 0.985 (company’s). The proportional QALY shortfall was less than 85% (but very close i.e., 84.4%) whilst absolute QALY shortfall <12.  Therefore, in its base case the EAG does not include a severity modifier, but presents EAG’s base case ICER adjusted for x1.2 severity modifier in Table 55. 

## **EAG comments:** 

- The company appropriately estimated the absolute and proportional QALY shortfalls, using preferred value sets.[40] 

- The EAG was able to replicate the QALY shortfall values in the company submission. 

- The EAG recalculated the QALY shortfalls based on EAG’s base case assumptions and arrived at different conclusions from the company’s i.e., a severity weighting does not apply for this appraisal. 

   - It is uncertain whether a severity modifier is appropriate for this appraisal.

## **5.2** _**Company’s sensitivity analyses**_ 

Uncertainty was explored via probabilistic sensitivity analysis, scenario analyses and univariate sensitivity analyses. 

In line with PSA methodology, each uncertain parameter in the model was 

represented as a probability distribution, based on published recommendations. One thousand simulations were performed for the PSA, allowing values to be drawn at 

121 



<!-- page 464 -->

random from each probability distribution, for every simulation.  Table 49 shows the results of the PSA for the analysis where QALYs are not adjusted for severity. The corresponding incremental cost-effectiveness scatterplot and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves are shown in Figure 8 and Figure 9. The scatterplot shows that the iterations fall within the ******************* indicating that epcoritamab is *********** and ************** than current 4L+ care at a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY. The probability of cost-effectiveness at similar threshold was **%. It is worth noting that for the PSA, the company did not apply the severity modifier directly to the incremental QALYs but to the WTP threshold. The company justified this approach on the basis that “as the PSA samples each parameter individually according to their mean and standard error, the output of the analysis cannot robustly incorporate a severity modifier as variations in individual parameters may impact absolute and proportional QALY shortfall”. By applying the severity modifier (x1.2) to the £30,000/QALY WTP threshold, the company concludes that, probability of costeffectiveness of epcoritamab is **% at the adjusted WTP threshold of £36,000/QALY. The NICE guidance is that the severity modifier should be applied to the incremental QALYs. However, whether the severity modifier was applied to incremental QALYs after PSA or the modifier was applied directly to WTP returns similar conclusions in company’s base case.

## **5.3** _**Model validation and face validity check**_ 

The EAG conducted an extensive review of the model submitted by the company. The model appears to reflect the assumptions made by the company and contained clinical aspects necessary to address the decision problem. The EAG sought clinical validation of (i) the model assumptions (both EAG and company’s) and (ii) model’s output ((LYG, QALYs) and relevant economic outcomes (e.g., treatment costs)). 

## **6 EXTERNAL ASSESSMENT GROUP’S ADDITIONAL ANALYSES** 

## **6.1** _**Exploratory and sensitivity analyses undertaken by the EAG**_ 

Following our critique of the company’s economic model, the EAG made changes to the company’s model to explore the impact of individual changes to the base case results. The suggested changes along with the EAG justifications are presented below 

- Using a naïve analysis to inform relative efficacy of epcoritamab vs. current 4L+ care 

In section 3.4.5, the EAG provides a detailed critique of the company’s MAIC and concludes that the MAIC is unhelpful and potentially mis-leading for decision-making purposes. The EAG believes that, whilst clearly flawed, a naïve comparison is probably the best approach to inform relative efficacy of epcoritamab in this case. The EAG has conducted an analysis to explore the impact on outcomes (LYG, QALYs) and costs of using a naïve analysis rather than MAIC to inform relative efficacy of epcoritamab (Table 52; Table 53). The analysis also uses Covid- 

127 



<!-- page 470 -->

unadjusted data contrary to the company’s approach where covid-adjusted data for epcoritamab was used in company’s base case. 

## • Epcoritamab OS extrapolation 

In section 3.2.5.1.1, the EAG highlighted that their clinical experts considered the company’s choice of lognormal model of OS for epcoritamab to be optimistic. If maintaining the COVID-modified data used by the company in their base case, the EAG explored the use of exponential extrapolation with the lowest goodness of fit statistics and most pessimistic extrapolation of models fitted to the data to evaluate the impact of using a model with fewer parameters and less prone to overfitting in view of the small sample size and number of events. 

- Using MAIC hazard ratios to the parametric extrapolation of the HMRN data to estimate the efficacy of epcoritamab. 

As outlined in section 4.2.6.1, the EAG explored using the MAIC hazard ratios on the parametric extrapolation of the HMRN data to evaluate the effect of this approach on the efficacy of epcoritamab. 

- Using COVID unmodified data of epcoritamab from EPCORE NHL-1 

As discussed in section 4.2.6.1, the company used COVID modified data to estimate the relative efficacy of epcoritamab but the EAG prefers the use of COVID unmodified data. A scenario analysis to assess the impact of using COVID unmodified data on the cost-effectiveness results was performed. 

- Using HMRN data to directly extrapolate the OS and PFS for the current 4L+ care. 

It was highlighted in section 4.2.6.2 that the EAG prefers to directly extrapolate the HMRN dataset due to the concerns with the MAIC. The EAG’s preferred 

extrapolation is a log-normal model for both PFS and OS, which had the lowest 

128 



<!-- page 471 -->

goodness-of-fit statistics and good visual fit. A scenario analysis was performed to assess the impact of this assumption. 

- Exploring alternative resource usage in the epcoritamab arm for 

haematologist consultant visits 

In Section 4.2.8.4, it was outlined that the clinical experts to the EAG indicated that haematologist consultant visits appear to be underestimated in the epcoritamab arm. They specified that haematologist consultant visits will be weekly in first month and then monthly thereafter because patients on epcoritamab usually have weekly infusions in the first month. The EAG has explored what impact this additional resource use will have on the cost-effectiveness results (Table 54). 

- Evaluate the impact of using proportions of AEs that represent AE for the therapies in the current 4L+ care basket. 

As discussed in section 3.2.6.4, the company used AE for R-CHOP to represent AE of the basket of care. The EAG evaluated the impact of using varying proportion of AEs that represent all the therapies in the basket. (Table 51)

Each adverse event proportion for a sub-basket was estimated by considering the proportion of patients taking the therapy that represent each sub-basket after reweighting the sub-basket proportions to sum up to 100%. 

New weights estimated are O-Benda – ******, R-CHOP – ******, and R[2] – ****** 

AE rate = proportion of patients taking the therapy x AE rate of the therapy……. (1) 

Weighted AE rate for the current 4L+ = Sum of AE rate of the therapies estimated from (1) …………………………… (2). 

Only AEs that occurred in ≥ 5% of patients were included in the model. 

- Estimating the impact of including grade 2 CRS that occurred in greater than 5% of patients in the EPCORE NHL-1 trial. 

As discussed in section 4.2.7.4 and section 3.2.7, the company model only incorporated grade 3 or 5 TEAEs that occurred in ≥ 5% of patients. CRS which is a major TEAE related to the use of epcoritamab was excluded in the model because it did not meet this criterion. The EAG indicated that grade 2 CRS required treatment with tocilizumab. The EAG’s experts noted that tocilizumab initial treatment costs are high. An exploratory analysis assessing the impact of the inclusion of all grades 2 CRS that required treatment in the optimization phase of the trial (data for expansion phase 4L+ not available) has been performed to assess the impact of company’s base case assumption. This approach has been taken in previous appraisals (see section 4.2.7.4) 

- Using same PFS utility for both epcoritamab arm and current 4L+ care and adjusting for PD utility with the utility decrement from wild et al, 2006. 

It was discussed in section 4.2.7.3 that utilities obtained by adjusting for CR status may be biased in favour of epcoritamab and that the EAG prefers to use the same PFS and PD utilities for both arms. A scenario analysis was performed to assess this assumption. 

130 



<!-- page 473 -->

- Applying AE disutility in the base case analysis. 

In section 4.2.7.3 , it was highlighted that AE disutilities were excluded from the 

company’s base case analysis. The EAG have included AE disutility to evaluate its impact on the cost-effectiveness results (Table 54). 

The EAG also corrected an error in the application of LDH cost in the company’s model (section 4.2.8.4).

## **6.4** _**Conclusions of the cost-effectiveness section**_ 

In summary, the model constructed by the company appears to be logical and company’s systematic literature searches comprehensive. 

142 



<!-- page 485 -->

The EAG has the following concerns regarding the cost-utility analysis (as detailed in Section 1.1): 

- Uncertainty in the estimates of relative effectiveness of epcoritamab compared with current 4L+ care obtained from the MAIC. The EAG notes the following concerns related to the MAIC: 

   - potential for relative efficacy estimates being biased by outcomes of a small number of individuals due to small sample sizes of the MAIC weighted population (n=40) and HMRN cohort (****). 

   - stricter inclusion/exclusion criteria of the EPCORE NHL-1 study means methodology of MAIC is unlikely to account for the differences between a trial and real-world population 

`o` Counterintuitively, the MAIC adjustment resulted in hazard ratios that favoured ************************* than in the unadjusted analysis, when one would expect the effect size to attenuate after adjusting, not improve. This further calls into question the face validity of the MAIC results. 

- Choice of data source to inform efficacy estimates for epcoritamab which results in widely varying estimates of QALY gains. 

   - Using covid-adjusted data for Epcoritamab appears inconsistent with approach used for HRMN data which does not appear to be adjusted for COVID-19 deaths. 

- Choice and source of data for modelling efficacy of comparator treatment which results in widely varying estimates of QALY gains 

   - The EAG generally agrees with the company that the HMRN dataset is probably the best currently available data on current 4L+ care in the UK. However, it is RWE data, that is missing key prognostic variables and where patient recruitment does not follow a strict inclusion/exclusion criterion. A larger real-world comparator cohort with 

143 



<!-- page 486 -->

more complete data on key prognostic variables could improve the validity of an adjusted comparison. 

- Other important factors that had an impact on the cost-effectiveness results (either costs or QALYs) included: 

   - Health state utility values applied in the model which differed between the treatment arms and were adjusted for complete response status. The EAG preferred to apply the same utility values to both treatment arms using data derived directly from the EPCORE NHL-1 study without adjustment for CR status 

   - Source of incidence data for adverse events for the comparator treatment which the EAG preferred to be weighted based on 3 out of the 4 treatments included in the sub-basket of care for current 4L+care and not based on data for R-CHOP only. 

The EAG could not explore any uncertainty in relative cost-effectiveness if the population under consideration fully matched that described in NICE’s final scope and UK marketing authorisation, ie., 3L+. 

The EAG have presented scenarios with a preferred base-case analysis. The ICER has **************** compared with the CS, except for PFS utilities where the ICER has *******. The EAG’s preferred naïve unadjusted comparison results in a ************** in the ICER. The EAG acknowledges the limitations of an unadjusted analysis but maintains that for the reasons stated above, this approach may better represent relative efficacy. Nonetheless, the EAG’s results of the cost-utility analysis should also be interpreted with caution. 

- Overall, in the absence of a head-to-head comparative study that evaluates efficacy of epcoritamab compared to current care, the relative efficacy of epcoritamab remains an area of great uncertainty.

**EAG report – factual accuracy check and confidential information check** 

“Data owners may be asked to check that confidential information is correctly marked in documents created by others in the evaluation before release.” (Section 5.4.9, NICE health technology evaluations: the manual). 

You are asked to check the EAG report to ensure there are no factual inaccuracies or errors in the marking of confidential information contained within it. The document should act as a method of detailing any inaccuracies found and how they should be corrected. 

If you do identify any factual inaccuracies or errors in the marking of confidential information, you must inform NICE by **5pm on 4 July 2025** using the below comments table. 

All factual errors will be highlighted in a report and presented to the appraisal committee and will subsequently be published on the NICE website with the committee papers.

## **1 Introduction** 

This addendum summarises the key issue “ _Disparity in the EAG modelling of COVID-unmodified survival data_ ” highlighted by the company (post initial factual accuracy check), followed by the EAG response. It also contains updated costeffectiveness analyses. A cPAS version of these updated analyses is provided separately. 

## **1.1** _**Digitisation and parameterisation of COVID-unmodified outcomes**_ 

## **Company:** 

The EAG’s digitisation and thus parameterisation of both the COVID-unmodified OS and PFS is different to the company analysis where survival has been estimated using patient-level data. In the case of OS and (to a lesser extent PFS) the EAG model underpredicts survival and using patient-level data for the COVID-unmodified survival reduces the EAG base case ICER compared with digitised curves. 

## **EAG Response:** 

The EAG acknowledges that analyses were conducted using digitised Kaplan-Meier data to estimate pseudo-IPD because IPD were not made available to the EAG. This approach is consistent with standard practice in HTA when IPD is not provided by the company. 

The EAG can confirm that the accuracy of the EAG’s digitised data produces is extremely high and are not the source of the difference between the EAG and company models. The observed differences noted by the company arise from the company’s implementation of background mortality, which applies a relative survival approach (adding background mortality to trial mortality). Whilst this was described in the company submission when describing background mortality, the CS also reported that standard parametric models were used, which led to this confusion. 

The EAG notes the company’s view that the survival estimated from the EAG’s extrapolation has slightly lower survival probabilities compared with IPD (table 1: Company FAC check v3). This is consistent with the application of excess 



<!-- page 564 -->

background mortality to the EAG’s extrapolations. The company has provided the parameters to survival models which account for background mortality, fitted to the COVID-unmodified data, which are used in the amended analyses presented later in this addendum, resolving this issue. 

## **1.2** _**Disparity in use of COVID-unmodified TTD**_ 

## **Company:** 

The EAG uses the COVID-modified TTD curve and appear not to have attempted to produce their own COVID-unmodified TTD as done for OS and PFS, creating an inconsistency in the modelling of outcomes. 

## **EAG Response:** 

TTD is a secondary outcome, capped at three years in the model, and therefore has limited impact on cost-effectiveness results. The EAG considered the company’s chosen log-normal extrapolation to be reasonable and judged that further exploration of COVID-unmodified TTD would not materially affect decision uncertainty. The EAG were not provided with the COVID-unmodified TTD Kaplan-Meier plot, and so it was not possible for the EAG to use this data. Given that the company had implemented updated OS models in their additional comments, the EAG understands the company could also have updated TTD if they considered this a major issue. The EAG is happy for the company to implement the option for extrapolations of this data to be utilised within the economic model, but anticipates the impact to be small. 

The EAG also notes an inconsistency in the company’s modelling of TTD for HMRN. The company’s approach to modelling TTD uses HMRN data, whereas PFS and OS apply hazard ratios to extrapolations of EPCORE NHL-1 data, and are therefore not based on the same population.

## **2 Supplementary information** 

In the updated economic model, the company has included an option to use reweighted epcoritamab curves to explore an independent modelling approach to “avoid a naïve comparison with HMRN”. 

The EAG stands by the naïve comparison for the base case. Reweighting to the HMRN still depends on the same fragility of the MAIC, including small ESS, differences in study design between RCT and real-world studies, and not being able to include known prognostic factors in MAIC. 

The company’s MAIC counter-intuitively decreased the HR, increasing the advantage of epcoritamab over current 4L+ care, and reweighting will not fix that concern. The EAG’s base case keeps both arms COVID-unmodified and directly models HMRN outcomes from its own data, which is both transparent and reproducible.
